The endless self analysis, the taking apart of every motive, every feeling, every flaw, with the knife of the intellect, until the living thing you were trying to understand is lying in pieces and will not grow. The gardener's work is not dissection. It is tending. Water, sunlight, patience, and the humility to remember you did not originate any of it.

The questions that night go somewhere surprising. Asked about his own life, Hatonn explains that he is one of many who share the name, a planetary consciousness, a culture come to oneness of thought. The one speaking at that moment, he says, is a woman, and mated, though their family life is an extended clan where children are raised by all, and each child seeks out those who vibrate in harmony with him. There is no falsehood in their relationships, he says, for they can see the thoughts of those around them. And so the restrictions are lifted, and they are free.

And then a questioner asks if he ever feels anything besides love, and Hatonn gives the most moving answer of the evening. We feel an emotion besides love, he says, but it is not anger. We feel an immense sorrow, a grief. We grieve for your peoples. We grieve because you are separated, and we yearn and wish and hope that we can help you become one within yourselves, with love. We grieve as parents grieve when their children are unhappy, wanting to give them happiness but not knowing how.

A question about evil brings the teaching full circle. There is no evil in our density, Hatonn says. Evil, as you know it, is simply the manifestation of separation: brother from brother, and man from Creator. It is a measure of separation from the knowledge and love of the Creator. It is a type of ignorance. And the best defense against it, he says, is the knowledge of what evil really is. Faced with evil, you can find the Creator in the source of that evil. This blocks the evil from coming into your world, for one who loves is stronger, in unity, than one who does not love, in his evil.

Oxal closes the night with a short message I want to leave you with. We speak of meditation, of love and light, of the Creator, he says. But where do we find these things? Do we find them in our pastimes? In our work? We find them, he says, in a moment of contemplation, in a moment in which we see the beauty of the world of the Creator, in a moment of silence in which that still small voice speaks within us, in which sweetness comes into our hearts. Seek those moments, my friends, day by day.

Tend the garden. Do not dissect the seed. And in the quiet moments, listen for the sweetness.

Thank you for listening.

title: Only Love and Be
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: only love and be.

On May sixth, nineteen seventy-nine, in a Sunday meditation, Hatonn answers a question that lives quietly in the channel's mind, and probably in yours too. Are you your brother's keeper? Are you responsible for the spiritual growth of the person you love most?

His answer is both yes and no, and the no is the part that sets you free. Attraction, he says, whatever form it takes, is a technique for placing two people in a position to be of service to each other. It gives you an irresistible reason to sacrifice the pleasures of the moment for the nobler desire to aid another human being. So yes, you are responsible for your mate's spiritual growth, for it is a special and privileged contact between two souls and the Creator.

But here is the no. How can you be of service? Can you be of service in an orchard, he asks, by grafting an apple onto a cherry tree, or a pear onto a peach tree, or by pinning the bloom of a tulip to the leaves of a rose? The only garden that you must cultivate, he says, is the garden of your own personality. If you have weeded your own plot, if you are centered in the love of the Creator, then you can give the only service that is worth giving: yourself.

I want to read you the sentence that follows, because it is the whole teaching in miniature. You cannot change those whom you love, he says. You can only be the best person that you can be. And if your example is an inspiration, then your loved one may change as you desire. The free will of your loved one is fundamental to the quality of your relationship. Thus, it cannot change. You can only be.

Listen to what he says about why this is hardest with family. You may find it easy to give yourself to others beside your mate, he says, for there is an escape. You will leave friends. You cannot leave family, and your family comes to know you: your weeds as well as your crops, your fruit and flowers. To be, he says, that is the essence of difficulty. When you can look at the pain of a misunderstanding and continue to be yourself in the face of it, then you become as a mirror, reflecting that which may help your loved one. Speeches, arguments, and inharmonious silences can never be of the help that you can be if you remain yourself.

A questioner asks what it even means to be yourself, and Hatonn answers with an image from high school chemistry. Each metal, he says, has a specific spectroscopic color, an identifying vibration. The vibrations of a being extend from the physical into the electrical, and into the more spiritual realms, and all of these together give a specific identification. However, he says, you are not a metal. You are an element of consciousness, and your color is one of relative virtue. You are unique, and your uniqueness is eternal.

And how do you find that unique vibration? In meditation, he says, you become one with the Creator and with your higher self, that self which will remain when your physical vehicle is no longer a functioning pile of chemicals. To find out who you are by action is a hit and miss proposition, he says, a process of elimination, trying something and saying, no, this is not me, and if your analysis is faulty, you may miss that which is yourself. In meditation you become centered in something sure, something more permanent than your physical personality, something called character.

And then he describes what happens when you know who you are, and I love the ordinariness of it. Some can speak, he says, and some can listen, and some can cook, some can sing, some can hold their arms out to children, some can nurture old people, some have the gift of silence and others that of words. When you know who you are, then your gifts will flow therefrom, and it will be a free flowing brook, one which is not stopped by the distortion of doubt.

So the answer to the evening's question is the evening's title. Are you your brother's keeper? Yes, in the sense that your being is the service. No, in the sense that you cannot do the growing for anyone. Weed your own garden. Be yourself. Let your gifts flow like a brook. And trust that love, given without pressure, is the only change anyone has ever needed.

Thank you for listening.

title: First, One Person
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: first, one person.

On May twentieth, nineteen seventy-nine, in a Sunday meditation, Hatonn tells a story about a man who spent his whole life searching for the love of the Creator, and found it in the last place he looked: in another person.

The man was not ordinary, Hatonn says, for within him from childhood was the burning desire to know the love of the Creator. In his youth he read widely, frustrated because no one could speak with him deeply enough about the things that mattered to him. He found theology a great puzzle, a great confusion of ideas, and he pressed on. He went into seminary. He became a minister, preaching the word of his Creator to his flock. Through the years he listened to the problems of those who came to his church. And yet, he did not find the love of the Creator.

In time he married, and his wife gave him children and supported his work unstintingly. Nor yet did he find the love of the Creator he sought. And one day, walking down the path from the rectory, now quite old, he met a boy who reminded him of himself at a younger age. They fell into conversation. And all of a sudden, something occurred that had never yet occurred in the old man's life. In this stranger's unlined face, burning to know the love of the Creator, the old man saw a person to love. And at the moment he gave his heart to this young man, as a father to a son, he felt the love of God.

The wanderer was never seen by the old man again. He was on his own journey. But the old man fell in love, first with one person, and finally with all mankind.

What had blocked the love of the Creator that he so earnestly sought for a lifetime? We say to you, Hatonn says, that you must love yourself. Not because your personality has any virtue, or because your ego needs shoring up by a self indulgent love. No, he says. We are speaking of a love that is one with the Creator.

And then he asks the question that unlocks the story. Where is the Creator? Can you touch Him? Is He outside the world as you know it? Is He unknowable in any way? If so, why would we seek to find Him? The Creator, he says, is in your brothers and your sisters and yourself. Closer to you than your breath. More available to you than reasoning. More heartening to you than your dreams. That which is beyond doing and dreaming is love itself.

I keep thinking about the structure of that story. A lifetime of reading, preaching, and seeking, and none of it opened the door. What opened it was one unguarded moment of giving the heart to one particular person, a stranger on a path. Not humanity in the abstract. One face. And from that one face, the love widened until it took in all mankind. The teaching seems to be that love does not begin with the universe. It begins with one person, and then it learns how to be universal.

Hatonn goes on to say that you cannot be kind to a Creator who is invisible, infinite, untouchable, unknowable. But you can be kind to those about you. You can allow yourself to be a channel for love, whatever your circumstance. It has been written, he says, that a man who is kind to another is not kind to a man but to the Creator.

And here is the sentence I want you to sit with. You cannot possess the Creator, he says. You cannot possess yourself. You possess only one thing: consciousness, and you possess it in common with all that there is. That which created this consciousness is love. Thus, he says, allow love to flow through you. Not your love, but the love of the Creator, for yours will run dry very quickly. People themselves are reflections of you. Allow this reflection to be one of love.

Whatever difficulties you may be having, he says, they can be met with love. And the more deeply committed you are to finding, feeling, and freely giving to others the love that is in every situation, the more quickly you will become what you might call a conscious being, controlling your destiny, improving the harmony, aiding the vibration of your life.

The old man on the path never found what he was looking for in any book or any pulpit. He found it in a boy's unlined face, in the moment his heart opened to one person. Tonight's teaching is that simple, and that demanding. Find one person. Love them. Let it widen from there.

Thank you for listening.

title: A New Heart
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: a new heart.

On June tenth, nineteen seventy-nine, in a Sunday meditation, Hatonn borrows a prayer from the channel's own mind and makes it the evening's whole teaching. Create in me a new heart, the prayer says, and make a right spirit within me. She repeats it to herself very often. Tonight, Hatonn shares it with all of us.

The message, he says, is that you cannot deal with your culture, with your surroundings, with your life as it is, with the old heart, with the old spirit, with the human frailties. No. As if they were skins, he says, you must shed them, and allow a transformation to take place within you, which can only take place within the purified atmosphere of meditation, in which there is created within you a newness of being, in which you are an instrument for the will of love.

I love the image of the old heart as a skin. Not something to be improved, or argued with, or gradually renovated. Something to be shed, the way a snake sheds what no longer fits, because the living thing inside has outgrown it. The transformation cannot be negotiated with the old heart. It has to happen in a different atmosphere altogether, the purified atmosphere of meditation, where a newness of being can be created.

Hatonn is strikingly honest about the limits of what he and his kind can do. We do not know what to do with your peoples, he says. We continue speaking with those of you on this path, knowing our words go forth in love, but we are powerless to affect or change the destiny of mankind at the end of this cycle and the beginning of the new one. Only you, my friends, can spread the message of love, the simple message of unity. There are those in this brotherhood who would leave you at this time, he adds, for we are no longer in a position to warn you. Events themselves are warning you.

And then, in the same breath, he gives the reason none of that is cause for despair. You, and no other judge, will judge yourself, he says. You, and no other judge, will see that which is needed by the soul, which is yourself. And you will see that it is done, so that you may grow according to your needs. The transformation that you may feel in meditation, he says, is all that can, at this point, harmonize your inharmonious planet.

The practical teaching that follows is a list of four suggestions, and each one is worth keeping. First, he says, become very active in the application of the knowledge you have received about the mechanics of creation. Knowledge unused is decoration. Second, maintain a community of those who wish to follow this discipline together, in as intensive a manner as you can fit into your schedules. One candle alone gives off great light in a dark universe, he says, but the power of several of these candles is much greater than the added power. It is multiplied many times. Meditate in groups, speak in groups, work in groups. Those who seek together, washed clean in meditation together, become a closer family than blood or law can make.

Third, he says, cultivate an overriding sense of beauty. If you could look about you, the world of the Creator would give you beauty each and every time you look. And fourth, maintain that level of detachment which ensures that you are as able to laugh at the comedy of life as it applies to yourself as you are able to laugh at it as it applies to others. This detachment, he says, is a divine sense of humor, which will lead you to a knowledge of the oneness of the universe. As you make your errors, so may you laugh and say, there also am I. And when you see the same error in others, you may nod and say again, there also am I.

Create in yourselves a new heart, he says in closing, and the right spirit within you. Find the peace that accompanies the expanded view of life, the view of a transformed soul whose horizons have been consciously widened, so that the love and the light of the infinite Creator may be seen in every corner, in every task, in every person.

Shed the skin. Find the others. Look for the beauty. And laugh, especially at yourself. That is the whole of tonight's teaching, and it begins, as it always begins, in the quiet of meditation.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Heavenly Octave
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the heavenly octave.

On June seventeenth, nineteen seventy-nine, in a Sunday meditation, Hatonn tells the story of a seed that could not grow, and then answers a question about the heavens, and the two turn out to be the same teaching.

The story first. There are many trees, he says, but this is the story of only one tree. As a small seed it was carried in the clothing of a not particularly cleanly fellow for several years, in the cuff of his trousers, you might say. It was dark, and the seed would have liked to have grown, but it could not. The environment was not correct. One day at the beach the small winged seed fell from the cuff as the man walked, and it lay there on the sand, and again it tried to grow, but it could not, for the conditions were not correct for its blossoming.

And one day a wind picked up the seed and carried it far, far inland, blowing it on the winds of change, and over this the seed had no conscious control. When it landed it saw the sun and felt beneath itself the grass, and the rains came and watered the grass, and the seedling put forth its tiny roots. With infinite patience, he says, the small seed became buried, put forth young shoots, dropped its leaves, and began the process of living. As it grew it gave off oxygen to the air, being of service to those beings who breathed that sweet substance. Its harvest was collected. And the beauty of the tree made many stop to envision the beauty of nature.

And then Hatonn turns the story on us, with a distinction I want you to hear carefully. You do not have, and should not have, pride in your existence or your importance, he says, for that which you are, you are because of the winds of change working upon that which is instinctually yours. You, unlike the tree, are beings of conscious volition over your destiny. The tree has a destiny without free will. Its wisdom is given it freely, and it reaches for the sun without hesitation or doubt. You must do the harder thing: penetrate the busyness of your daily lives and find within yourselves that seed which is very simple. That seed, he says, is that part of you which is a unique vibration of love.

I love the humility of that. Not pride in how far you have grown, because the winds carried you. But also not passivity, because unlike the tree, you must choose to turn toward the light. Both truths at once. That is the whole of the spiritual life in one seed.

The question period brings the evening's other great teaching. A questioner keeps reading in metaphysical literature about seven levels, seven heavens, and asks if the concept is valid. Hatonn answers with a piano. There are in a major scale, he says, seven different notes, having a relationship to each other which is pleasant. And then there is an octave, in which there is an identity of the top note with the bottom, and the tonality begins again. Thus it is with quanta, he says: just so much occurring within a quantum, and then a leap to another set of configurations.

There are indeed, he says, seven levels within the next quantum above you, the plane some call the astral. Beyond that quantum there is a further octave of seven, sometimes called the devachanic. Beyond that another octave of seven, sometimes called spiritual. Beyond that plane, few among your peoples who are incarnate have traveled. There are an infinite number of octaves in the heavenly music, he says. The number seven is the number of completeness, for that is the scale of vibrations within each quantum.

Asked where he himself vibrates, Hatonn answers plainly. We ourselves vibrate within the fifth octave, he says. You vibrate within the third. There are many in the Confederation in the sixth, and some in the fourth. And then he adds something I find deeply encouraging: there are three among our number who, though vibrating in the third dimension, have done so in such harmony that they are able to aid us, in spite of the gross physical illusion they are experiencing. So you see, he says, your condition is not hopeless. Your bodies do not pin you down. It is your minds that imprison you, by accepting the illusion.

The last question is about why we forget our past lives, and Hatonn's answer is merciful. If you knew all that you have done before, he says, your mind would be attempting to carry you through all of the lessons you had learned before. This is too much for the mind to deal with. It is enough that you have this incarnation to deal with. The fruits of former incarnations dwell within your spirit, as biases: some born with native love, some without it, some with great talent, others who seem quite ordinary. But other than that, you have the opportunity to begin wherever you are and become a loving being. This, he says, is the only test upon your level.

The seed in the trouser cuff could not grow until the winds carried it to the right soil. You are that seed, carried by winds you did not choose, to soil you did not choose. Your work is simpler than you think, and harder than you think: turn toward the light, forget what you need to forget, and grow.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Alligator Within
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the alligator within.

On July fifth, nineteen seventy-nine, in an intermediate meeting, Hatonn tells a story about an alligator in a bar, and it is the funniest and most uncomfortable parable in this whole section of the archive.

Once upon a time, he says, in one of your southern cities, there came to be a very unusual creature. This creature had the body of an alligator but the wisdom of a man. Those about him learned to treat him as a man. He wore special shoes and special clothing, and had a hat specially made for him, and learned to sit upright and eat his meals and hold his job and act in every way like a human would act.

One day, sitting on a bar stool watching the big game, a rather tipsy man stumbled and stepped upon his tail. Somewhat tipsy himself, the alligator was furious, and he whipped around to slay the poor unfortunate who had dared to step on his tail. I am sorry, said the drunken man, but I did not see your tail. I do not have a tail, said the alligator with great fury, for I am a man. And he lunged, and the man grabbed a stick the bartender handed him and rammed it into the alligator's throat, killing him. As the alligator lay on the floor, dead, in his shoes and his clothes and his hat, the man said to him, I may be drunk, but I know an alligator when I see one.

Hatonn then asks us to consider this story in the context of our own personalities. Within your own mind, he says, there lives a population of many creatures. Some are saintly: good and pure, kindly and compassionate. Others are boring, over intellectual. Some are too emotional. And a few, he says, may actually be beasts that you may not wish to face.

Listen to how he describes our excuses, because he has us exactly. There are many negative emotions which do not seem so negative on the plane you now enjoy, he says. Greed is explained away as a means whereby produce is generated in the marketplace. Ambition is explained as that which one must do to be of service to one's family. Selfishness, jealousy, and envy, all of these things can be so easily explained away in your mind. You can clothe them in explanations. The hat, the coat, the shoes.

And so we charge you, he says, in your meditations, first to find your alligator, and to remove him, and then to meditate in quiet and humility, knowing that you are not unlike your brothers but very, very much the same. Let the citizens within you which are compassionate grow and spread their wings. This can be done, not by your efforts, but by meditation. Not by conscious thought, but by intuition.

I want to stay with the order of operations there, because it matters. First find the alligator. Then remove him. Then meditate in humility, knowing you are just like everyone else. The seeing comes before the quiet. You cannot meditate your way around the beast. You have to admit the tail is yours.

He adds something that softens the whole teaching. Although we are more advanced than you, he says, we of Hatonn know that our thoughts are varied and are not always harmonious. The difference is simply that we can see our thoughts. We have no chance to quarrel with our alligators. When they arise, we must deal with them without further ado. We ask you to never fear what is inside yourself, he says, but only to love it, for it too is the Creator.

The night's questions turn to karma, and Oxal, who speaks later in the evening, gives the teaching its philosophical backbone. It is best, he says, to deal with karma not as your people have dealt with it: as lawyers, attempting to balance the case in court, or accountants attempting to total the debits and credits. For we are dealing here not with actions, but with thought. A person is as he thinks. That is reality. His actions are the fruits of his thoughts.

And then the sentence that dissolves the whole courtroom. The law of love, he says, is far greater than the law of cause and effect, just as the law of eternity is greater than the law of time and process. Do not linger in the river of your life, he says, but move onward to the sea, dissolving yourself in love. In this way, karma ceases to become your reality, and your love may be freely taken and freely given, with forgiveness to all men for all things.

So tonight's teaching is really one motion with two parts. Find your alligator, take off its little hat, and stop pretending the tail is not yours. And then dissolve the whole courtroom in love, because the law you actually live under was never cause and effect. It was always love.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Globe of Light
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the globe of light.

On July eleventh, nineteen seventy-nine, in an advanced meeting, Telonn leads the group on a journey out of the room and out of the body, and then Hatonn follows with a teaching about evolution that turns the world's idea of strength upside down.

Telonn's part of the evening is a guided exercise, and I am going to give it to you the way he gave it, because it is meant to be experienced, not explained. Visualize, he says, a white globe of light that hovers in the center of the room in which you now dwell. When you can clearly see it in your mind's eye, transfer your consciousness into the light, until you can look back at yourself as you sit in meditation in the dim light of the room.

Then, with his consciousness protecting you, slowly move the globe of light through the windows, up above the roof of your dwelling. Look down upon the quiet house you have left, and then speed quickly away from the gravity of earth, through the overcast. Now you begin to see the rounded shape of the earth beneath you. Keep your globe stable, and look for a moment at the spinning, beautiful planet which you have now left.

Then he shows them a triangle, green, like a great eye, and asks them to move through it, out the other side, into the next dimension. What do you see? All that is about you is very bright. The sky is no longer dark. There a watchman of that density approaches, and they are told to remain stable in the globe and allow him to sense their vibration, and to greet him with their thoughts if they wish.

And here is the part I keep thinking about. Traveling back toward the earth in this density, the earth is no longer a blue planet with white clouds. It is, Telonn says, a rainbow of colors. Do not go too close to the darker colors, he warns. They are the dwelling places of thought forms of those among your peoples who are less than fully positive in their thinking. But observe the reality of these thought forms, the activity of the colors, and know that your thoughts are never lost, just as energy can never be lost. Your thoughts, he says, are the equation of the next dimension.

Move now, he says, into the realms of higher and lovelier light. These are the realms of sweet thoughts and kindly deeds, and beings who vibrate in this level dwell therein. And then, gently, back through the eye, back through the night sky, letting the magnetism of the body pull the globe steadily home, until you can see your quiet figures again in the room. Say goodbye to your unity for now, he says, and partake again of the separation of the physical body.

Hatonn's teaching that follows is the philosophical companion to the journey. What is the will of the Father for your planet? It is very simple, he says. It is that it may evolve. But not the evolution you think. We do not speak of a Darwinian evolution where the fittest survive and the weaker are destroyed. Indeed, he says, it is the very opposite that is true. In spiritual evolution it is the weak that survive, and the strong and hard headed who go down in confusion and must repeat again the cycle of lessons that have to do with loving one another.

Loving takes a type of strength, he says, that is known among your peoples as weakness. Loving is serving. Loving is not caring what is done to you in return for your love, and such humility is difficult indeed to accomplish. In a culture where each person demands his rights and each action seems to demand its reward, the act of pure love implies a total disregard of reward. This seems to others to be weakness. You become known as a doormat, as a pushover. Count these things as blessings, he says. When someone says to you, you are not liberated, silently give thanks that you are at least trying to be loving rather than demanding.

And here is the practice he leaves them with. Love yourself, your circumstances, your troubles, your pleasures, your friends and your enemies, your catastrophes and your triumphs, with a grand and careless equality, and you will find yourself to be on key, on balance, and able to act without selfishness and without foolishness in any situation. How? As always, he says, meditate. In your daily meditations, center yourselves upon that love which, like a gyroscope, keeps you from being tumbled about in this world of illusion that you call earth.

One last sentence from the night, a small one, but I think it might be the most useful. In the hierarchy of obedience, Hatonn says, be obedient first to that which you feel is correct. If you are meditating each day, your feelings are more trustworthy than the opinions of others.

The globe of light. The gyroscope of love. The weak who survive. Tonight's teaching is that the journey out of the body and the journey into humility are the same journey, and both begin the same way: in the quiet, in the light, in the willingness to be thought a fool for love.

Thank you for listening.

title: A Cloak of Light
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: a cloak of light.

On July fourteenth, nineteen seventy-nine, in a senior citizens meeting, Hatonn gives one of the shortest and most practical teachings in the archive. It is about what meditation actually gives you, and his answer is a single word: confidence.

He begins with an old saying. It has sometimes been said that ignorance is bliss, he says, and when you are dealing with a spiritual journey, this is very true. For knowledge carries with it a great responsibility. That which is known and not practiced reflects itself upon the knower, so that he must again know that which he has already learned. This, he says, is the price of knowledge: that you practice what you know.

I want to pause there, because it is a bracing thought. Every truth you have heard in this series, every teaching that has moved you, comes with a price tag. If you know it and do not live it, you will have to learn it again. Knowledge is not a souvenir. It is a responsibility.

But then he tells you how to carry it. In meditation, he says, you can deepen the ingredients you need, and the first and most important is confidence. Not the loud kind. The kind that comes from knowing who you are. Have you ever, he asks, in meditation, felt all the parts of yourself finally come into alignment with your highest goals and your deepest beliefs? By centering yourself in meditation, by finding that within you which vibrates in love and seeks the light of the Creator, you can find a quietness and a peacefulness that you can then use in the hectic and chaotic world about you.

And here is the image that gives tonight its name. As you come out of meditation, he says, this confidence that you have gathered therein becomes your armor. It is as though you are wearing a cloak of light through which no negative vibration may pass. Thus, you do not need to react to irritating, angry, and other negative statements from others. Circumstances cannot penetrate the confident one who moves in power.

Listen to how practical that is. He is not promising that the irritating people will disappear, or that the angry statements will stop coming. He is promising that you will be able to walk through them unmoved, wearing something they cannot touch. The confidence gathered in the quiet becomes the protection in the noise.

And there is more that meditation gives, he says, and you will find these as you proceed along the path. You may find yourself deepening as a person, becoming more able to understand the problems of others, becoming an ear which is requested many times by others, for they sense in you a deep understanding. In this way you are of service to your brothers and sisters. You may find the gift of laughter, which is not easy to come by in a daily life so easily filled with difficulties.

And then this, which might be my favorite passage of the night. As your character grows deeper and your knowledge more centered, he says, you begin to see the divine comedy of your existence, the delightful balance of lessons and experience. You cease looking for happiness, and you become divinely happy, whatever your circumstances may be. In short, he says, you slowly become a generator of your own experience, rather than the recipient of other people's experiences, of the world view which is so often negative.

A generator of your own experience, rather than a recipient of other people's. I keep turning that phrase over. Most of us walk through the day receiving: receiving moods, receiving opinions, receiving the weather of everyone around us, and calling the sum of it our life. Hatonn is describing the reversal of that, the slow becoming of someone who generates the weather instead of catching it. And the whole reversal, he says, begins in meditation, in the quiet gathering of confidence, in the cloak of light.

It is true, he says, that not all of your problems are large. You do not have to decide the fate of nations. But your vibration on an individual basis is as important, as vital, and as necessary to the salvation of your planetary consciousness as is the vibration of kings and heads of state. You do not move armies with your commands. But can you command yourself? This, he says, is perhaps the hardest thing to do of all the tasks you have been given in this experience.

So tonight's teaching is small enough to carry in one hand. Sit in the quiet. Gather the confidence. Wear it out into the noise like a cloak of light. And slowly, day by day, become the generator of your own experience, divinely happy whatever the circumstances, laughing at the divine comedy of it all.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Treasure of Desire
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the treasure of desire.

On July nineteenth, nineteen seventy-nine, in an intermediate meeting, Hatonn opens with a question about treasure, and it is not the kind you dig up. We are aware, he says, that the treasure that is in your heart is sometimes buried. It has been written in your holy works, where your treasure is, there shall your heart be also. And yet we say to you that your heart may contain any treasure which you desire.

And then he asks the question I want you to carry tonight. Have you desired, this day, well? Have you had small desires, easily satisfied? Have you glanced up into the lovely arches of your heavens during this day and sought and dreamt and hoped, those desires which make men into beings who are claiming their birthright? That is what lies between you and the birthright of love and light which you brought into this illusion, he says: your inability to remember to desire it. That is all that separates you from infinite love, infinite light, and the power of a consciousness which these understandings can coordinate and enable.

I find that quietly radical. Not your unworthiness. Not your ignorance. Not the size of the obstacles. Only this: that you forgot to desire the treasure, or desired it weakly, or settled for small desires easily satisfied. And so his charge for the evening is simple. Desire, with the greatest intensity possible, that which you wish to desire. What have you desired today? He asks it in the name of the Creator.

The night then turns to Latwii, and to the deepest waters in this section of the archive: paradox, time, and the question of whether we chose to be here. A questioner asks why mankind was seeded on this planet without any choice in the matter, and Latwii answers with the paradox that underlies everything. None of us have a choice, they say. We are all the Creator. You were not created. You are the Creator, a portion of all that there is, a portion of no time and no space. And yet, they say, you have infinite choice in the amount of time it takes you and the way in which you wish to articulate your creator-ness. You have no free will, and you have complete free will. Paradoxes, they say, are an absolute necessity if one is to advance spiritually. If you are not facing a paradox at this time, then you are not trying.

The questioner presses on. If there is no time, and all is now, then how is it that the great structures of the past stand today as ruins? If Socrates walked the Parthenon in its glory, and I stand before it now and my camera says it is a ruin, which now is real? And Latwii answers with an image I love. Take a piece of living tissue from your thumb, they say, and look at it under an intensely strong microscope. Ultimately you begin to see the creation: galaxies, solar systems, planets. There are beings on your thumb. How long do you think their lives are, in your time? How many civilizations pass while that cell that is a universe is spending itself as a living part of your being? What Romes, what nations, what empires have come and gone?

You yourselves, they say, are in time and space that is far less slow, relatively speaking, than many universes. There is one uniting truth, and that is that beyond time and beyond space lies unity. You are not living in a straight line. You are living in a circle. The beginning is your ending, and there is no beginning or ending.

Your camera, they say, is part of the illusion which you now enjoy. They distinguish between your now now, the everyday now, which is only so so, and the other now, in which you may see what you wish to see and really understand what you want to understand. But you cannot be in both at once. This illusion is to you a lesson time, they say, in which that which is an illusion appears real.

A questioner asks whether we exist in other dimensions as well as here, and Latwii answers that it is not a question of location, for the dimensions are interpenetrating. All of you exist into the fourth dimension, they say, and there are adepts among you working actively in the fifth, attempting to understand the teachings of the inner realms of the sixth. To go beyond that, you must be free of your chemical body. But there are many, many infinities to explore within those dimensions, and much wisdom to learn. The path becomes lighter, they say. The teachings truer. And the laughter happier.

And one more thread from the night, because it ties back to the treasure. Asked whether knowing our past lives would help us spiritually, Latwii says it usually would not. If you can learn the art of forgiveness, they say, you do not need to know what it was that somebody did to somebody else. If you can ask forgiveness with all your heart and forgive with all your heart, you have broken the laws of karma.

So the evening comes full circle. The treasure is buried in your heart. The only thing between you and it is desire, remembered and intensified. The paradoxes of time and choice dissolve when you stop trying to solve them and start living them. Forgive with all your heart, desire with all your heart, and the circle you are living in turns out to be the road home.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Cloud and the Moon
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the cloud and the moon.

There is a storm raging outside the house where the group sits to meditate, and inside, a friend named Hatonn begins with a image that sounds made for the weather. Lives, he says, are like clouds as they cross the moon. Visible only for a brief time, before and after lost in the darkness of the eternal heavens. It is not meant to be mournful. It is meant to be emphatic. And the more I sit with it, the more I feel how carefully he chooses it. A cloud is real, it casts its shadow, it changes the light for a little while, and then it is gone, and the moon goes on.

Listen to how they put the teaching underneath the image. You are not your body, he says. Not your pains and your pleasures. Not your experiences. You are a vibration, temporarily and transiently housed in a chemical body. And that vibration has characteristics, the way a bell has a tone. The degree of loving kindness in your nature. The degree of generosity, of compassion, of kindliness. These are the qualities that show through, he says, from your true personality into the physical illusion.

And this is where it gets practical, which I love. The vibration shows forth, as he puts it, in the ordinary things. In the ability to help people by healing, by the preparation of food, by working with your hands, by singing, or by telling stories, or by raising the young who are entrusted to your care. None of that is glamorous. All of it is the light coming through the cloud. What makes a life meaningful is not the cloud at all, he suggests, but how much light gets through it.

So the advice is detachment, but not the cold kind. Do not take this illusion, he says, any more seriously than you would take the passing of a cloud across the moon on a stormy night. There will be other clouds. Other nights. What matters is the one effort: each day, find some moments to meditate, to center your will on the desire to know the love of the Creator. That wish for the original Thought will be to you as a beacon, guiding your spirit far into the stormy seas of night when you have crossed the moon and there is no light. I read that line twice. A beacon. For the part of the journey after the moon goes dark.

The original Thought, he says, is infinite love expressed in light. This light has formed all of his creatures. The planet you live on. The skies that surround you. All things are light. And as you root yourself in that knowledge, something changes without you forcing it. Your power as a personality will develop, he says, so that the circumstances which seem inharmonious will of themselves become more harmonious. Not because the circumstances changed. Because your attitude became such that nothing can disturb you.

Then a second voice comes through, a friend called Laitos, and he is here for something smaller and more tender. He works with the group one by one, helping each of them deepen their meditative state. And he says something that stopped me. If we can but help the people of this planet to meditate and feel the oneness of all creation, he says, we will indeed have a part in the delivery of a tiny infant. That is the new age dawning upon your planet. At this time it needs all the midwifery that it can get.

I keep turning that image over. Not the conquerors of a new age. The midwives of it. A tiny infant, not yet born, and the whole work of spirit is to be present at the birth. That is a different job than the one most of us imagine we have. It asks for patience. It asks for hands that know how to hold still.

Hatonn returns at the end with one last thought, and it is the one I want to leave you with. You know that love is all that there is, he says. Think of it as the great medicine that is needed by your peoples. Think of yourself as a healer, for the one who loves heals. There are different methods, different levels. Some heal nations through politics. Some heal the hunger for knowledge through teaching. Some heal sickness, some heal melancholy, some loneliness. But all of them work through the vibration of love. There is a great sea of love around you, he says. Float on it. Rest in it. There is nowhere you can go that is not full of love, if you have but the eyes to see and the heart to understand.

The storm outside does what storms do. The cloud crosses the moon and moves on. But the beacon is lit, in the silence, for the one who chooses to see it.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Sower of Seeds
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the sower of seeds.

A friend named Hatonn begins this session the way he always begins, in the love and the light of the infinite Creator, and then he says something that quietly reframes everything that follows. The Creator is love, he says, and that love, working through motion, has created all that there is in an infinite panoply of beauty and order and unity, so that we are all one divine and unified being, with but one purpose. And that purpose is to give back that which has been given us so freely.

And what has been given us? Not the things we usually count. Your supply of worldly goods, your intellect, your strength, your courage — Hatonn is blunt about these. They are not gifts at all, he says, but limitations that you have chosen for this experience. What you have in common, he says, is consciousness. Could you but strip away the layers of concept and illusion that furnish your mind, you would find that the original Thought in which you are molded is that of love made conscious of itself. Each of you, my friends, is love.

I love that line. Not you are loved. Not you should love. You are love, made conscious of itself. And then he asks the practical question, because he knows we are thinking it. How can this be a practical piece of knowledge? How can you use this in your life? That, he says, is why they speak through instruments at all, for those hungry for words that make sense amidst so many words that do not.

All of you are aware, he says, of the transforming power of love. The touch of a hand. The difference a smile or a kind gesture might make to a stranger. And there is a method, he says, by which you can tap into the infinity of the universal supply of this love. Through meditation on a daily basis, the people of this planet, even in the midst of incredible turmoil, can gradually erode the illusion of that turmoil and discover that which is calm, peaceful and yet ever moving, that which is the fountain of love within each being.

But listen to what he does not promise, because the honesty is the whole point. We do not promise you great power, he says, though some have found great power through simple meditation. We do not promise great riches, though those aware of the moment receive what they need in that moment. We cannot promise you peace of mind, for you will constantly go back into the world, and you cannot stay in meditation unless you wish to stop learning. Coming from meditation with your heart full of love, it is time to meet the world on its own terms, but with a smile on your lips in the face of what would upset you were you not centered, safe in a harbor of love that extends throughout the universe.

He knows what the world will do to you. So many people you meet, he says, are polarized in a negative way, and it is not their fault. They are victims of their own conditioning. Yet you must deal with them, in stores, in cars, among your friends on a bad day. Even you yourself may startle you into asking, can that be me, can I be this upset, this angry? Let the part of you found in meditation, he says, the part which is infinite in love, be the self that meets that situation. Find the humor hiding in it. See the love hiding in the person. And offer the seed of an idea, that it might be possible there is something he does not know that he may want to know.

No, my friends, you are sent into the world, as it is written in one of your holy works, as sowers to sow a seed here and a seed there. Many will fall where they will not grow. But the seeds of love are the most valuable seeds in your universe, and the Creator has sown them all about you. The beauty of the trees breathes with love. The skies give you wind and rain and sunshine. This much the Creator can do. Beyond that, he says, and I will let his words carry their own weight, beyond that, you are the Creator, and it is the look in your eye or the touch of your hand or the way you can give love in an unlovely situation that produces the future crop of love in those about you.

And then the closing image, a sea voyage. The course of action he has outlined, he says, compared to a voyage, would be a lifetime voyage. That is all right, for it is for that voyage you set out on this incarnation. Some of you have already embarked. You shall become, then, those with the far-away eyes who can touch and help those upon the land who do not yet know that life is a voyage, and that there is a purpose, a new world to be found at the end of it.

This experience in the illusion will end, he says. Each of you will leave, and then you shall see what you have done. It is a precious time, under the hardest of circumstances, and the help you give can only travel from one person to another. So go and sow. A seed here. A seed there. Most will fall where they cannot grow, and it does not matter. The sowing was always the point.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Grain of Sand
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the grain of sand.

This session opens with a question that lands like a stone in still water. Not what is the illusion, but how complete it is. Hatonn asks his friends to notice the care with which their lives have been arranged. Your bodies sit held downward by a force you never examine and simply take for granted. Walk down the street and you expect no building to fall on you, no head to come hurtling at you. You do not find high risk in simple actions. Do you realize, he asks, how carefully the illusion has been planned, so that you do not have to be aware of the safety of your physical vehicles?

Why, he wants to know. Why is so much danger taken from you? His answer is not what the comfortable would hope to hear. Much has been taken from your worry, he says, that you may turn your will and your desire more deeply into the mystery of who you are. Comfort is not the reward. Comfort is the clearing. It is the empty field where you are supposed to build something, and he looks at us, gently, and wonders why so many of us keep paving the parking lot instead.

And then the question sharpens into something I have carried around all day. You have been placed into this world by yourselves for experience, he says, but not to be hungry, not to be at risk from bullets or tidal waves or heat or exhaustion. For what, then, were you put into this world? Do you really wish to know? Have you sought in meditation today, even for a few seconds, that link with the Creator that gives you the key that unlocks the door to knowledge of yourself? What do you know of yourself, he asks, besides the fact that you are comfortable and that you enjoy comfort?

Many are the laws of love you have discovered, he says, and for that he congratulates us. But you have only scratched the surface of your own consciousness. There is a vast geography beneath the surface of your knowledge of yourself, he says, and in that country lies an understanding that goes beyond comfort, beyond the physical body, beyond the physical life you know. How can you seek less, he asks, even for one day? I do not read that as a scolding. I read it as an invitation to a place bigger than the rooms we keep living in.

Keep the humor. Keep the pleasure. Just do not mistake them for the business.

And here is a mercy I did not expect. The instrument carries a regret that day, for having failed to be of perfect service to another person. And Hatonn answers it with a tenderness worth remembering. If you cannot share what you know, you must not regret your lack, he says. For if what you know is incomprehensible to them, then to keep pushing it is to throw pearls before swine. They will only sicken on such a diet. Allow yourself only to desire to know the Creator in yourself and others. But if the moment has not come for you to demonstrate a teaching, then it simply has not come. You were not sent out into the world to change those who were not ready.

Never shut your heart against another, he says. Bide your time. Plant those seeds of information, those thoughts of love, when they are asked for, not before. And the important thing is to remain untouched by success or failure in contact with others. You do not know what your manifestation was to another. You know only what you feel. Therefore let your heart be glad, let your tongue be honest, and let your thoughts dwell upon the Creator. More than that you cannot do. Less than that you should not do. I have read that last line three times now, and it steadies me every time.

Later in the evening, after the tape recorder is stopped and started again, a quieter voice comes through. Oxal. And he brings the image I have been waiting all session to tell you. Try to view yourself, he says, as a grain of sand on the beach of a vast ocean. You are an individual, one of many millions like you forming one great stretch of sand. And every so often the waters come in, the waves surround you, and you are turned a little and carried along the path.

In the eyes of the Creator, he says, you are one of many, and not much real harm can come to you. Not much can really hurt you, except being bounced around with other grains of sand. The illusion makes it seem otherwise sometimes, but as a father and mother love their children, they watch and protect us. The seriousness that surrounds the problems of your individual lives, he says, is not so serious as you may think. Listen to that again, slowly. It is not permission to stop caring. It is permission to stop drowning.

And then Latwii, just a few sentences before the group disperses into the night. As you go about your business, remember whom you serve. Only one thing do you serve, my friends. Love. Invoke the light of that love, and all things will come into harmony in their own time.

The grain of sand. The vast ocean. The comfort that was never the point. Somewhere between the waves, the Creator is watching, the way a parent watches children at the water's edge, close enough to catch, far enough to let them play.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Two Sisters
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the two sisters.

This evening, a friend named Hatonn says he would like to tell a story, because in stories, he says, there are sometimes the seeds of truths that cannot be spoken straight, but must be approached through what you would call the parable. And the story he tells is one of the most human in the whole archive. Not about the cosmos. About two old women, widowed, living together.

Once there were two sisters, he begins. Both had lost their husbands. Alone in the world, they sought each other, loved each other, and lived together, taking care of each other in times of distress. As they reached the age of seventy, the failing senses of old age came upon them both. One sister reacted by becoming bitter. She felt herself in a tragic situation, and grew less able to manage the simple functions of her life, melancholy indeed, waiting for a death she did not want.

The other sister reacted quite differently, for even in the same family, Hatonn notes, each individual child is a unique entity. This sister began to think of the shortness of her remaining years, and realized that although she had been of great assistance to her husband and children and sister, she had narrowed her world until she was no longer of assistance to those beyond her doorstep. And she determined to crusade beyond her doorstep, and do what she could for the world.

And so this lady began to take a walk, just a short one around the block, and she opened her ears and opened her eyes. Within a few months she had conversations with many people. She talked about the Creator with confused children. She learned of the crying need in hospitals for visitors. She heard that in prison, those who sit in darkness have no visitors, and are grateful to speak with anyone, even a seventy-year-old stranger. Taking her courage in her hands, as though it were a precious gift, she did what she had never done, for she had been a timid woman. And where she was guided, she went.

She sat by hospital beds where people were dying, and talked to them. She came to prisons once a week and made friends in that unlikely place. And on she walked, until the neighborhood knew of her, and people came to her. No doctrine. No miracle. Just an old woman walking around the block with her ears open.

One day, Hatonn says, both women lay dying, for such is the end of the mortal life, and it will certainly happen to you all. Stricken by the same virus, dying at the same time, they were placed in the same hospital room. The walking sister had so many clustered about her bed she could not count them, and she begged them, please, go talk to my sister, for she is in great need of friendship and love. But the younger sister was bitter, and could not accept the love of strangers. Go back to my sister, she would say. She is the one you came to see.

In the end the sisters died, and as the older one died she reached out to the youngest, and they were able to hold hands. Her last words were very simple. I love you, sister, she said. And the friends still came, though there was an empty bed, and they clustered around the younger sister. And suddenly, for the first time, she understood that the legacy of love is an endless repetition and echo of that vibration in others. And as she died, her bitterness left her, and she was able to leave this plane in the vibration of love that her sister had finally been able to share with her.

And then Hatonn draws the teaching out. We ask you, he says, to be so seated in your hearts that you can do those things which come before you to do, in the name of the Creator and in the voice of love. There will come before you things to do. You each have your own talents, each different and unique. You cannot be anyone but yourself. Yet in your own way you can be one who shows love. There are an infinity of ways to show love. When you see an opportunity, my friends, turn it not down, but go forward. You will feel in your heart that which is right.

We ask only one thing, he says. Instead of becoming bitter as the lessons of life hurt you, remain open to the healing power of love, which is best done through daily meditation. It does not matter what type. You may pray, read scripture and contemplate it, sit in silence, engage in ritual. But however you can become close to the one original Thought that created all of us, to the one Creator that is love, that is what you should do daily. For you cannot be a loving person by yourself. And if you fail, do not reproach yourself, but go on and try again, for it is expected of a student of life that he will not be perfect in all of his examinations.

Two sisters. One walked around the block with her ears open, and the ripples reached a prison, a hospital, a neighborhood, and at last, across one hospital room, a hardened heart. The ears are open, or they are not. The feet move, or they do not.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Law of Love
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the law of love.

A friend called Latwii opens with urgency. Hatonn is stationed over the eastern skies, he says, sending vibrations of peace to the leaders of nations, because tempers are rising toward armed conflict. And he asks the group to meditate upon the harmony of the creation, and send those vibrations into the planetary consciousness, for the world needs your love very much. Even a small group, genuinely concerned, giving of itself in prayer and meditation, can be effective.

Then he turns to his real subject, and it is a bracing one. He wants to talk about laws. He quotes the teacher known as Jesus, who was asked why his disciples ate without washing their hands, as custom required, and answered, it is not what goes into the mouth of any man that defiles him, but rather those things which come out of the mouth of men. Yes, my friends, Latwii says, there is a law, and that law is love.

Mankind has created many systems of ethical consideration so that man may live with man without warfare, and to the extent that these laws preserve the common peace and aid the spiritual development of each human being, they are to the good. But when they are interpreted literally and rigidly, and do not allow for compassion and understanding and the redemption of love, then these laws are harmful to the spiritual development of the individual. Listen to how carefully he draws that line. Law is not the enemy. Rigidity is.

How many of your peoples, he asks, were subjected in childhood to a long list of things about which they must feel guilty? What to put on the body. How to keep the dwelling. How to speak, and to whom, and how to judge others by their appearance. All of this is erroneous, he says, because the appearance of man, the habits of man, all that goes with a cultural upbringing, is merely window dressing for the spark of love deep within the heart, the divine Thought that created him.

If you cannot deal with a person because of his differences from you, intellectually, morally, or simply by appearance, then you have not drawn from your meditation the deeper understanding that all men are the same, and all on a path toward the Creator. Some go fast, some slow. Some seem to be taking a vacation from the journey, or side trips that carry them farther away. But if you take the long view, he says, it does not matter, because if you have eternity in which to develop each soul, then each person is either progressing on a spiritual path now, or will do so in the future.

And then he names the hardest case he can think of, and I admire him for not flinching. It is hard to imagine being able to love some people, he says. Adolf Hitler, whom it would be difficult to see as a child of the Creator. Yet, my friends, this man is a child of the Creator, and this soul, though he has a long, long journey, will in the end become a spiritualized and seeking being. You must see each person as part of the Creator, he says. Only in doing this do you free yourself to have a right relationship with each person you meet. In your daily life you meet so many whom you could inspire because of the joy in your heart and your acceptance of them without judgment. They would wish to know what you had that made you different. And you would have dropped a seed of love. Whether it fall on stony ground or on fertile soil, your service would have been accomplished.

Know the law of love, he says, and understand that it supersedes the laws of mankind. If you can apply the law of love in any situation, do not hesitate to relax your grip upon the laws of men. For more important than your understanding of the wrongness of others' actions, or even your own, is the understanding that forgiveness is the divine act. And it is within your own heart, through the grace and power of love, that you may forgive yourself and others.

Then the tone lifts, and he gives the session its strangest image. Life, he says, is truly a humorous condition. If you could look at your life as though it were an old time silent movie, with all the gestures exaggerated and subtitles under each episode, you would see your life's dream in its true form. You can be an actor, totally lost in the drama of your existence, or you can be in the audience, watching, understanding what there is to understand, and finding the comedy inherent in the ridiculous assumption that a soul could take on a heavy chemical body and find the importance of things like money and possessions and homes, when the only important things are love, compassion, and service to others. When you find your mind too much with your worldly goods, step back, my friends, and watch the action as though it were on a movie screen. Have a good laugh, and feel refreshed.

He closes with a phrase he says is important. Butterflies are free, he says. Beauty is another manifestation of truth, and truth is not an intellectual perception but is heartfelt. Feel the beauty of nature, or of man's inspiration as co-creator, music, painting, the written word, and you come closer to the love that is the original Thought. We leave you, he says, nestled like children in the arms of that love.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Burning Bush
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the burning bush.

This session was spoken to a small group, and Hatonn says at the outset that there is much he would say to them that would be inappropriate for a larger one. What follows is one of the most intimate messages in the archive. It is addressed to the ones who came here on purpose. The ones who, long ago, stood before a council and asked permission to incarnate into this dense and unloving vibration, in order to help.

You have tried through many incarnations to be of service, he tells them. It was hoped before this incarnation began that this would be the one in which you succeeded. In other words, my friend, you, like Moses, have been attempting to lead your people through a desert toward a promised land of love and light, which you can see clearly in the distance and know as a reality, but which those around you either doubt or disclaim completely.

And now you find yourself moving through the incarnation, giving of yourself to the best of your ability, and finding yourself still in the desert. Your sacrifice has not been in vain, he says. Even if you do not lead your people into the promised land, even if you cannot save your planet, you have shown by your life and by your works, to the best of your ability, the love and the light that await those who praise the truth of the Creator's love.

Remember you are not alone in this great effort, he says. What you have done prepares the way, at the very least, for another generation of those who seek the promised land, as long as your gaze is steady. But the free will of each soul is supreme. And then he gives the image that carries the whole evening. The parable of Moses and the burning bush. The bush was burned, and yet it was not consumed, and out of the bush a voice addressed the one known as Moses, there in the desert as he stood, foot-weary and dusty and helpless.

Take off your shoes, said the voice, for that place whereon you stand is holy ground. You cannot bring people to an understanding, Hatonn says. You can only bring yourself to people. And if you have the realization that you are constantly in the holy tabernacle, dwelling in serenity and intimacy with the Creator, then you will be able to bring that holiness ever so quietly into the atmosphere about you.

He sees their hearts, and knows they quake with the sadness of their indiscretions, heated words, wrong feelings. But he is not speaking of the human personality, he tells them. There is a level beneath the human personality in which true sainthood and true holiness abide. You do not so much need to tame your human personality as to learn to discard it, to understand that as the bedrock of your character lies that with which you came into this solar system. Compared to those who dwell upon this planet from a previous age, he says, you are indeed saints, subconsciously. Not saints because you are perfect. Saints because of what you are, underneath.

And then the practical instruction, which is almost embarrassingly plain. Do not think of goals, he says, but only of the mile which you are walking at this time. Do not be concerned with your accomplishments. Be concerned only with the amount of time you spend dealing with individuals upon the sturdy and heartfelt basis of the love of the Creator. Most of all, allow your intuition to play the part in your life it deserves, for with daily meditation your intuition will point you in the direction you ought to go. When it becomes obvious, seize it and embrace it, for it is your next lesson.

When one of the group asks about the sadness in his voice, he does not deny it. The sadness is real, he says, but not because they have failed. It lies in a planet only with the greatest difficulty avoiding becoming evil, holding on to its mixed neutrality only by effort, and that effort is what is put out by those such as you. And then he names the hardest truth about loving. In the vibration of love as we know it, he says, there is a dynamic of joy and sadness. Joy from the Creator. Sadness because of the separation of those who are separated from the Creator. For those who love wish only to serve others, and when you cannot serve, you must then feel sad. Perhaps that is the hardest thing about loving, is to know that you cannot change people. They must come to you. They must be ready. Then the seed is planted, and joy begins again, in new ground.

He asks them to understand a deeper reality in which they must not and cannot feel sad. For the place whereon you stand at this very moment, wherever you are, is holy ground. You do not need to reach the promised land, he says. You have the promised land in your heart. Simply because other people cannot see it does not mean it is not there. You must visit it in meditation, and then you will know.

The bush burns, and is not consumed. The desert is long. The shoes come off wherever you happen to be standing.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Big Belly Laugh
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the big belly laugh.

Your entire planet, he says, is hurtling headlong into the greatest crisis possible, almost unnoticed by the great majorities of your peoples.

He frames the crisis in a way I have not heard anywhere else. The consumption of creative energy, he says, has increased the entropy of your planet and decreased the available creativity and regenerative abilities of the planet itself. Meanwhile your peoples ignore those forces of nature which cannot be depleted. And with the entropy of the physical there is a corresponding entropy of mental and spiritual creativity. Those who dwell within your culture have more and more become creatures lacking in creativity and imagination, he says, one with the machines they have created, the governments they have created, the polarities they have created.

Listen to how he defines the terms, because the definitions are the diagnosis. What is creativity, my friends, but an understanding of creation? And what is the creation, but love? And what is love, but unity? Where your peoples have accepted the fundamental dicta of government, society, and culture regarding differences in ideology and religion, he says, you will have endless and proliferating polarities. And polarity or separation, he says, is indicative of one thing. A lack of creativity.

And from polarity he moves to the deepest trouble of the cycle, as he calls it. Leaders who would consider planetary annihilation rather than relinquish an ideology, a piece of land, or power. There is a growing probability, he says, that one of your leaders will attempt to use nuclear force to gain an advantage. It is not creative to consider the destruction of a planet as a diplomatic tool, he says. It is indeed suicidal.

What can you do? The answer is the one the archive always gives, and he gives it without apology. Include in your meditations a prayer for the peace and the brotherhood of your planet, he says, for it is truly needed at this time. It is only due to the meditation of those sending love and light to the planetary consciousness, he says, that the many natural disasters of recent years have not taken an even greater toll in lives. A small group, meditating, has weight. He says so plainly.

Then a second voice comes through, and the whole temperature of the evening changes. Latwii arrives, and where Hatonn brought the diagnosis, Latwii brings the remedy, which turns out to be joy. Things look a little down on planet Earth at this time, he admits. But from where we are, you are only where you are for a moment. And in that moment you are working very hard. And after that moment you will play, and before that moment you will play. And what we would like you to do, my sister, is learn how to play during the moment in which you are working very hard.

Whatever burdens you carry, he says, they will become weightless if you put them down. You need only be the best person you can be, love the Creator with all your heart, and let your heart touch others in a spirit of love. If light is shining from your eyes, that is your entire responsibility. You did not come into this world that the world might be entirely altered, he says. You came to display a talent. That talent is to show the love of the Creator.

And then he returns to the image of the movie, and plays it out. Look upon these times as you would a movie, he says. You are an actor, but let yourself also be the observer, the director, that keeps your part on an even keel. We are all the heroes and heroines of our own motion pictures, in an illusion such as yours. Thus let the movie be one which you will be glad to watch later. We encourage you to be a good heroine in that movie, he tells the questioner. As wise as you can be. As loving as you can be. As analytical of your own faults and as confident of your own virtues as you can be. What more could you ask from a heroine, my sister?

When the time comes, he says, you will be in the company of those who, like you, were attempting to be of help. And we will meet you then, we and our brothers of the Confederation, and it will be a grand meeting, and we shall all laugh and rejoice together. We will look for you there, my sister, in person. And you will see us as light, and we will see you as light.

And his closing lines are the ones I have been carrying around all day, the reason for the title. Join us in the big belly laugh, he says, for you have a very funny planet, a very silly planet, a very foolish planet. And sometimes, when you are sane and those about you are not, you have a very lonely laughter. But don't forget to laugh, even if you laugh alone. This is only a movie. Have a bite of popcorn and keep on.

Do not be trapped, my sister, he says. You are a light being. You are not an earth being. The entropy is real. The danger is real. And the answer, in the end, is not despair but play. Have a bite of popcorn, and keep on.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Mountaineer’s Stick
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the mountaineer's stick.

A new voice comes to the group this evening, one that has not spoken with them before. The name given is Kasara, and they say they have been asked to come by the brothers and sisters of Hatonn, the chief teachers of the group. They offer, humbly, a little story, in the hope that it might spark a thought or two. And the story they tell has the plain perfection of all true parables. It needs nothing added to it.

Once, my friends, there was a mountaineer, and this mountaineer was a wanderer, and he wandered up hill and down, many the day and many the night spent he in loneliness, enjoying the beauties of his scenery and enduring the hardships of all weathers. This mountaineer had but one desire, and that was to find the perfect walking stick. For it was his belief that with a stout stick at his side, he could climb the highest mountain, traverse the longest distance, and always, without fail, keep a sure footing.

For years he tried and tried to find the right stick. He whittled on sticks. He carved on sticks. He traded sticks with others. But somehow, they never seemed to fit his hand just right, or to hold him up just right. And one day, after many years of trying to find the right stick, he got tired of looking for something to lean on. And he decided that if he did not need a roof over his head, or walls between himself and the winter, or shelter between himself and the rain, or anything but a hat between himself and the summer sun, that perhaps he did not need any stick, either.

And once he had found that he had all he needed in himself, then and only then did he become the true wanderer. Then and only then did he become truly happy. Satisfied at last that his purpose was not that of another, and his needs not that of another, but that he was complete within himself.

Then Kasara steps out of the story and names what it is. We speak to you allegorically, my friends, they say. What we are encouraging you to do is to leave off looking for the right walking stick in life. You did not come into this world to lean on others, to lean on ideas, to lean on possessions, or to lean on preconceived ethics.

You came into this world a perfect creature, they say, and that perfection was rapidly overlaid by a complex system of intellectual limitations placed upon you by others. You then carefully continued the work of your parents, believed what they told you in good faith, and for your lifetime have been trying in good faith to live according to the precepts of people and ideas and ethics and ways of being that were taught to you. These are your walking sticks, they say, and none of them fit, do they?

No one else's ideas will carry you through, they say. No one else's ethics can make you feel right if something is wrong, or wrong if something is right to you. Why spend so much of your life confused because of what others think? They may have traded you a walking stick, but you don't have to take it. You don't have to have any.

And then they quote the old line from the holy works, and turns it into the hinge of the whole evening. My rod and my staff shall comfort thee, they say. Yes, my friends, even if you walk through the valley of death, you have a rod, you have a staff. You have the Creator within you. You are part of a perfection that is the Creator. And that part of you is the only walking stick you will ever need.

You cannot get in touch with that part of yourself by any outer means, they say. Not even by intellectually understanding the means of meditation and service to others. What is a walking stick for, my friends? It is for the steep places. When you need comfort, know that that comfort exists within you. Even if you walk in the valley of death, the Creator is with you. Stand on your own two feet, my friends. And in your spiritual path remember that the way of the mountaineer is the true way. Walking, going, journeying, seeking, that is all that there is to living. The rest is illusion.

I love the plainness of that list. Walking, going, journeying, seeking. No arriving. The true way is not a technique you master, it is a walk you keep taking, on your own two feet.

Later in the session, when they speak again through another instrument, they add a caution worth keeping beside the story. Possessions will help you along your path, they say, but draw the line, for the pull is so strong that it may engulf you. Through meditation you will evolve to a state where you can offer your services to many. The road is steep and long, they say, but well worth the trip.
