You have begun a sequence of events, gotten on a track from which there is no removing yourself. And his answer is immediate and absolute. My friends, this is not so.

It is a condition of the illusion, he says, reinforced only by your belief in it. There is no track that cannot be replaced with one which you more truly seek. The secret lies not in catching the right train, but in knowing yourself. Knowing enough about yourself to seek your deepest desires.

I want to stay with that distinction, because I think it undoes a whole way of living. We spend so much energy trying to catch the right train: the right job, the right city, the right timing. And he says the train was never the point. The point is the passenger. Know the passenger, and any track can be replaced.

He goes on to name what keeps us locked on the wrong track. You have heard from many sources, he says, a great variety of things that should be, ought to be, must be, and need to be the models for your expectations of yourself and of others. And we come to you and suggest a substitute for all of these things. The substitute being love.

Then he quotes your holy works, and the line he chooses is perfect for this. Love is not puffed up. Part of what makes the freight train feel so complete in your existence, he says, is your belief in a puffed up, proud sense of the rightness of certain ways of being. If something in your existence is not pleasing to you, reexamine those concepts of which you are proud, and evaluate them in the simple, single, all-encompassing light of love.

Wash yourself clean in that love, he says, and so purified, reexamine your concepts. You will find that the path you are on is not what is making you less than comfortable, but rather your expectations, your preconceptions, and your feelings about how things should be.

The discomfort is not the track. The discomfort is the map you drew of where the track should go.

Toward the end of the evening, through another channel, Hatonn lifts the whole teaching into a larger frame. This time, he says, is a very important time in the history of your planet. The lessons that have been learned are about to culminate. Graduation is at hand. And the lessons to come, he says, will be ones where love is understood not as an intellectual concept, or an expression of feeling toward others. Love will be understood as a living being. Understood in all of its essence as the foundation for everything that is.

Love, not as an idea about which you have feelings, but as a living being you can meet. I do not know what that will be like. But I know I want to be on whatever track leads there. And if the track I am on is not that one, I am glad to know it can be replaced.

Thank you for listening.

title: Radiation and Relationship
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: radiation and relationship.

The session of March twenty ninth contains one of Hatonn's most quietly profound teachings, and it takes the form of two pictures. He asks you to hold them side by side and consider them. Consider, he says, two models of love.

The first model is the concern and love of a parent for a child. How careful the parent is. How concerned. How totally committed to the care of this being, this perfect entity which is a representation of the Creator. Of what service, he says, in this great love of parent to child.

The second model is a rose. Let us look at the first rose as it blooms, he says. First a bud, then sweet smelling and fresh with the dew. It opens to the sun, sharing its scented beauty with the breeze, and the glory of its radiant color with all who pass by. Or with no one at all, if there is no one to pass by.

I love that last clause. Or with no one at all. The rose does not check whether it has an audience before it blooms.

Then Hatonn names the difference. There is much to consider in these two models of love, he says. One is a radiation. One is a relationship. And then he turns the question back on you, the way the best teachers do. Are you in a relationship with the Creator, he asks. Do you feel the radiance of the Creator? Is there a point at which it is necessary to understand the difference?

He does not answer his own question. He leaves you these thoughts to ponder. And I have been pondering them, so let me offer what I see in the two pictures.

The parent's love is love with its hands full. It watches, it worries, it commits. It is love aimed at someone, love that knows a name. The rose's love is love with its hands open. It simply shines. It asks nothing of the passerby, not even that there be one. One love moves toward. The other simply radiates.

And the quiet suggestion underneath is that the Creator's love is both, and that your love can be both. There are moments to be the parent: careful, committed, tending what is yours to tend. And there are moments to be the rose: blooming because blooming is what you are, whether or not anyone is watching.

Most of us, I suspect, are fluent in only one of the two. We either love by gripping or love by glowing, and we mistrust the other mode. Tonight's teaching is an invitation to practice both. To hold someone the way a parent holds a child. And to shine the way a rose shines at no one.

One is a radiation. One is a relationship. You contain them both.

Thank you for listening.

title: Guests at the Costume Ball
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: guests at the costume ball.

The fifth of April brings a session about patience, and Hatonn opens it with a line from your holy works. I have waited for the Lord, he quotes, more than the watchman for the morning. More than the watchman for the morning.

He says he wants to speak of the love that manifests itself to you more slowly than you would perhaps wish. It is very difficult for your peoples to wait for anything, he says, for among your peoples it is understood that each entity has rights and privileges, and these include prompt results from any energy output. And yet, he says, when your day is done and you look back on it, you find that all too much of your precious time has been spent waiting for inconsequential and petty things. Things which shall not outlast this transient illusion.

There is a waiting that is profitable, he says, and it is the waiting for the truth. Not the truth of a circumstance, or the solution to an apparent problem, but the truth of who you really are and whence you truly came. This is worth much waiting. The Creator makes itself known in an eternal present, and you live day to day, so you have little natural access to that sphere. It takes patience to set aside the time to wait upon the Creator.

And then he gives you the image that carries the whole evening. Each of you, he says, is like a guest at a costume ball. Each with their own mask and costume, each playing a part which in a certain way expresses the Creator for that individual, in a way that has meaning for that entity.

Most at the ball, he says, know not that they wear costumes. Most believe they are who they seem to be in their daily round of activities. But most also suspect that there is more to their expression of life than meets their own eyes. And each, on occasion, peers into the mirror of their own being to examine that which is the self.

And each entity, at the appointed hour of their own illumination, shall discover that they are but one thing in truth. They are the Creator. And upon that discovery they shall also realize that each of the other entities at the costume ball are also the Creator. There is nothing but the Creator.

I love what he says next, because it is not what you expect from a teaching about illusion. He does not tell you to tear off the costume in disgust. The patience of playing the parts, he says, is a prime requisite for playing the part well. Enjoy the ball. Enjoy your costume. Enjoy all the manifestations of the creation, for each expresses the Creator in an infinity of ways.

Enjoy the ball. After all the warnings about illusion across these sessions, here is Hatonn telling you to enjoy it. But enjoy it knowingly. Know that it is a costume you wear, a play in which you partake, an illusion in which you are immersed. And know also that there is a truth in which you are an integral part: the truth of the love and the light of the infinite Creator, that shines from deep within your very being.

So wait, he says, like the watchman for the morning. And while you wait, dance. The morning will come. And when it does, you will find you were the dawn all along.

Thank you for listening.

title: Where Is the Love
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: where is the love.

The twelfth of April. Hatonn speaks at length about how your people see the world, and his diagnosis is blunt. Your perception of creation, he says, sees objects, interactions, ratios, particles broken down as though they were bricks and built back up as though they were buildings. It is, if you will pardon our expression, somewhat of a mechanical view of creation. A view which does not see far beyond the exterior appearance.

Against this he sets another way of seeing. When you view the Father's creation, he says, if you look with your heart, if you look with your inner eye, if you look with your interior perceptions, you might become aware of a binding force which holds all of creation together. A force which serves as not only the binder, but also that which is bound.

Without that binding force in view, he asks, is not all that is seen somewhat chaotic, somewhat disjointed, without rhyme or reason? For within the creation there is an ordering, and that ordering of the Father is love. Love which seeks to be known. Love which seeks to know itself. Love which calls. Love which listens.

And then the practice, in the form of a question. As you perceive that which is round about you, he says, keep within your mind, within your heart, within your being, the consideration of what it is you see. Ask yourself: where is the love? For surely, my friends, it surrounds you always.

Where is the love. Four words, and I think they might be the most practical instruction in the entire archive. Not a doctrine. A question to carry into the grocery store, the argument, the traffic, the ordinary Tuesday. Where is the love here? It is somewhere. It surrounds you always. The question is only whether you are looking with the eye that can see it.

Later that evening, a man asks about the Kingdom of Heaven, a phrase he has been turning over in his mind from the Bible. And Hatonn's answer is as plain as anything he ever said. Mull no longer, my friend. The Kingdom of Heaven is that place one reaches when one understands and shares the existence of oneness in this universe and all universes.

He gives it an image. Just as in a well exercised and cared for body, he says, all cells work joyfully and share one set of vibrations, so also could be represented the Kingdom of Heaven.

All cells working joyfully, sharing one set of vibrations. That is the kingdom. Not a place in the sky. A condition of harmony, entered the moment you understand oneness and begin to share it.

And when the man presses him, asking whether beings like Hatonn are part of that kingdom, the answer is wonderfully honest. Both yes and no, he says. Yes, in that whether one realizes his perfection or not, he is still a part of the Kingdom. And no, in that they have not yet attained that form of perfection. And when the man asks how they have fallen short, Hatonn answers: my brother, if we knew that answer. If we only knew.

I love that they do not pretend. They are ahead of us on the road, not at the end of it. And the road, it turns out, is the same question all the way down. Where is the love? Ask it of the world. Ask it of the kingdom. Ask it of yourself.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Lesson of the Willow
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the lesson of the willow.

Easter Sunday, the nineteenth of April. Hatonn gives the group a teaching about meditation, and he gives it as a comparison between two trees.

Perceive yourself, he says, not as the willow, whose green color is always the first to show in the spring, and whose beauty is unparalleled, but as the mighty cedar or oak. The willow has roots that move shallowly in the earth, drinking eagerly and quickly, feeding and growing and ripening and bearing fruit in haste. Yet the storm comes, and the wind blows, and the willow is torn from the ground.

It takes a mighty wind indeed to topple a cedar, he says, for the roots go deep. It takes a great wind to fell an oak, for the roots seek downward, ever downward, into the deeper sources of moisture, of life, of food.

In your meditation, my friends, he says, know that you are a thing growing. Growing quietly, nourished and nurtured from the earth of your silence. Do not be satisfied with your own quick results. Do not be fooled by the constant taking of your own spiritual temperature. Simply and patiently, seek ever deeper in silence for the waters of truth, that they may nourish you and lift you up, that your fruits may be strong and good and ready for the harvest time.

I want to linger on that phrase: the constant taking of your own spiritual temperature. How often the seeker treats the inner life like an illness to be monitored. Am I better yet? Am I enlightened yet? Did that meditation work? Hatonn says: stop checking the thermometer. Be the oak. The oak does not check.

Earlier in the same session, he names what the deep roots are reaching for. Within all of the creation of the Father, he says, there is a space which contains all of creation. The space between all things. The space within all things. That vacuum, as it were, that needs to be filled with love, and in fact is filled with love.

That is a sentence to read twice. The emptiness you feel is not empty. The space between things, the space within things, the hollow place in your own chest on a bad night: it needs to be filled with love, and in fact it already is. You are not trying to fill a void. You are trying to notice that it was never void.

Many try to fill that empty place, he says, with substitutes. Thoughts, things, ideas, accumulations. Much time and effort is spent gathering what it is hoped will fill the void. But the substitutes are transient, and they are only catalysts for your growth. They are not the substance.

And his closing that night is one of the loveliest in the archive. Remember the lesson of the willow, he says. True answers come from deep within your being. The shallow ones may be moved by the storms of your illusion.

The shallow answers blow away. The deep ones hold. So do not be the willow, beautiful and first and torn up by the first storm. Be the cedar. Be the oak. Let your roots go down into the silence, and let the silence do the growing.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Virtues of Dissatisfaction
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the virtues of dissatisfaction.

On the twenty sixth of April, a rare voice takes the floor. Oxal does not speak often in this archive, and when he does, he wastes no words. His subject for the evening is dissatisfaction. And his first move is to tell you that your whole approach to it is backwards.

In your illusion, he says, dissatisfaction is the watchword. Few indeed among your peoples can be said to be satisfied with their condition, physically, mentally, emotionally, or spiritually. And the universal reaction is to try to eliminate dissatisfaction by correcting whatever causes it. The consumer pressures the producer. The partners try to fix the relationship. The individual buys volumes purporting to give advice upon correcting the defect within the self.

The mechanisms for erasing dissatisfaction abound, he says, and are considered appropriate and normal. And then he asks the question that rearranges the room. Were we to ask you what the primary reason for your existence is, he says, the answer would not be satisfaction. Of this we are certain, for those who seek will never be satisfied.

Those who seek will never be satisfied. Read that as a promise, not a curse. If you are a seeker, satisfaction was never the destination. So what is dissatisfaction for?

He gives you an image. When an unthinking being such as a horse or a donkey does not wish to move forward, he says, it is goaded. Consider your sources of dissatisfaction, he says, and look within yourselves for the causes, for the defects, for the stimulus to seeking.

The goad. Not the enemy. The prod that moves the animal forward. Your dissatisfaction is not a sign that your life is broken. It is the instrument that keeps you moving. And the mistake, he says, is to carry dissatisfaction beyond the function for which it was intended: to be dissatisfied with the state of your dissatisfaction, to make a problem out of the prod.

So what do you do instead? When you find yourself dissatisfied, he says, know that the source is yourself. Without condemning the self, clear the mind, step away from the illusion of time and limitations, and do your work. Not to seek satisfaction, he says, but to understand the stimulus. And he gives you the question to dwell in, patiently, humbly, quietly: what do you seek?

What do you seek. Not what is wrong. Not how do I fix it. What do you seek. Dwell in that question, he says, accepting your dissatisfaction, and you will find the combination most fruitful.

Later that night Hatonn adds the other half of the teaching. His words have been heard by many upon your planet, he says, but very few have put these words to use. They hear the words. They understand the words. But there is more to our communication than the hearing and the understanding. The important step is the next step: putting into action that which we bring to you. That, my friends, is the only important step. The first two are necessary. The third produces the result.

So the evening gives you both halves of a whole practice. From Oxal: let your dissatisfaction goad you, and ask what you seek. From Hatonn: then act on what you hear. Hearing is necessary. Understanding is necessary. But the result comes only from the third step, the living of it.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Soft Heart of the Creator
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the soft heart of the creator.

The third of May. Hatonn speaks through several channels in turn, and his message is the simplest one in the archive, which is also, he admits, the hardest one to live. The message is of what you would call universal love, he says, for this is what the people of your planet need at this time.

He says something striking about how this message travels. They have been beaming it to the population of Earth for many of your years, he says. Not so much in an intellectual sense, but in what you might call a subliminal way. A quiet increase in the awareness of universal love, moving through a portion of your population like light through water.

And yet the vast majority remains unaware, he says, and so you find yourselves immersed in a sea of troubles. These troubles are the creation of the individual members of your planet, he says. Manufactured by thinking. And this creates a difficulty for those who seek awareness of love and then attempt to put that awareness into practice, because all about them they find the continuing problems created by those who have blocked the truth.

His advice for living inside that difficulty is one of my favorite practical teachings. Look upon each of the problems generated by those who do not seem aware, he says, as simply a small test of your awareness. If you successfully pass that small test in each and every day, in each and every way, you will have learned the very simple lesson that will open to you the gateway to your Creator.

The rude driver, the cruel headline, the colleague who blocks the truth at every turn: small tests. Not punishments. Not proof the world is hopeless. Small, daily examinations in the one subject.

He is also honest about the strange economics of this path. The confusion upon your planet, he says, is the logical outgrowth of an illusion pursued to its ultimate completion. The illusion in which you live is not what sustains you, not the goal of evolution, not the goal of the Creator. It is simply the means. Simply the catalyst. Simply the opportunities presented time and again to learn to seek within, to seek from within the center of your own being the love of the Creator.

The illusion has this simple purpose, he says: to teach you that it is not real. That is all it was ever for.

Toward the close, he speaks of those who seek hardest and find the established paths hardest to walk. Many of those who seek the hardest, he says, are those who do not wish or need the bones, the hard skeleton of churches, ashrams, or synagogues, but rather need the soft heart of a living and loving Creator.

The soft heart of a living and loving Creator. Not the skeleton. The heart. I think that is what tonight's title is really pointing at: the difference between religion as structure and love as something alive, beating, warm to the touch.

And his farewell that night is one of the great goodbyes of the archive. I leave you naked, yet strong, he says. Alone, yet full of love. Pilgrims, yet accompanied by the hosts of heaven.

Naked, yet strong. That is the seeker without the skeleton: no armor, no institution to hide inside, and somehow stronger for it. Pilgrims, yet accompanied. Alone on the road, and never alone at all.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Lens of Service
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the lens of service.

The tenth of May is Mother's Day, and Hatonn opens the session by noticing something beautiful about it. It is a custom on your planet to honor mothers on this day, he says, and the cumulative effect of this vibration is the creation of a state of receptivity across an area of your planet often responsible for much strife. The result has been an increase in peace within the hearts of many entities, not only where you reside but across the surface. For peace, he says, has a cumulative effect that increases beyond its original numbers.

Peace has a cumulative effect. I love that as physics. A day of honoring mothers measurably softens a planet. Keep that in mind the next time someone tells you small kindnesses do not scale.

But the main teaching of the evening is about service, and Hatonn frames it as a way of seeing. Consider the unity that binds each of you with each person that you meet, he says, with each activity which you undertake, with each thought that you think. And as you go your ways over the days and months ahead, as you face the various difficulties, the various joys, the various experiences, consider your response to each as an act of service.

Look through the lens of service, he says. That is the whole instruction. He will not explain completely what he means by it. He leaves the majority of that understanding to come as a result of your ponderings. The lens is not a rulebook. It is a way of looking, and you have to grind the glass yourself.

What does it change, to look through that lens? The difficult colleague becomes someone you might serve rather than someone you must endure. The boring errand becomes an offering rather than an interruption. The joy becomes something to share rather than something to hoard. Same events. Different eyes.

He is clear about why they serve at all, and the reason is not what you might expect. Those who have traveled the trail of conscious evolution, he says, incur a certain responsibility that is a privilege as well: to serve those who have not traveled quite so far. And by such service we not only aid those who seek, he says, but we aid ourselves. For are we not all one? As one becomes illumined, the All shines just a bit brighter.

The service is not charity handed down. It is the one serving the one, which is to say, yourself. And he adds the line that steadies every anxious servant: we do not seek recognition for this service, for the service is its own reward.

There is a sterner thread in the evening too, in answer to questions about the use of power, about names that can command other beings. And his counsel there is entirely of a piece with the lens. Any power has the tendency to corrupt, he says. Guard yourself against lightly held commands. Preface any use of your abilities with careful preparation in compassion and acceptance, for the creation of the Father is interrelated by webs of love and service.

Webs of love and service. That is what you see when you look through the lens. Not a hierarchy. A web. And your place in it is wherever your hands happen to be.

Thank you for listening.

title: Perfect Love Is Perfect Freedom
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: perfect love is perfect freedom.

The seventeenth of May. Hatonn announces that he wants to speak about some aspects of love which are not recognized by your peoples, aspects which blur the image of love past all recognition. And the aspect he chooses is freedom.

Many times, he says, it comes to the attention of all those who seek that there is a concept called right and wrong, virtue or sin. This concept is much like one who willingly builds a jailhouse and locks himself within it.

He is quick to add what he is not saying. We are not suggesting in any way that lawlessness prevails, he says, or that nihilism is an appropriate stance for those who seek the truth. He suggests only that that which is appropriate for each being is known to some portion of that being. Is known within. And the entity which seeks the counsel of society, of accepted modes of conduct, without discrimination, is like unto the willing prisoner.

And then the sentence that became tonight's title, one of the great sentences of the archive. Perfect love is perfect freedom, he says. Perfect love is an entrance into a fresh field of flowers from the dark dungeon of fear.

From the dark dungeon of fear into a fresh field of flowers. That is the whole movement of the spiritual life in one image. Not from wrong to right. From fear to freedom. The jailhouse was built by your own hands, out of rules you never examined, and the door was never locked.

What replaces the rulebook? This: take the responsibility for the use of discrimination, he says, in ascertaining those actions which are appropriate. Not in the eyes of others, or of a society which is faceless, but in the eyes of the self facing itself in meditation.

The self facing itself in meditation. That is the only courtroom he recognizes. And he calls this the law of love, which binds and unbinds. When used correctly, he says, it causes the entity to take upon itself the raiment of the co-creator that each of you really is.

There is a companion teaching later in the evening, from a question about how to direct light to the planet in prayer. And Hatonn gives a visualization so simple you could teach it to a child. See the planet first in darkness, he says, as a blackened void. Then begin to see points of light in different locations beginning to shine. Continue until the light grows in size and brilliance, until finally the light completely encompasses your planet, until it glows as though it were a sun.

He explains why this works, and his reasoning is pure oneness. Each being upon your planet has areas of darkness, he says. Each area of your planet has areas of darkness. Each being and each location has areas of light. For each particle of your creation is composed of polarities of light and dark. And if all are indeed one, then all must be treated the same.

All must be treated the same. The dark places are not the enemy of the light places. They are the same planet, waiting for the same dawn. Perfect love does not divide the world into the saved and the damned. It sees the whole blackened void, and it begins, point by point, to light it.

Thank you for listening.

title: Beyond Justification
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: beyond justification.

The twenty fourth of May. Hatonn takes up one of the heaviest words in the human vocabulary: justification. And he sets out, gently and completely, to take it away from you.

How often, he asks, have you acted and thought on the basis of the illusion that there is such a thing as being justified? How many times have you condemned yourself because you were not justified in your own mind?

When one has not sufficiently sought to know the self, he says, one is liable to accept the belief that the ethics and dogmas of your peoples have an independent propriety. How much sadness, guilt, grief, and consternation has been caused, he asks, because your peoples do not go within to seek for what is right for them?

And then the flat statement, with no cushioning at all. To the best of our understanding, he says, there is no justification. You are never justified. You cannot ever be justified. Nor can you be wronged. Nor can you wrong, except intentionally.

You are never justified. Sit with how strange that feels. We spend our lives building cases: for ourselves, against ourselves, for others, against others. And he says the courthouse is empty. There was never a trial. There is only the question underneath the trial, which is whether you have gone within to seek what is right for you.

He takes one of the most quoted sayings of Jesus and re-reads it through this lens. I am the way, the truth, the life, the saying goes. No one comes to the Father but by me. This saying, Hatonn says, has been much misunderstood, and it is very central to what we have to say.

His reading is this. The entity known as Jesus often went to be by himself, to seek within himself that knowledge which is not justification but rather the knowledge of love. And when he became one with that love, he also became one with the knowledge of what creative actions he might take in harmony with the rhythms of his existence. And when this entity was in that state of love, he was one in consciousness with the Creator, with love itself.

And you also, he says, when you find that consciousness, when you find that selfhood, that I which is beyond justification, concerns, and worries, that I which may move mountains, you too will be the way. For love is the way. The truth. For is not love the truth? And the life? And you will be one with the Father, for there is no road to the Father but by love.

I am the way becomes: love is the way, and you can be it too. That is quite a different teaching from the one most of us inherited.

There is a small, human moment near the end of the session that proves the teaching in real time. A telephone rings. The channel's concentration breaks. She is embarrassed at having forgotten some duties. And Hatonn folds the interruption straight into the lesson. For a disturbance to occur may not be justified, he says, but that it does occur is a perfect part of a creation of love. When you feel that you have failed, when you feel that you are not justified, step back, and know that it does not matter.

Failure. Success. Justification. These are illusions, he says, and dreams within a dream. Know yourself as one who is learning from failure, from success, from striving and from not striving, and accept all those things in yourself and in others.

Beyond justification, then, there is not chaos. There is love, which was the point all along.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Radiant One
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the radiant one.

The thirty first of May. Hatonn says he will speak in parables, and the parable he tells is one of the most human stories in the whole archive. It is about two young men on a freight train.

Once there was a young man, he begins. This young man roamed the highways. He was homeless, and carried what little he had upon his back. This young man was consumed with the knowledge of his imperfection. When he looked upon himself, he saw nothing but error, mistakes, imperfections, and faults.

Notice what he could still see, even in his despair. With his ears he could hear much beauty, Hatonn says, for birdcall and the rustle of the wind are the friends of those who live by the road. With his eyes he witnessed an unending panorama of the creation. His skin was touched with sun. The flowers greeted his nose with that beauty that is so careless that it gives itself regardless of the witnesses it may have.

The world was still beautiful to him. He just could not include himself in the beauty.

One day the young man catches a ride on a freight train, and finds he is not alone. He is joined by another young man much like himself. This man, however, dirty and ragged and poor though he was, was radiant. A light shone from his eyes.

My friend, the radiant one says, what is wrong with you? Are you hungry? May I help you? And the young man answers: no. It is hopeless. I cannot help myself, for I have done many things of which I am ashamed.

What are they, asks the other. Have you raped? Have you killed? Have you stolen? Oh no, says the young man, startled. But I have lied, and I have run, and I have hidden, and I am not clean, and there is no hope of my overcoming these faults in character.

And here comes the turn. Sit up, my friend, says the radiant one. You were made in the image of the Creator. Where is the fault in that?

Why, no fault, replies the young man. But you do not understand. Has your Father not told you to be perfect? asks the other. Yes, cries the young man in anguish. That is what I cannot be.

Ha, says the radiant one. How foolish. To think that the Creator would ask you to be perfect, unless He thought you could be. The radiant eyes seemed to burn into the young man's very soul. Touch the places within yourself that you feel are at fault, he says, and know that the Creator is waiting confidently for you to be perfect.

The young man closes his eyes and prays. He touches his iniquities, his harsh words, his ill feelings, his half truths. Whoever you are, he says, I cannot find the truth that you give me, for I can find no health in them, much less perfection.

Aha, says the radiant one. But you have touched them. You know them. Now open your eyes, my friend. Do you not love me? The young man opens his eyes, startled. Yes, of course I do. The radiant one smiled. There, you see, said he. Is that not perfection? Continue, then, to love.

Is that not perfection? He could love the radiant stranger, and that love was perfect, and it was his. That is the whole argument. You do not have to become someone else to be perfect. You already love. Continue, then, to love.

A man in the group asks the obvious question afterward. Can you truly love others without loving yourself? And Hatonn answers: the process of loving the self may begin at any point, for all is one. When an entity can truly love any other entity, then the entity has made a start in loving the self, which will become as a chain of reactions, each feeding the other, until the channel of love is open within the entity and flows freely, the waters of love touching all.

The love of the self for the other, for the self, for the other, for the self. A chain reaction. It only takes one link to start it. One moment of real love, aimed anywhere at all, even at a ragged stranger on a freight train. Especially there.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Slow Climb
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the slow climb.

There is a particular kind of tiredness that only seekers know. It is the tiredness of trying very hard and getting nowhere, of straining toward the light and finding your foot lands exactly where it started. Tonight Hatonn tells a small story about that tiredness, and about what happens when you finally stop forcing the climb.

Once, he says, long ago and in a distant place, there was one of their own brethren who was a seeker. He felt his efforts were not enough, and yet he could not see the next step. The more he tried to gain a foothold on the next slope, the more his outstretched foot passed straight through his illusory goal, and down he came again onto the all too solid earth beneath him.

I love that image, the foot passing through. Anyone who has meditated or prayed or tried to be a better person knows exactly what that feels like. The goal dissolves the moment you reach for it. And the seeker in the story did what many of us do. He despaired. He decided to give the whole thing up and climb back down to where he had started, to become again a simple half-conscious being, lost among a crowd of other half-conscious beings.

But he could not do it. And listen to how Hatonn puts this, because it is one of the strangest sentences in the evening. The way of the lonely one is not the path of the blind. Once you have started to see, you cannot unsee. So the seeker turned around, painfully, arduously, and retraced his path of growth, feeling that to be alone and trying was better than the company of the blind. And when he arrived at the place where he had been stuck, he found his path no longer blocked. He could continue. The ascent resumed.

What changed? Nothing, except that he had stopped trying to force it. That is the teaching Hatonn draws out, and it is worth hearing slowly. There are times, he says, when the harder one tries, the less one seems to accomplish. One does not grow by attempting to force change. Rather, one must wait until the flow of the universe guides one into his proper path.

So the advice is not to strive less but to strive differently. Do not be hasty, Hatonn says. Welcome and cherish the experiences before you, for it is on this plane that you will establish the growth you need for the next. The very frustrations that feel like wasted time are the material. The slope you keep slipping on is the slope.

And then, through a second voice in the circle, Hatonn adds something that sharpens the whole evening. Many have heard our words, he says, and gone away feeling that what they heard was of value. But the value is not what you hear. It is in what you do with that which you have received. We could reveal a great deal of knowledge, he says, but unless you have the initiative to employ that knowledge in your everyday actions, our mission has been of no use.

That is a bracing sentence to sit with. All the listening in the world, all the transcripts and tapes and notes, amounts to nothing until it is lived. The archive is not a library to admire. It is a set of instructions for Tuesday morning.

The questions that followed that night circled the same theme from another angle. Why, one of the group asked, do so many of our questions get refused? And the answer is worth keeping. We cannot, Hatonn says, smell flowers for you. We cannot feel the air for you. We cannot offer you predigested enlightenment without losing our ability to speak clearly on what matters. The questions they will answer at any length, at any cost, are questions of love, of light, of the Creator. Everything else, the personal specifics, the proofs, the predictions, they leave alone, because to hand them over would be to stunt the very growth they came to serve.

So the evening ends where it began, with the seeker and his foot and the illusory slope. Growth cannot be forced, wisdom cannot be handed over, and love cannot be proven to you. Each of these must be walked into on your own two feet, at the pace the universe sets. The good news, if the little story is true, is that the path unblocks itself the moment you stop trying to kick the door down and simply keep walking.

Thank you for listening.

title: The One Security
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the one security.

Of all the things people chase, security might be the most quietly desperate. Not the loud ambitions, but the low hum underneath them, the wish to finally feel safe. Tonight Hatonn takes that wish apart, gently, and shows what it is made of.

He starts with the obvious candidates. Is security found in the accumulation of worldly goods? Apparently not, he says, for many who have amassed a comfortable amount of them are painfully insecure. Is it found in work? This is the widespread belief, that what an entity does lends it a reality it does not have on its own. To do, then, is to be. And to do is to be secure.

But sit with that a while, Hatonn suggests, and it palls too, for it becomes clear that you are more than what you do, and the security vanishes again. Listen to how simple his conclusion is. There is only one security, he says, and that is the knowledge of the nature of yourself. To know that you are not a transient being is to be secure. To know that this life is an illusion you are passing through, and that there is an infinite woven into your makeup, is to feel secure.

That knowledge, he admits, is hard won. Serenity, long sought after, is seldom won permanently. So day by day you must seek it again, in meditation, whatever form your meditation takes. It does not matter what the technique is. It matters only that you desire to know the truth of your own nature and your oneness with love.

And here is the turn I did not expect. Through a second voice, Hatonn gives security a second definition, and it sounds like the opposite of the first. True security, he says, lies not in that which one possesses, but in that which one gives away. If you would seek security, seek it in service.

He reaches for an image to make this concrete. Service, he says, acts as a sort of solvent. It dissolves density the way water dissolves crystalline forms clinging to something less solid, freeing it of unnecessary weight and rigidity. Or think of a spring pressed down and coated with something hard, so it can never release its pent up energy and expand. Service dissolves the coating. It lets the spring be a spring.

What I love about these two definitions is that they are the same teaching seen from two sides. The knowledge of yourself dissolves the illusion that you are small and temporary. Service dissolves the habits and prejudices that keep you compressed. Both are a kind of unclenching.

So Hatonn closes with an old saying, offered without irony. Hitch your wagon to the nearest star, he says, and let it bear you where it will, ever onward and ever upward. That is the objective of your striving. Not a house, not a title, not a role. A star. Something you can never possess and never lose.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Gift of Confusion
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the gift of confusion.

Confusion has a bad reputation, and Hatonn would like to do something about that. Tonight he argues that the state of not knowing what to do next is not a malfunction. It might be the most honest state there is.

He asks you to look closely at what confusion actually is. Activity has been brought to a halt, because certain messages do not jibe with your ideas, your preconceived notions of what should be. You have traveled a path up to a point, and the path leads no further. You are unsure which way to go. Around you a multitude of directions presents itself, each path a possibility, each path an impossibility. Confusion.

Now, he says, consider your options. Charge down the first path that appears? You may only find more confusion. Wait and assess? Still confusion. Do nothing? The confusion persists. So what moves you forward? His answer is disarmingly simple. Accept the state. Claim it. It is, after all, your state at the moment.

It is no sin, he says, to be confused. And here is why it might be a gift. If you can accept that you do not know, then there is an openness in you, a love of the state itself, that acts like a magnet. The proper course of thought is drawn to you the way a magnet draws iron filings. But if you insist you know exactly what to do, if you bull ahead with any plan simply to have a plan, you are like a cup that is already full. Nothing more can be poured in.

Listen to how he puts the counsel, because it is startling. We of Hatonn would counsel foolishness, my friends. We would counsel that you know very little, that we ourselves know very little. Wisdom, he says, is like the forces that fill a vacuum. It is all around you, always available, but only to those who make a place for it inside themselves.

Through another voice he widens the frame. Without some disorder, he says, there is no creation. Think of how the fruitful things multiply, with a minimum of neatness and an excess of enthusiasm. Confusion offers you that same minimum of neatness. It is the breeding ground of new beginnings, of transformations, of wisdoms.

Confusion is balanced by meaning, he says, and meaning by confusion. You will not find the meaning in each moment without accepting the confusion, the foolishness of how little any of us understands. If you can hold both at once, how small a part of creation you are and how perfect a part, you will have achieved a great deal.

The questions that night reached for the practical. How does one touch infinite intelligence, someone asked, with all this confusion in the way? And the answer is the whole evening in miniature. It cannot be achieved quickly or lightly, Hatonn says, but must be sought through all confusion, through all self doubt, through all tribulation, constantly seeking, constantly asking, constantly waiting, constantly knowing that what is sought will be found. At some unknown moment, he says, it will occur, and in that moment you will know the joy of love and light and infinity.

So if you are confused tonight, consider the possibility that you are not stuck. Consider that you are an empty cup, and that the universe is very good at filling those.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Chair and the Throne
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the chair and the throne.

What is your relationship to your things? Not in the moralizing sense, not the minimalism lecture. Hatonn takes a stranger and more interesting angle tonight. Your possessions, he says, are not the problem. Your grip on them is.

He begins where most spiritual teachers begin, with the pilgrim's reaction against things. When you start walking the path in earnest, you notice how much emphasis is placed on objects, and there is often a great backlash, as if things themselves were unspiritual. Hatonn gently disagrees. You are one portion of the original Thought, he says, and the first thing you possess is your physical body. Without it you would not be here at all. So it deserves appropriate, loving care. And so it is with your possessions.

If you can view your things as invested by you with love, he says, you create in them vibrations of peace and harmony and light that touch everyone who comes near them. Perhaps you have entered the home of someone serene, and felt it in the very walls, each thing comforting and comfortable, an atmosphere exuded from the woodwork itself. That is what he is describing. In themselves, things have no importance. But imbued with love and held without clinging, they become instruments of service.

And then, through a second voice, the image that gives this episode its title. The value of a physical object, Hatonn says, lies not in its existence but in the use you put it to. If you use a chair as a tool, a means of supporting you comfortably at rest or at work, then the chair acts in service. But that same chair used as a throne becomes a different matter altogether. In the first case, the chair releases. In the second, the chair, through your will, restrains.

I keep turning that sentence over. The chair releases. The chair restrains. Same chair. The difference is not in the object but in the posture of the soul sitting in it. Are you being supported, or are you being enthroned? One posture serves the journey. The other anchors you to the perch.

He extends the same logic to the inner furniture, our emotions. Each person who enters your life is your teacher, he says, for a true teacher is one who prompts the student to teach himself. And our reactions to these teachers, even the sharp ones, the warnings, are simply tools. Some serve to teach, others to warn and correct.

Listen to the image he offers for what to do with a reaction once it has done its job. If you were serving a meal, he says, you might use a pan known as a skillet to warm the food. But would you cling to the skillet throughout the meal, after it has served its purpose? Your reactions, he says, are like that. They warn you and prepare you. But once they have served, release the skillet. Your actions can be consciously chosen. Your reactions are a choice to place your actions at the whim of another.

So the evening's teaching fits in a single gesture of the hand. Hold your things lightly. Hold your reactions lightly. Use the chair. Do not be used by the throne. Pick up the skillet. Put it down again. Everything you own, everything you feel, is a tool for the journey, and tools are meant to be set down when the work is done.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Underground Rivers
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the underground rivers.

It was raining the night this session was recorded. You can almost hear it in the background of the words, the rain on the roof of the house where the group sat. Hatonn begins there, with the weather, and follows the water down into one of the most beautiful images in the archive.

The rains come, he says, and moisten the surfaces of your thoughts. But inspiration does more than moisten. It goes deep beneath the surface of your mind and heart. This rain, which you may call grace or love, feeds the deepest rivers that flow at the very heart of your being. These rivers are never dry, he says, no matter what the outer surface of your reality may seem. They are always enriched, forever full of the waters of love, and in each meditation you may come to these waters and be bathed and cleansed in their sweetness.

I find myself returning to that phrase, the outer surface of your reality. How easy it is, Hatonn says, in the hurly burly of daily life, to mistake the surface weather of your moods and emotions for the deeper sources of your being, to think that you are as you feel. It is good to know how you feel, he says, to keep careful track of it. But the true self is deeper than any weather. It bears, he says, often no resemblance whatsoever to your thinking or feeling on the outer planes.

And then he asks a question I love. Where does the rain on the roof come from? Does it come from elsewhere, from some outside source? No, he says. That rain was once part of the deepest underground waterways, surfacing in sea and lake and stream, taken up into the air, to fall again in service upon the good earth. So it is with love. It is not something you need to seek on the outer planes, for it is within you. And as it comes to you, so it has flowed from you. To seek love is to give love, in the unending cycle of service.

The questions that night turned to solitude, and the answer belongs with the rivers. Other people are mirrors, Hatonn says, reflecting back the part of yourself that most needs attention. Solitude is a mirror too, but a deeper one. Without others around, your attention is driven further inward, until you begin to see that all about you is your being, that you create your reality in your response to what you experience. It is a powerful tool, he says, and like all powerful tools it must be used with discretion, for in solitude the reflection is harder to ignore.

And then, almost as an afterthought, the evening takes a delightful turn. Someone asks about dragons. Were there ever dragons? And Hatonn answers with complete seriousness about the mass mind, the ancient fears, the images of power that peoples carried. But the heart of his answer is this. Each entity, in his or her life, faces many unknowns, many dragons, many threats. And many are the opportunities to confront and face and slay the dragon, and thereby pass yet one more test in this course of learning.

So tonight's teaching runs like water through all three images. The rivers beneath the surface that never run dry. The solitude that drives you down to them. The dragon waiting at the deep end, which is only the unknown wearing a frightening shape. None of it is elsewhere. It is all within, it has always been within, and the rain on your own roof is proof.

Thank you for listening.

title: No Success, No Failure
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: no success, no failure.

If there is one idea our culture will not let go of, it is the scoreboard. Winners, losers, the successful, the failures. Tonight Hatonn takes the scoreboard off the wall, in every area of life, and shows you what the wall looks like without it.

He walks through the three great arenas. First, work and money. Those who garner great amounts of money or power or prestige are admired simply because they have succeeded, and those whose accomplishments are modest are regarded with kindness or pity. But it is all an illusion, Hatonn says. You cannot know whether the work you are doing is succeeding. You can only do it with love. It is the love in your work, not the remuneration, that will affect your eternal self.

Then relationships. Those with many friends or a devoted spouse are counted successes. Those whose relationships end, or who walk alone, are counted as having somehow failed at the personal side of life. And yet again, he says, it is not the length of relationships or the number of them. It is the love given and received between yourself and strangers, enemies, acquaintances, friends, lovers, family, any self whatsoever, that accounts for the true value of your channel of love. For it is in giving that you receive. Not in this illusion, but in that which remains, your eternal spirit.

And then the most frightening arena of all, the spiritual one. How does one know if one is among those who will be with the Creator? How can one monitor one's behavior to be sure? Here Hatonn stops, and says the sentence this episode is named for. There is no success or failure. There is no judgment. There is, in each of you, the Creator.

Sit with that a moment. The Creator seeks to express itself through you, he says, in whatever way it may, to a world much unused to the original Thought. Your values may look ineffectual, even perverted, when offered freely to a world that does not believe anyone would love without gain. But be glad, he says, to fail in the eyes of the world, if through that mechanism love can best be channeled.

I love the tenderness of what follows. As you find the blockages in your minds and hearts, turn within to the original Thought, for it is simple, unlike your paradoxical illusion with its great ideas of success and its poor ideas of failure. There is a comfort in knowing you cannot run out of spiritual food. You cannot be hungry. You cannot be thirsty. You have only to turn within.

What a treasure you have, he says. What a wonderful treasure room is locked within you. There is no limitation and no difficulty that can remove the key to that treasure room from your hand. Feel merry then, and with utmost gladness seek the original Thought, that fire that blew upon creation and formed the planets in their courses, the suns in their brilliance, your tiny delicate island home, your Earth.

And if you want a single test for whether you are on the path, he offers one in the questions afterward. The mark of the spiritual journey has one sign only, and it is love. When you come in contact with love, he says, you shall know it, for it shall enlarge your field of perception, enlarge your capacity to feel the glory of creation, and it shall be unmistakable to the depths of your very being. When you do not find love in what you are doing, take it as a sign you may be embarking on an empty journey.

No scoreboard. No final judgment. Only the treasure room, only the key in your hand, only the question of whether love is in the work. That is the whole of the evening, and it is more than enough.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Light Touch
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the light touch.

Some evenings in the archive are crowded. Tonight's session brings a whole procession of voices, including a brand new one, and the thread that ties them together is a question the group could not stop circling. With so much talk of coming cataclysms and doom, how should a seeker hold all of that?

The new voice belongs to one who calls himself Orcas, of fourth density, recently graduated, contacting the group for the first time. His area of service, he says, is guidance in surviving future events on the planetary surface. But listen to how carefully he frames it. He will not provide a strategy, for that would infringe on free will. What he offers instead is a way of seeing. Identify yourself with the Earth's realms, he says. Become aware that a oneness exists, traversing the first and second and third levels of your world, and let that understanding assist you. On his own world, he says, his people attained such an attunement with their planet that the necessity of cataclysmic events simply fell away.

I find that quietly radical. Not stockpiles and bunkers, but attunement. The advice is not to brace against the Earth but to belong to it more completely, to live in a sharing between yourself and the living levels of your world.

Then Latwii arrives, and the temperature of the evening changes entirely. Where Orcas is careful and measured, Latwii is, by his own cheerful admission, liveliness itself. He has been away, he says, because the configuration was not right, and tonight the group finally holds the balance he needs. His perspective, he explains, is that of light rather than love. Love is the moving force that creates all of creation, but in the light of wisdom the creation can be clearly seen, so that love might be used in a balanced fashion, and one does not run headlong into difficulties with a completely uninhibited open channel of love.

And it is Latwii who answers the doom question, the one hanging over the whole evening. Yes, he says, cataclysms have begun and more will come, of that there is no denying. But one's response to such doom saying is what matters most. Do you wish to be swayed by prophecies of doom? If so, you have your choice of many. But we of Latwii, he says, have what might be called a light touch upon this matter, and do not see such things with the same gravity as many who speak of them.

A light touch. I keep coming back to that phrase as the title of this episode, because it describes not only Latwii's view of catastrophe but his whole manner. He teases, he jokes, he yields the floor to the punster of rank among the group. And underneath the playfulness is a serious teaching. Hold even the end of the world lightly. Choose, in each moment, what you will give your weight to.

He leaves practical counsel too. One of the group asks about meditation that leaves him drained and tired, and Latwii suggests a small ritual with real meaning, leaving the cares of the day by the door before entering the quiet, so that the meditation does not magnify the very energies that drain you. Choose what you open to, he says. An indiscriminate opening lets everything in.

So the evening gives you two teachers for fearful times. Orcas, urging attunement with the living Earth. Latwii, urging a light touch and a ready laugh. Neither of them says the storms are not coming. Both of them say the storm is not the point. The point is who you are while it passes.

Thank you for listening.

title: Marriage as Service
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: marriage as service.

Tonight's session is a short one, led by Laitos, the voice that specializes in training new channels. But tucked inside the channeling lesson is one of the clearest statements in the archive about what marriage actually is.

The relationship you call marriage, Laitos says, is a vehicle for service. The polarity between two entities draws them together and forms within each a bias to be of service. That is the basis of it. That is the whole of it. Everything else, the structure, the expectations, the heaviness, is extra weight the vehicle was never designed to carry.

I love how practical he is about this. When dealing with the relationship in daily life, he says, clear your mind of all thoughts of the necessity the marriage bond seems to suggest, and focus instead on the bias toward service that caused the relationship to begin. Go back to the origin. Two people drawn together by the urge to serve each other. Everything true in the bond flows from that.

He names the responsibilities plainly. Offer yourself in service. Express yourself as undistortedly as you can, so that you are a clear self to the other, communicating, teaching, or offering the ability to one in need of teaching. And be the friend and protector of the children, offering them the basic orientation of service to others, and the remembrance of their relationship to the Creator.

Notice what is missing from the list. Nothing about rights. Nothing about what is owed. The responsibilities all point one way, outward, toward giving. That is the vehicle, and it only moves in one direction.

The rest of the evening belongs to the craft of channeling itself, and it is worth hearing because it tells you something about how all of these sessions came to exist. One of the new channels asks about accuracy, how much of what comes through is really the Confederation and how much is the channel's own mind. And Laitos answers with unusual precision.

The channeling is always imperfect, he says. It is their intent to retain at least a quarter of the contact for the channel's own resources, so that the message finds a unique expression in each instrument while keeping the basic tenor, which is always the explication of the original Thought of love. Never be concerned, he says, if you find some of your own experience worked into the material, for it is their precise intention to use your experiences to illustrate the love and light of the Creator.

That sentence reframes the entire archive for me. These are not dictations from on high. They are collaborations, three parts received wisdom to one part human life, the eternal filtered through somebody's particular memories and vocabulary. The imperfection is not a flaw in the system. It is the system.

Thank you for listening.

title: Stepping on Water
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: stepping on water.

Imagine yourself on a ship, Hatonn says, out on open water. There are many configurations in the sky and no land in sight. The ship has a rudder and a sail, and the wind is keen and swift. And yet there is much to be done before you can set sail and move before the wind.

That is the human condition, in his telling. Each of you is on a path which, like the trackless seas, offers no apparent signpost. Daily life is a great confusion. So how do you get your bearings? How do you read the skies?

His answer is that the instruments are already aboard. There is within you, he says, the ability to create the knowledge you need to be master of your destiny. A knowledge of constellations, and the sextant to measure them. It is not hidden at any great depth. It is separated from your conscious mind only by a veil, and that veil may be penetrated by meditation, contemplation, and the desire to seek.

I love the modesty of that image. Not a revelation from the heavens, but instruments you already own, a little rusty from disuse. The sextant is in the cabin. You only have to pick it up.

And then Hatonn tells the story that gives this episode its title, from one of the holy works. A disciple sees the teacher known as Jesus walking toward his boat across the water, and calls out, if you truly be he, bid me come and walk to you. Come, says the teacher. And so the disciple steps out onto the water. As he doubted, he sank. As he asked, he walked.

Listen to what Hatonn draws from it. In meditation, he says, you find more than the tools for plotting your course. You find a feeling, a sensitivity, an openness to what your course may be. This is the function of what some call faith. It is not necessary to have rigid beliefs in order to progress. In fact, quite the opposite, for the path, like the ocean, is ever changing.

It is important, however, to reach, to seek, and to dare. To step out upon the water is not a sensible thing to do, and yet the disciple was instructed to do what he felt. Many times, Hatonn says, you will begin to sink. Many times you will clamber back into your boat and wonder if you will make error after error in your search for the truth. Nevertheless, if you seek and yet again seek to know the truth of who you are, why you came to be here, and why you make this pilgrimage in this particular way, you will find your path opening more and more fair before you.

The evening's second voice, Latwii, adds a lighter grace note. All who strive, he says, are beautiful points of balance within creation. And when asked about the body, about reincarnation, he answers with characteristic practicality. The body is merely a tool, he says, as you would use a screwdriver or a spoon to accomplish a task. We create our tools, use them, and lay them aside when the learning is done.

So tonight's teaching is really one teaching in two images. The ship, with its instruments waiting in the cabin. The disciple, with the water holding him up exactly as long as he dares to trust it. In both, the lesson is the same. The equipment for the crossing is already yours. The only thing missing has always been the step.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Lesson of Love
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the lesson of love.

There is a question the voices return to, the way the tide returns to the shore. Not because they have forgotten the answer, but because we keep forgetting the question. Why are we here? What is this life for, underneath the noise of it? Tonight, the one who calls himself Hatonn gives the simplest answer in the archive, and then spends the rest of the evening proving that simple does not mean easy.

You cannot walk your streets, he says, you cannot sit in any chair, climb any mountain, or live through any single event of your day, that does not contain one facet of the lesson of love. Everywhere it is taught. And yet, he says, so many do not seem to notice that this is the lesson they came to learn.

Many seek other things instead. The positions of power. Social eminence. The rewards of the monetary system. The recognition of others for one achievement or another. Hatonn is gentle about this. He does not call these seekings irrelevant. Inside every one of them, at the core, the lesson of love is still there, waiting. But he suggests that when you chase only the outer trappings, the lesson arrives hollow. And after a while, disappointing.

And here is the turn that makes this more than a scolding. That very disappointment, he says, is also a lesson. It points the seeker in another direction. Because deep within the being of every person on this planet there is a knowledge of why they are here. The hollow feeling is not a failure. It is a compass.

So where do you go? What can you actually do to find what rings true in the depths of your being? Look at the outer world, Hatonn says, with its jangling vibrations, its disturbed thoughts and activities, and it is clear this is not a place built for efficient seeking. But there is one sanctuary, he says, which no one can bar you from, beside which no fence can be built. It is the sanctuary of your own inner self.

This is the true tabernacle. There, none may pass. None may distract. None may say you nay or discredit you in any way. It is common, when you begin to seek, to want to share your amazement at the mysteries with others, and to find in their reactions little support, only the confusion of those who do not wish to be moved from the illusion they have arranged. But each of you has the capacity to seek within, in the sanctuary of your own silence. Within you lies a great knowing, a great peace, a path that can guide you step by step through what looks, to the outer eye, like chaos. To the inner eye, there is a purpose in every circumstance. There is a learning. There is a blessedness about all of it.

None can take this capacity from you. None can discourage you from it. You have only to meditate, to listen in silence, and to wake with the echo of the still, small voice. You may hear nothing at all. And yet, at the moment you must choose which way to go, the love you have been seeking will speak to you in the silence, and your choice will be made simple.

For love, Hatonn says, and by this he does not mean the love so confused among your peoples, is the great simplifier. As you seek, so shall you find.

He borrows a line from the teacher known as Jesus. My house shall be a house of prayer. Houses, Hatonn says, can be shaken and scattered. The winds of chance may remove everything that is physically yours in this illusion. But the one house which is always yours, through whose doors you may always pass, is the house of your own body, your mind, and your spirit. Let that house be, habitually, a house of meditation and silence and listening. For love waits within. The creation, of which love is the great ingredient, waits within.

And then, the closing note, which might be the most important sentence of the evening. Listen to our words, he says, not as if we were wise, for we are not. Not as if we were perfect, for we are not. But as if we were your brothers and sisters. For this we are.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Blessing of Seeking
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the blessing of seeking.

It is said, Hatonn remarks tonight, that one must go blindly into the darkness to discover the significance of light. There is some truth in it, he says, though the analogy has lost something in translation. Blindness and darkness are not necessary. But they are, he admits, beneficial tools.

What follows is one of the most startling passages in this stretch of the archive, because Hatonn refuses to condemn the dark. Your illusion, he explains, is maintained by light energy. Follow either polarity to its maximum, total light or total darkness, and the illusion begins to disappear. In darkness there is no light energy to maintain it. In total lightness the illusion can no longer be focused, and the light overwhelms it until only what is real stands in evidence.

It is difficult, he acknowledges, for minds trained in right and wrong, good and bad, to look with love upon those who struggle in the opposite direction from one's own. And yet, he says, even those who strive toward darkness, the absence of light, shall in their striving overcome the illusion. Then the sentence I keep returning to. It is a blessing to follow either path, for no matter what the path, the blessing exists in the seeking, and in seeking one will always find.

I want to be careful with that sentence, because it is easy to misread. Hatonn is not praising cruelty. He is saying something stranger and, I think, truer. That sincerity itself, the honest pursuit of what one takes to be real, carries a blessing regardless of the direction. The seeking is the thing. The path is almost incidental.

He encourages his own path, of course. He would have you increase the light in your lives, for such is the tool that has served his people so well. But he asks one thing of those who walk it. Learn to see the value of your brother's struggle. Appreciate your brother as one struggling for spiritual nourishment, even though his path may not be your own.

The opening of the evening belongs with this too. Hatonn speaks of the calling he feels from your peoples, their sorrow, their pain, their frustration, their desire. We feel all of it, he says, for we are as one being, and any feeling that any entity feels, we feel as well. We come however we may, in dreams, in inspirations, in intuitions, in whatever manner each mind will accept. But never, he says, may we infringe upon any entity's path back to the Creator, for we cannot learn lessons for an entity. That would be robbing the entity of experience. And upon your planet, all experience has one purpose, and that is to teach.

There is a humility in that I find moving. Beings who have journeyed the path of seeking love longer than we have, who come with greater understanding, and still they will not do our homework for us. They will sit with us in the dark, they will lend us their light, but the seeking remains ours. Perhaps that is why the blessing is in the seeking. It is the one thing nobody can do on your behalf.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Child in the Wilderness
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the child in the wilderness.

Tonight Hatonn tells a story about a child abandoned in a wilderness, a place antagonistic to his growth and survival in every way. And the strange thing is, the child thrives. Being a child, he is not aware of the hostility around him. He sees only what he wishes to see. And so, unaffected by his surroundings, he grows and learns, happily, successfully, in the middle of the wasteland.

The child, Hatonn says, is yourself. For is it not true that you came into this life, this illusion, which is unquestionably hostile to your spiritual growth, and yet here you are, growing? Your illusion entitles you to a multitude of distractions and setbacks, designed primarily to prevent your growth. And still you grow.

His counsel is the child's counsel. See through your illusion. You have within you the power of creation, so use it. Create the garden you so fervently desire to return to. For the only return to Eden you will experience, he says, is a return through developing your own ability to transform disorder and chaos into balance and beauty. And like the child in the story, see in your world and in your brothers and sisters only what you wish to see. Only beauty. Only love.

I know how that sounds. Naive, maybe even irresponsible. But Hatonn is not describing denial. He is describing a discipline, the deliberate exercise of the will to be conscious of the illusion without being immersed in it. Your schools, he says, give you problems about the mysterious appearance and disappearance of apples and oranges, and you solve them without believing the apples are real. Life's problems are like that. Resolve them, hone your skills on them, but do not drown in them.

Through a second voice he turns to the fruits of all this seeking, which is service. And here he is wonderfully sharp about the difference between real service and its counterfeit. Many among your peoples, he says, may be likened to weeds. What they offer may appear pretty, but it takes the place of good growing things and gives back neither fruit nor scent nor true beauty. Many who truly wish to serve speak again and again, believing they are aiding their fellows, and all the while judging, limiting, and divorcing themselves from them.

True service, he says, is like the rose. It not only blooms, it has a sweet scent, and when cut, it wishes only to serve by growing again. And then the sentence that holds the whole evening. The essence of service, my friends, is an effortless cheerfulness, a lack of judgment, and a willingness to serve as others would have you serve them.

Effortless cheerfulness. Not grim duty, not martyrdom, not the tight smile of someone keeping score. Sometimes, he adds, this means you cannot serve a person at all, because they are not ready. Accept this with cheerfulness, he says, and let the cheer itself be the service.

The questions afterward go deeper into why the wilderness is so wild. The distractions and obstacles, Hatonn explains, were designed before your incarnation, by your own higher self, as the lessons you wished to learn. There is a forgetting after birth, or the lessons would carry no weight. It is your task, he says, to remember. Time and again you will get the opportunity to learn the simple lesson, that there are no obstacles, that there is only the one infinite Creator, that there is only love, and that this love may be found in each part of your experience.

So the child in the wilderness was never really abandoned. He was in school. And so, if Hatonn is right, are you.

Thank you for listening.

title: Above the Clouds
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: above the clouds.

Tonight Hatonn tells a story about a mountain, and it is one of those stories that rearranges the furniture in your mind. There was once a very steep mountain, so steep that clouds formed across the face of the cliffs. Those who lived in the valley never saw the sky. Those who lived on the heights never saw the valley.

In the valley there was plenty, and jealousy, and harshness, and disharmony reigned under the clouds. On the peaks there was almost nothing. Game was scarce, little grew that could be eaten. And yet those people lived in peace. Their leaders were wise and fair. All was shared, because all had so little it had to be pooled to survive. And because they did not think of possessions, Hatonn says, harmony was handed down like an heirloom, from generation to generation.

One mountain, he says. One location. One illusion. The conditions varied, but the difference was not in the conditions. It was in the level at which the people chose to live.

And here is the turn that makes the story yours. You, yourself, he says, may choose the level at which you wish to experience the conditions of your existence. When it seems that though you have plenty, nothing is harmonious, put yourself to the task of scaling a cliff within yourself. Move beyond the cloud that hides the ever present pinnacle towering out of sight above the fog.

I love that phrase, scaling a cliff within yourself. He is not asking you to change your circumstances. He is asking you to change your altitude. At that higher level, he says, you may feel certain losses, but you will recognize them as only the needs you have discarded, seeing their illusory nature. And in their place, a freedom to be joyful that you could not see from underneath the cloud.

The cloud is part of the illusion, he says, and it is most easily penetrated by meditation. But at any moment, by an act of desire, you can mentally climb the precipice and see the stars, the points of light and love and truth invisible from below. And there is a gift waiting at the top, above most others. A sense of the honor it is to dwell with those about you. For each is a unique and beautiful part of a creation that is vast and free and resplendently lovely.

Think, he says, of someone who once honored the life within you, whether you honored it yourself at the time or not. What a gift such a person gives. The gift of recognition. For are we not all one being, one part of an infinite Creator, each part fully worthy of the utmost honor?

Latwii closes the evening with a smaller image that belongs beside the mountain. Think of the oyster, he says. When sand gets inside it, the oyster does not say to itself, ah, sand, now I will make a pearl. It tries as hard as it can to remove the sand. But the sand remains, and the pain of its remaining is borne, and somehow, something of great beauty comes to be. The sand in your existence, he says, is not there to make you swear, though you do. It is there to create the opportunity for you to make those things of beauty in your nature which shall be of eternal worth.
