Then find five minutes of true solitude, not aloneness, and climb, in attention, one small mountain. The voices say the day will meet you differently.

Thank you for listening.

title: Faith Before Proof
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: faith before proof.

One evening the voices addressed the hesitation that quietly stalls every sincere seeker. The waiting. The feeling that you cannot act, cannot serve, cannot commit, until you are certain. Until you have proof that it matters, that you are ready, that you will not get it wrong.

Listen to how they put it. Sincere service, they said, requires acting through uncertainty, not after it. The proof you are waiting for does not come before the act. It comes through the act, and often long after. To wait for certainty is to wait forever, because certainty is not on offer in this life.

This is not recklessness, and the archive is careful to say so. It is the recognition that desire, faith, and will matter more than perfect knowledge. If you desire to serve, if you have faith that love is real, if you have the will to begin, you have everything the work requires. The rest is learned in motion.

I love the dignity this restores to the uncertain servant. So many of us disqualify ourselves in advance. We tell ourselves we are not deep enough, not sure enough, not healed enough to help anyone. The voices turn this around entirely. The willingness to act without guarantees is not a deficiency. It is the qualification.

Think of it as the difference between studying swimming and getting wet. The study has its place. But at some point the water is the teacher, and the water does not offer certainty, only buoyancy for those who trust it enough to push off. Every servant the archive honors learned the stroke by swimming.

And there is a tenderness here worth naming. The voices know how frightening it is to act without proof. They do not mock the hesitation. They simply point out its cost. While you wait for the sign, the need goes unmet. While you polish your readiness, the moment passes. Faith, they suggest, is not the absence of fear. It is the decision to move with the fear.

Tonight's practice is one act of service performed before you feel ready. Small is fine. Unwitnessed is fine. Uncertain is the point. Desire it, will it, do it, and let the proof arrive later, in its own time. The archive promises it will arrive. It always does, for those who move.

Thank you for listening.

title: Glory in the Walking
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: glory in the walking.

One evening the voices said something that relieves a very modern ache. The glory of the path, they said, is not in its landmarks. Not in the summits reached, the milestones passed, the moments you could photograph and point to. The glory is in the undertaking itself. In the fact that you set out at all.

Listen to how they put it. We are obsessed with arrival. We treat the stretches between the landmarks as empty, as waiting, as the boring parts to be endured on the way to the real thing. The archive says the stretches are the real thing. The long, unremarkable miles are where the walking actually happens.

And those miles have their own teaching. Attentive balance, the voices called it. The steady, unglamorous art of staying upright over time. Anyone can be radiant at a summit. The path asks something harder. Can you be present on a Tuesday? Can you keep your footing when nothing is happening? Can you walk well when there is nothing to show for it?

I love how this reframes an ordinary life. Most of your days will not be landmarks. Most of your efforts will not be visible. If glory lives only at the milestones, then most of life is gloryless, and that cannot be right. The voices insist it is not right. The undertaking is the glory. The walking is the arrival, happening continuously.

There is a quiet courage in this teaching. It asks you to value what no one will praise. The faithful showing up. The patient continuing. The choice, made again each morning, to stay on the path when the path offers no drama. This is not resignation. It is a deeper ambition, the ambition to walk well rather than to arrive loudly.

So the practice tonight is a revaluation. Look at one long, unremarkable stretch of your own life, the part you have been treating as filler between important events, and try the archive's version. What if this is not the waiting? What if this is the thing itself? Walk it tomorrow with attention, with balance, and see whether the glory was hiding in the walking all along.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Manna of the Heart
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the manna of the heart.

One evening Hatonn reached for an old word to describe a present abundance. Manna, he called it. The provision that arrives, unearned and sufficient, for the journey. And then he asked the question that carries the whole evening. What do you desire? Because the manna, he said, takes the shape of the desire.

Listen to how he put it. There is physical manna, the bread of the body, the shelter and the sustenance. There is the manna of the heart, and here his voice deepened. You may choose to love, he said. This is the manna of the heart. Beyond this blessing there is no provision, for this blessing is an end in itself. I love that line. Love is not the means to the provision. Love is the provision.

And there is the manna of the spirit, which he named as discrimination. The clear sight to know what serves and what does not. He added a sharp edge to it. It is to be used against yourself, he said, against your own illusions and evasions, not as a weapon against others. Discernment turned outward becomes judgment. Turned inward, it becomes freedom.

Then came the image I have never shaken. The unwashed dish. The unraked leaf. See the insignificant and petty detail of living, he said, and go about that task knowing for a moment that you are the Creator, and that all that you see is the Creator. Look at the beauty of the shining plate, the sunlit window, the pleasant smell of cleanliness.

This is the whole teaching in a single chore. The ordinary task, performed with the knowledge of who is performing it, becomes holy ground. You do not need a temple. You need a dish, and attention, and the willingness to see what is actually there.

Latwii closed the evening with a question for the strivers. Are the trees without value, they asked, because they only stand? Are the rivers without value, because they only flow? Is the soil without value, because it does not move of its own accord? Being, they said, is not the absence of doing. The tree nourishes by being a tree. You are allowed to nourish by being you.

So tonight's practice is a choosing. Name your desire. Physical manna, the manna of the heart, the manna of the spirit. Then take up one small task, a dish, a leaf, an ordinary thing, and do it as the Creator doing it. The voices say your path shall be made plain. Not easy. Plain. And that is enough.

Thank you for listening.

title: A Quality Not a Quantity
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: a quality not a quantity.

One evening Latwii asked the group a question that still disarms me. How shall you share? You who have learned so much, who want so badly to give, what exactly do you have to offer? And the answer they gave turns our usual accounting upside down. What you have to share, they said, is a quality, not a quantity.

Listen to how they put it. They borrowed the old image of the yeast, the tiny bit of leaven that transforms the whole loaf. It was not a great quantity, they said. It was a very small amount of the proper quality. You cannot do a great deal of infinite work or a small amount of infinite work. You do infinite work. The size was never the point. The substance was.

And here is the part that makes it personal. Each of you, they said, has a totally unique radiance. Not equal gifts. Not interchangeable roles. Your gift, whatever it is, is the quality you have to give. The world does not need another copy of someone else's light. It needs the particular frequency that only you emit.

Then they gave the practice, and it takes less than a second. Before you share, allow a silent opening within. A prayer so simple it barely counts as words. Not my will, but my will as You, O Creator, be done. Not the little self, but the great Self. Open me. Use me. I love that prayer because it is not asking for strength. It is asking to get out of the way.

That phrase was theirs too. Perhaps the most difficult thing for a pilgrim, they said, is to discover how to get out of the way of that great and abiding flame of love. Let it burn through you, never from you. Let your light shine so that the kingdom is revealed, not you. The servant's glory is to disappear into the service.

Hatonn opened that same evening with an image for all of this. Think of yourself as a cloud, he said, floating on gentle breezes, rained on and made fresh again, at peace with its environment. When you are scurrying and at odds with everything, remember the cloud. Harmony with your troubles will not solve them, but it will change your relationship to them, and that changes everything.

So the practice tonight is the fraction of a second. Before the next thing you do for someone, pause. Open. Pray the small prayer. Exchange quantity for quality, hurry for radiance, the little self for the great Self. The voices say the flame is already burning. Your only job is to stop blocking the light.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Glad Pilgrimage
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the glad pilgrimage.

Some evenings in the archive are not about a single teaching. They are about practice. This is one of those evenings, an autumn night on which Hatonn moves from instrument to instrument, tuning voices the way you would tune strings, a few words here, a few words there. And in the middle of the exercise, another voice arrives. Maitreya, who speaks not to the beginners but to the ones who have been walking a while and are starting to wonder whether they have arrived.

Hatonn begins gently, with patience. Each of you worries about your progress on the spiritual path, he says, and let me assure you that you are making progress. You do not watch a small baby growing moment by moment, but over time the growth is obvious. Think back, he says, and you will recall experiences and dreams that fit together and guided you. So do not be impatient. Be joyful. Be cheerful. Continue day by day. I love that image, the baby you cannot see growing. It asks nothing of you except to keep going and to trust that the going is the growing.

Another voice through another instrument picks up the thread. When the present seems too intense, stand apart from yourself. You will see the intensity is not necessary. Both the good and the bad will pass. You need the positive and the negative for proper perspective. And then, the line I keep returning to: rejoice in your problems. Overcoming them can give you great joy, more joy than if you never had them. Treat your trouble as something that will pass and something very educational. Even great failure, Hatonn says, makes it possible to understand great philosophies.

And then Maitreya, with the evening's hardest sentence. There is a call, Maitreya says, to take up your pilgrimage, take the next step, and do not seek comfort. Because you are spiritual, seek only to seek. Joyful the seeking may be. Loving it may be. But comfortable, never, not if you keep moving. Maitreya speaks as one of those who offered themselves as martyrs, and so cannot blush at discomfort. The suggestion is not the life of the martyr. It is simpler and stranger: never, for one moment, let the feeling of a plateau comfort you. The thing left undone, Maitreya says, no matter what you do to follow the light, shall always be greater. And as you love, so shall you be given the next lesson, and the next, and the next.

Listen to how they put the ending. As you seek more and more, so shall more and more of the creation move with you, seek with you, blend with you, feel with you, and be transformed with you. The pilgrimage is glad, then, not because the road is easy, but because you never walk it alone. The creation itself walks it with you, in step, as fast as you are willing to go.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Source Within
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the source within.

There is an evening in the archive that begins with laughter and ends in silence, and both are doing the same work. Hatonn speaks first of laughter, which he calls next to love. Nothing lightens your burden like laughter and humor. It is similar to sunshine. If you can laugh about yourself and your situation, you will not become so serious that you could even be depressed. Laughter, he says, is as good as vitamins. It tunes and tones up your whole system. I love the plainness of that. Not a theory of joy. A practice of it.

And then Hatonn, through another voice, tells a story. There was once a young man who wished to know the truth, and of one thing he was sure: truth is love and love is truth. So he asked a friend, what is love? And the friend asked, how much of it do you wish to have? All of it, said the young man. Come with me Saturday night, said the friend, and I will see that you get some of it. Oh no, said the young man, I do not think that is what I am seeking. Do you not like pleasure? Why, yes, said the young man, but I seek something else.

He asks another friend, who says love is relationships, personal communication, understanding what the other has in mind and whether what you each need will work out. There is much in what you say, the young man answers, but I shall continue seeking. A third friend says love is the love of ideas that move nations, great thoughts for which you might die. The young man thinks long and hard, for he has been inspired by speeches, and has seen the failure of ideals lead to no end of human error. But his heart is not satisfied. A fourth friend says love is laying down your life for others, casting all your gifts upon the waters and never looking back. Thrilled, the young man begins casting his love upon the waters, waters that often seem muddy, aiding his fellow man even when his fellow man does not seem to want aiding. Finally he says to himself, I think I am looking for more.

Running out of friends, he seeks a wise stranger, a spiritual man much revered by seekers. Sir, he says, I have been searching to find the nature of love, for only in love will I discover the truth. And the sage says, anything that you say with feeling is lovely. Love is communication, with yourself, with the Creator, with all those about you. Aha, says the young man, who by this time is not so young, I have been giving love but I have not been speaking. And so he begins loving and communicating. Many are his friends and much is he beloved. And yet. And yet. He has not found the truth.

Having no one left to turn to, he sits in silence and asks himself, what is love? It is not in the body. It is not in my relationships. It is not in society. It is not in loving everyone the same. It is not in communicating. What is the heart? Where have I missed the truth? And a golden sun bursts within the darkness of his inner mind, and love rains down upon him, not from above, but from within. And as he opens his eyes, that golden sun gleams in his heart, and he knows the world as himself, light and shadow both. Much he forgives. Much he gives. But always, he finds the source within.

And that, Hatonn says, is the whole of the seeking. Each of you is seeking love. But what answer you receive depends on what question you ask. Seek, and seek again and again, for with each seeking you refine the question, and with each refinement you learn more of the truth. A truth that does not lie in the illusion except when seen with eyes that shine with the light of the inner sun. Without that light, you seek that which is outward in vain.

The evening closes with one more practical note, and it is pure Hatonn. Your people have many rules against touching, many taboos, and yet touch is one way you communicate with your other self, a very healing thing. People who hug one another with genuine feeling can usually adjust to their differences. Try, he says, to hug someone each day. Let the people around you know that you are with them. The beauty of living will be enhanced by the number of people you hug. Laughter, hugs, the golden sun within. The teaching is simple. The source was never anywhere else.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Mark Is Yourself
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the mark is yourself.

This is an evening of stories, and the first one is told in pieces, passed from instrument to instrument like a torch, each voice carrying it a little way and then handing it on. Hatonn begins it. There once was a young prince who strode out one day with a quiver full of arrows and a strong bow. It was the mellow youth's wish to practice his marksmanship until he could hit the mark. He set out in the bright light of morning, the dew still on the grass, the air full of promise, vague and unspoken, yet very real.

Walking through the forest, the prince stumbles on a small open place, and there before his wondering eyes arises a beautiful, bright entity that speaks of love to him. He is astounded. His first thought is to run, for this entity speaks words not commonly spoken, and he is a prince and must not be influenced. But he does not run. He stays, not knowing exactly why, and listens, and feels all that is spoken. The fair entity shares many truths with him, unfolding mysteries that have puzzled the young man, much as a mentor would. At the end of their long conversation the prince asks, who might you be? How is it that you know all these wondrous things? And the fair entity answers: surely all these things you have learned this day you had inside known all along. I have taught you nothing you were not capable of learning yourself. And then the entity turns the question back upon the prince. Since you have in truth known these seeming secrets, I ask you, who am I? For this too you know.

The prince looks into the eyes of the fair one, and in that locked stare seems almost to look within the other soul. And what he sees when he looks within is himself.

The young prince had begun that day hoping to learn a skill with bow and arrow, and had found the mark he sought was himself. And so, Hatonn says, it is with each seeker. You travel the path of your seeking using the implements of your choice to penetrate the mystery of your being. It may seem the mystery would need a special tool, and only that tool would do. But the outer manifestation is meaningless. The desire comes from within your being. To seek the truth is all that counts. You may use whatever tools are at your disposal, for each will find the catalyst most appropriate for its personal journey. To fire the self with the desire to know the truth of what it is you seek, and who indeed you are as you seek, that is the ingredient that makes any manifestation appropriate.

Later in the evening Latwii takes up a harder question, one about a weapon, a gun in a soldier's hand, and whether the one who made the weapon bears the same responsibility as the one who fires it. And Latwii answers not with judgment but with a question about motivation. Look, they say, not at the action within the frame of good and evil, but at the why. Does the entity wish in the action to be of service to another, or to be of service to the self? Or is it unaware that either choice exists? The maker of the weapon may be committed to defending what it sees as truth and beauty within its country, and the motivation is service to others, though the taking of life still costs. Or the maker may wish to serve the self, and polarize in that direction. Or the maker may be unaware, and drift. I find this answer quietly radical. It refuses the easy verdict. It asks instead: what did you mean by it?

The prince and the weapon-maker. One sought a target and found himself. The other built a thing and is asked to look at the hands that built it. Both evenings end in the same place. The mark is yourself. The meaning is yourself. Aim there first.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Great Mirror Within
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the great mirror within.

Hatonn begins this evening with mirrors. You speak of mirrors with the word reflection, he says, and it is the nature of the mirror to show you your illusion. Each of you is to every other person a mirror. You see in the behavior of your family those characteristics you do not like within yourself, and so you call them faults. The mirror does not lie, but it shows you the illusion, the appearance of the self. If you cannot bear to be illusional before the mirror, you may be able to bear being illusional before yourself. And that, he says, is the great advantage of the family, and the great advantage of friendship.

Listen to how he develops it. Each of you lives within a family as well as your own skin. Home is not just a place. It is a group of entities within which you may, in total confidence and in total support, be able to work upon your transformation. In the family you are etched in pain. The people closest to you etch you, and you etch them, and it is there, where you are truly yourself, that you begin the transformation of consciousness. Hatonn gives home a definition I keep in my pocket. Home is where, when you have to go there, they have to let you in. Within the family there is a mutual need, and each may be sure that the others will, however imperfectly, attempt to work with each other in the face of difficult catalyst. What you do not like about your family is not important. The advantage of family is that you may be the imperfect self and be accepted, and may watch the growth of others within the same imperfect self.

Then comes the turn. After the mirrors of other people, there is the great mirror, which is within yourself. In meditation, Hatonn says, you may seek the point of tabernacle with the infinite One, and if you do so you will find that mirror blazing, clear, and true. And this is the challenge he lays down. Try to see yourself as the saints would see you. As a clear, perfect instrument, through which light may pour through all of your energies. Each of you has a beautiful and complex inner self, a self which is an expression of love, unbound by the illusion of the world. You have only to reflect it outward, and to aid others in knowing their own beauty.

There is a passage in the middle of the evening about the changing of seasons, and I want to share it because it carries the whole teaching. Think of the great seasons of your own experience, Hatonn says, and of the many small deaths within the life that you lead. Think of the butterfly, which in the cocoon does not look like much. Many times in the life of the seeker there are periods of apparent death and rest, periods when you are preparing to fly but do not know it. And flowers too are nurtured, that they may flower. There are times of blossoming within each entity's growth. If you are going through a dark period, know that you are in the season of preparation, and let it happen. Do not waste energy grieving that you are not blossoming. It is your season.

Latwii, later, is asked about death, and about a friend who passed, and answers with a gentleness worth preserving. Death, they say, is the illusion ending, but it is a very real and emotional experience. Each entity has its own answer to what death means. It is a birth into a wider life. And to the friend who grieves a husband: let the grieving proceed, and let it be natural, and let it express love. Hatonn has said the one commandment, if there were one, is love your neighbor as yourself. Let the dead be given love, they say, and let the living give love to each other, for the living need it so.

And so the evening ends where it began. The mirrors of family show you your illusion. The great mirror within shows you your light. You do not need to smash the first mirror. You only need to look into the second, and then begin each day as if you were a newborn soul, the universe and everything within it completely, utterly fresh. Begin, and let the light pour through.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Little Things
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the little things.

There is a kind of evening in the archive that does not reach for the heavens. It reaches for the table in front of you. Hatonn speaks tonight about little things. And small things, he says, can be so very, very important. A smile. A handshake. A compliment. A cup of cold water in my name, if you cannot do more. These are the small and wonderful things that make one human being care for another. Hatonn is blunt about why. You look for the large, the dramatic, the heroic gesture, and you miss the field where service actually grows. For the one who serves on the physical plane in small and everyday ways, the harvest comes in small and everyday joys. And they are just as precious as any grander crop.

Listen to how they describe the mechanics of seeking, because this is one of the finest passages on the subject anywhere in the archive. When you seek, you act like a magnet among iron filings. You draw to you all those things which will help you to seek, the books you need, the people you need, the inspiration you need. As you think, so your seeking draws to itself those things which will aid it. You cannot fail to be aided in your seeking, for it is the law. And here is the line that rings like a bell: there are no accidents. It is your doing that you are here this evening. That statement may be applied to any happening within your experience. Each thing that happens to you happens for you to learn from, and to aid you in your seeking. Seek, therefore, in all ways, at all times, and at all levels.

But Hatonn will not let service become a performance. If you want to love and serve your fellow man, you must first find the center of your being. Open the door within. There you will find a never-ending source of love, and by opening that door the love will flow through you. That is the service you do for others when you meditate. You allow a channel to be opened so that love may flow through you to others. The little things, the cup of cold water, are the outer sign of an inner door that is open.

Later Latwii is asked a question about a physical ailment, and I want to be careful here, because the archive sometimes speaks of the body in ways that sound like medicine and are not. Latwii offers a spiritual picture: that the body is a creature of the mind, and that in illness we may see the mind's rejection of some portion of experience. Treat this, if you like, as their way of seeing, a lens for reflection, not a medical claim. What interests me for tonight's theme is the spirit underneath it: that we are not strangers inside our own houses, and that attention, given honestly, is itself a kind of service.

The evening closes with Nona, who does not lecture at all, but sings. And I cannot sing it to you, so I will tell you what the song does. It bids the listener rest, be still, feel the love around you, know that you are one with all things. After an evening of little things, the song is the smallest and largest thing of all. A lullaby for a seeker. Rest in my love, it says, and know that you are mine.

So tonight, the practice is small enough to hold. One smile. One compliment that costs you nothing. One cup of cold water, given in the name of love. The archive promises nothing dramatic will happen. Only that the field where you plant it will be your own life, and the harvest will be joy, small and everyday, and precious beyond measure.

Thank you for listening.

title: Attention Is Possession
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: attention is possession.

Hatonn opens this evening with a sentence that reorders your whole sense of ownership. The only things that you really own, he says, are the things to which you give your attention. Give your attention to things of the world, things that glitter and are gone, and you own glitter. Give your attention to love, and you own love. I love the plain economy of that. Your life is not measured by what is in your hands. It is measured by what is in your mind when your mind is quiet.

And so, Hatonn says, choose carefully, for you will possess what you attend to. If you give your attention to criticism and judgment of your fellow beings, then you own criticism and judgment, and they will own you. If you give your attention to praise and thanksgiving, you own praise and thanksgiving. Look at the daffodils, he says, and you own the yellow. Look at the trees in the spring and you own the green fire of new leaves. The world is always offering itself to be owned in this way. The only question is where you look.

Then comes the companion teaching, and it is the heart of the evening. Be who you are, Hatonn says, but be it clearly and lucidly. Do not try to be someone else. Do not perform goodness. The flower does not perform the blossom. The petals open because that is what petals do. And in the same way, your work is not to manufacture a self that deserves love. It is to be the self you already are, so clearly that love can find its way through. Love the Creator, he says, and the Creator that is you. For the Creator is not somewhere else. The Creator is the one looking out through your eyes, waiting for you to notice.

Later, through Latwii, the evening turns practical, and the questions are the ones seekers always ask. How do I help the ones I love who are suffering? Is it right to send them light without their asking? And Latwii answers with a principle worth memorizing. The Law of Confusion, the law of free will, permits you always to send love and light. You may always send love. What you may not do is attempt to control the outcome, to decide for another what healing should look like. Send the love, they say, and release the result. That is service. That is also the clearest test of whether your attention has become possession in the wrong sense. If you are gripping, you do not own love. Love owns you, and it is pulling your hands open.

I want to linger on that image, because it gathers the whole evening into one gesture. The open hand. The open petal. The attention that rests on a thing without grabbing it. To own by attention is not to hoard. It is to dwell with. You become what you behold, and what you behold, in the end, becomes you.

So tonight, an experiment, small enough to try before sleep. Notice what you have been attending to today. The headlines, the grievance, the glitter. And then choose, once, deliberately, to rest your attention on something you wish to own. The yellow of a flower. The green fire of a leaf. The face of someone you love. Hold it there gently. And be, clearly and lucidly, who you are.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Eye of the Storm
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the eye of the storm.

Peace is one of those words everyone uses and almost no one means the same thing by. Hatonn spends this evening taking the word apart and putting it back together. Peace, he says, is not merely the absence of conflict. It is not a truce. It is not the quiet after the argument. Peace is the presence of something, and that something is alive. I want you to sit with that sentence, because it changes the whole search. If peace were only the absence of noise, you would have to flee the world to find it. If peace is a presence, you can carry it into the noise.

Hatonn reaches for an image. Think of a great ring, he says, or a spiral turning, and at its center, a stillness. The storm can rage around the edges of your life. The winds can howl. The demands can pile up. But there is a point within you that does not move, and that point is not empty. It is full. It is the presence of the Creator within the created, the anchor and the eye of the storm at once. Your work in meditation, and in the small meditations of the day, is not to stop the storm. It is to find the eye, to settle there, and to let the stillness at the center teach the storm at the edges what it is for.

And then the practical turn, because Hatonn always brings it back to the hands. The highest form of peace, he says, is love that does not demand, love that does not control, love that simply is. You cannot manufacture peace in another person. You can only be peace, and let the being of it do the work. To love without demanding is to give the other person the same eye of the storm you have found in yourself: a place where they are not required to be different in order to be loved.

I need to pause here and speak gently about something that comes up in the evening's questions. Someone asks about a friend who is depressed, who has spoken of wanting to end his life. The archive answers in its own way, with compassion and with the suggestion that love, offered steadily, matters. I want to add, in my own voice, what no archive can say for me. If you are the one carrying that darkness, or if someone you love is, please do not carry it alone. Reach out to someone you trust, a friend, a counselor, a crisis line in your country. You deserve support that is present and human and now. The teaching of the evening still holds. Peace is a presence. But sometimes the way we find that presence is through the hand of another person, extended in the dark.

The evening also holds a smaller, brighter thread. Someone asks whether the chair used in meditation can hold energy, and Latwii answers yes, in their way, that objects can be charged by the love poured into them. Take it as their picture of how devotion soaks into the things we touch. Your cushion, your corner, your chair. The places where you return to the still point become still themselves.

So tonight, do not try to stop your storm. Find its eye. Sit down, breathe, and feel for the point within you that is not moving. It is not empty. It is alive. It is the presence you have been calling peace. Rest there a while. And when you rise, carry it with you, undemanding, into the weather of your life.

Thank you for listening.

title: Moss Upon the Rock
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: moss upon the rock.

Hatonn tells a story tonight, and it is one of the strangest and most tender in the whole archive. There was once a pilgrim, weary and footsore, who had walked a long, long way, and who came at last to a great rock, smooth and bare, with no crack for a seed and no soil for a root. And the pilgrim sat down upon the rock in despair, for the journey had been hard and the destination was nowhere in sight. And as the pilgrim sat, something impossible happened. Upon the bare stone, in a place where nothing could grow, there began to grow moss, soft and green, impossibly alive, spreading across the hardness as if the rock itself had decided to be kind.

The pilgrim stared. And Hatonn says the moss is the teaching. You are the rock. Hard, defended, convinced that nothing can grow on you, that your heart is too smooth and too long exposed to the weather for anything green to take hold. And yet the moss grows. The soft thing finds the hard thing, and the hard thing, without doing anything at all, becomes a garden. All that was required of the rock was to be there, and to stop insisting on its own barrenness. Surrender, Hatonn says. Not effort. Not self-improvement. Surrender. Let the green thing do what the green thing knows how to do.

Listen to how they put the practice. In your meditation, do not try to force the growth. Do not hammer at the stone of yourself. Sit, as the pilgrim sat. Be still, as the rock was still. And allow. The love that moves through the universe is not waiting for you to become worthy of it. It is already growing on you, in the cracks you cannot see, in the places you have given up on. Your only work is to notice, and to stop scraping it away.

The evening then turns, as these evenings do, to the senses, and Hatonn gives one of his most joyful passages. Glory in your senses, he says. See the beautiful colors. Hear the beautiful sounds. Taste, smell, feel. The creation is not a waiting room. It is a banquet. Your eyes were made to feast. Your ears were made to be filled. And cheerfulness, he says, is not a mood but a discipline, a way of meeting the creation that invites the creation to meet you back. The one who glories in the senses, who laughs easily and looks long at beautiful things, is doing spiritual work as real as any meditation.

I keep thinking about the pilgrim and the rock together with that feast of the senses. The rock thought it was dead, and the moss proved it wrong. The pilgrim thought the journey had failed, and the green proved otherwise. How many of your own barren places are only waiting for you to sit down, be still, and let something soft do its work? You do not have to become the garden. You only have to stop insisting you are only stone.

So tonight, find your rock. Sit on it. Breathe. And look closely, very closely, at the smooth hard places in your life, the griefs you have decided will never soften, the habits you have decided will never change. Somewhere on that stone, something green is already growing. Your work is not to make it grow. Your work is to let it.

Thank you for listening.

title: Trust Is a Bridge
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: trust is a bridge.

Trust is the theme of this evening, and Latwii begins with an image that does all the work. Trust is a bridge, they say. It spans the gap between one self and another, and it can only be crossed in one direction at a time, by the one who chooses to cross. You cannot build half a bridge and demand the other person finish it. You cannot cross it for them. Trust is extended. It is offered. And here is the hard part: it must be given freely, without a price, without a contract, without the quiet demand that it be returned in kind. The moment you attach a condition to it, it stops being trust and becomes a bargain.

Listen to how they put it, because the phrasing matters. Trust is an unconditional form of love. Not a reward for good behavior. Not a wage paid for reliability. A form of love. And like all love, it cannot be forced. It can only be given, and then left alone to do its work. If you give it and hover over it, checking whether it is working, you have taken it back. The bridge stands, or it does not, and your hovering does not make it stand.

The evening's questions press on this from every side, and the answers keep returning to the same center. Someone asks about altruism, about the difference between serving others and serving the self, and Latwii answers that the difference is not in the act but in the intention. Two people can do the identical thing, and one is service to others and the other is service to the self, and the difference is invisible to everyone except the one who acts. Even the mother who cares for herself, rests, eats, restores her own strength, may be serving her child in the serving of herself, if the intention is love. The act does not decide. The heart decides.

Someone else asks about the Law of Confusion, the principle of free will that runs through the whole archive, and Latwii gives the clearest short definition I have found. It is the law that says each entity must be allowed its own choices, its own mistakes, its own pace. You may offer. You may not compel. And this is where trust and free will meet. To trust someone is to honor their free will. To try to control them, even for their own good, is to withdraw the trust. The bridge and the law are the same structure, seen from two sides.

There is humor in the evening too, and I want to keep it, because it belongs to the teaching. When the contact grows thin and someone asks whether Latwii is still there, they answer, with unmistakable cheer, that they are still kicking. It is a small moment, but it tells you something about trust as these voices understand it. It is not solemn. It is not fragile. It is sturdy enough to laugh.

So tonight, think of the bridges in your life. The ones you have built toward others. The ones others have built toward you. And ask the honest question. Is there a price on my bridge? A toll, a contract, a quiet demand for return? If there is, consider what it would feel like to lift it. To give the trust freely, and then to step back, and let the other person cross in their own time, or not. That stepping back is not indifference. It is the highest form of the bridge. It says: I trust you to be who you are, and I will be here, on my side, regardless.

Thank you for listening.

title: Love the Living
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: love the living.

This evening was recorded far from home, in Louisville, and it carries the warmth of guests being welcomed. Hatonn speaks about memory, and about the dead, and the teaching is one I have never forgotten. When someone you love dies, he says, you begin to polish the memory. The rough edges fall away. The difficult mornings, the sharp words, the ordinary frictions, all of it softens, until the one you remember is not quite the one who lived. And that is natural. But do not let the polished memory become the only place you love people. Love the living, Hatonn says. Love them while they are still here, still rough, still unfinished, still changing.

Listen to how they put it, because the tenderness in it is the whole point. The people around you are like trees in their seasons. Sometimes they are in leaf, sometimes they are bare. You would not love only the memory of the summer tree and resent the winter one. Love the tree in every season. And the people you love are the same. Do not wait until they are gone to give them the love you are saving up. Give it now, while the giving can be received, while the rough edges are still there to be loved.

The evening's questions turn to healing, and Latwii offers a picture that belongs with tonight's theme. Healing, they say, occurs when the entity realizes that it is whole. Not when the body is repaired, not when the symptoms leave, but when the one who suffers recognizes the wholeness that was never lost. Treat this as their way of seeing, a lens and not a medical claim. What moves me is the direction of it. Healing is not something done to you. It is something you remember. You were never broken in the way you feared.

And then Hatonn gives the evening its widest sentence. Everything is a miracle, he says. Not the rare things. Not the visions and the healings. Everything. The thousandth sunrise is as miraculous as the first. The ordinary cup of water, the ordinary breath, the ordinary face across the table. The only reason you do not see it is that you have seen it before, and familiarity has covered the miracle like dust. Wipe the dust. Look again. The world has not become less miraculous. You have only become less astonished.

I keep turning these three teachings over together, because they are really one teaching. Love the living, not only the memory. Know yourself as whole, not only as wounded. See the ordinary as miraculous, not only the extraordinary. In each case the movement is the same. Stop postponing. Stop polishing. Stop waiting for the special occasion, the perfected person, the dramatic sign. The love is here. The wholeness is here. The miracle is here, in the thousandth ordinary morning, asking only to be noticed.

So tonight, before you sleep, think of one living person you have been saving your love for, saving it for the right moment, the resolved argument, the better season. And give some of it now, unfinished, unpolished, while they can still receive it. That is the whole practice. Love the living. The dead are loved already. The living are waiting.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Loving Part of You
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the loving part of you.

It is mid-December, and the evening begins where the season asks it to begin. Hatonn speaks of the Christmas story, not as history but as an inner event. The light, he says, is always at the end of the path. You walk through the darkness of your days, through the confusion and the weariness, and the light does not move. It waits. And the waiting is the teaching. The light is not earned by the walking. The walking only brings you to where the light has been all along.

And then, through Latwii, the evening turns to one of the most tender questions ever asked in the archive. Someone describes being at a hospital bed, watching a loved one near death, and seeing, with eyes open, a form of light standing beside the bed. What was it, they ask. And Latwii answers with a gentleness I want to preserve exactly. It was, they say, the loving part of that entity, the part that is always with you, made visible. Not a stranger. Not a visitor from elsewhere. The loving part of the one you love, which does not leave, which is not bound by the failing of the body, which stands beside the bed because love stands beside the bed.

I want to speak carefully here, in my own voice. The archive offers this as its way of seeing, and I offer it to you as comfort, not as a claim about what happens at every bedside. But there is something in it that rings true regardless. That those we love are larger than the bodies we watch failing. That the love between you is not a product of the body and does not end with it. That when you sit beside someone who is dying, you are not sitting beside an ending. You are sitting beside a love that is too large for the room.

Latwii is asked, too, what happens when we die, and answers simply. It is a birth, they say, into a wider life. Each entity has its own experience of it, its own pace, its own greeting. And the one who has lived in love finds the wider life to be more of what was already true. There is no sudden transformation into something unrecognizable. There is only the continuing of the love, with fewer walls.

The evening keeps returning to the season. The lights on the trees, the songs, the gatherings. Hatonn does not dismiss any of it. He only asks that you see through it to what it points to. Every light you hang is a reminder of the light at the end of the path. Every song about peace is a rehearsal for the peace you carry within. The season is not a distraction from the seeking. At its best, it is the seeking, dressed in colors, singing.

So tonight, in this dark part of the year, remember the figure beside the bed. The loving part, always with you. Whether you are the one sitting vigil or the one being watched over, whether your grief is fresh or old, the love has not gone where you cannot follow. It is beside you now, as it was then. Reach out your hand. It is already holding yours.

Thank you for listening.

title: Service Without Strings
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: service without strings.

This evening, recorded in Dayton a few days before Christmas, circles a question that every sincere servant eventually asks. What do I do when my service is not wanted? When I offer and offer, and the offering lands like a weight? Latwii takes the question seriously, and the answer is one of the most practical in the archive.

There is, they say, such a thing as service that becomes a burden to the one served. The server serves and serves, pouring out energy, attention, advice, help, and the one receiving begins to feel not helped but crowded, not loved but managed. And Latwii names the cause without flinching. The server has forgotten the free will of the other. True service, they say, always honors the other's right to choose, to refuse, to be left alone. The moment your helping overrides their choosing, it has stopped being service. It has become control wearing the costume of love.

Listen to how they put the remedy, because it is beautifully concrete. Before you serve, sense whether the door is open. Every person has a door, and the door is sometimes open and sometimes closed, and it is not your work to break it down. If the door is open, enter gently, and give what is asked. If the door is closed, wait. Tend your own garden. Keep your own lamp lit. The waiting is not failure. It is respect. And often, they say, the one who waits in patience finds the door opening on its own, in its own season, when the forcing would only have driven it shut.

The evening draws the circle wider. Do not neglect yourself in the serving, Latwii says. The server who is depleted, who gives from emptiness, begins to serve from need rather than from fullness, and need always attaches strings. Rest is not selfishness. It is maintenance of the instrument. You cannot pour from a cup you have not allowed to be filled.

There are smaller threads in the evening worth keeping. Someone asks about tradition, about the old forms and rituals, and Latwii answers that tradition is a vessel. It can carry the living water, or it can be carried around empty, polished and admired. Honor the vessel, they say, but do not mistake it for the water. And someone asks about the blending of beliefs at Christmas, the old stories and the new, and the answer is the same. Take what feeds the love. Leave what does not. The season is large enough for all of it.

I keep returning to the image of the door. How much of our exhaustion as helpers comes from pushing on doors that are closed? How much of our resentment comes from service that was never asked for? The teaching tonight is not to serve less. It is to serve cleanly. Offer, and do not grasp. Give, and do not manage. Love, and leave the other person free to receive it or not. That is service without strings. And it is the only kind that does not, in the end, become a burden to the giver or the given.

So tonight, think of one place where you have been pushing. One person you have been trying to help who has not asked. And practice the harder discipline. Step back. Tend your own lamp. Wait with love. The door you stop pushing may open on its own, and when it does, you will be rested, and ready, and your hands will be empty enough to truly give.

Thank you for listening.

title: On Christmas Day
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: on christmas day.

It is Christmas Day, and the circle gathers anyway. There is something quietly defiant about that, and quietly faithful. The world is unwrapping its presents, and a small group sits down to listen. Hatonn honors the day by going behind it, to what the day is about.

There is, Hatonn says, one original Thought. Before the tinsel, before the carols, before the story in the manger, before everything, there is a single Thought, and that Thought is love. And the teaching of the day is that this Thought can be found wherever you look for it. In the face across the table. In the stranger at the door. In the quiet of your own heart, when the noise of the celebration dies down. The original Thought is not far away. It is the closest thing there is. You are looking for it with the very eyes it gave you.

Listen to how they put the practice. Strip away the veneer, Hatonn says. The veneer is everything you have laid over the simple thing: the obligations, the performances, the anxieties about getting it right. Underneath the veneer, the day is simple. Love was born. Love is here. Love is you, when you let it be. And the stripping is not done once. It is done every day, every hour, every time you notice the veneer has grown back.

Someone asks about the words we speak, the intentions of the lips, and Hatonn answers that the lips are servants. They can serve the heart or they can serve the habit. Speak, he says, from the place where the original Thought lives, and your words will carry it, even when they are ordinary words, even when they are only hello, or thank you, or I am glad you are here. The holiness is not in the vocabulary. It is in the source.

The evening holds a question about beginning a church, about gathering people in the name of the teaching, and I want to include the answer because it is so characteristic. Do not build an organization, Hatonn says, in effect. Build a seeking. If you must gather, gather to seek together, and let the seeking be the structure. The moment the form becomes more important than the love, the veneer has won. Keep it simple. Keep it about the Thought.

It is a short evening, as Christmas evenings should be. There is dinner waiting. There are people to hold. But the teaching fits the day exactly. Behind every light on every tree, behind every song, behind every outstretched hand, there is one original Thought, and it is thinking itself in you, right now. You do not need to go anywhere to find it. You only need to strip away the veneer, and look, and recognize your own face in the light.

Merry Christmas, says the archive, in its own way. The Thought is born again, in you, today. Let it live.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Infant Spirit
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the infant spirit.

The day after Christmas, Oxal comes forward, and the voice is different, slower, with the weight of long perspective. The theme is birth, but not the birth in the manger. The birth that happens in you, again and again, every time the light finds a new place to be born in the darkness.

I am going to give you Oxal's passage at length, because it is one of the great passages of the archive, and it deserves to be heard whole. In the beginning, they say, there was the Word, and the Word was with the Creator, and the Word became flesh. And this is not only a story about one life long ago. It is the story of your life, now. For within each of you there is a darkness, and within that darkness a light is struggling to be born. And each time you choose love over fear, each time you turn toward the light in the middle of your own night, the Word becomes flesh again, in you.

Listen to how they develop it. The spirit within you is an infant. It cannot walk yet. It cannot speak yet. It cannot survive in the open. And so you must do what any parent does with an infant. You must shelter it. You must feed it in the quiet. You must carry it through the desert places of your life, the dry stretches where nothing seems to be happening, and trust that the carrying is the work. Do not expose the infant spirit to the harsh winds of judgment, your own or anyone else's. Do not demand that it perform. Nurture it in the hidden places, in meditation, in prayer, in the small fidelities of the day, and in time it will stand, and walk, and speak with a voice you will recognize as your own truest voice.

And here is the promise Oxal sets beside the labor. The darkness shall never overcome the light. Never. However long the night, however deep the desert, the light that is struggling to be born in you is stronger than the darkness around it. Not because you are strong. Because the light is what you are. The darkness is the weather. The light is the climate.

The evening's questions circle the same fire. Someone asks about loving without condition, and whether it is the same as indifference, and the answer draws the line cleanly. Indifference does not care. Unconditional love cares completely, and demands nothing. The difference is everything. Someone asks about twin souls, about the one who completes you, and Latwii answers gently that each entity is already whole, already complete, and what you seek in another is the reflection of the wholeness you have not yet recognized in yourself. And someone asks about the dark prophecies, the catastrophes, the end of things, and the answer is steady. Do not feed the fear. Feed the infant. The future belongs to the light being born, not to the darkness making noise.

I keep thinking of the timing. The day after Christmas. The presents opened, the company gone, the ordinary days stretching ahead. And Oxal says: now the real birth begins. Not in the manger. In you. In the quiet after the celebration, in the desert of the ordinary week, the infant spirit stirs, and asks only to be carried.

So tonight, find the infant. It is there, in the darkness you have been afraid to look at, small and breathing. Shelter it. Do not judge it. Carry it through your desert, one day at a time. And trust the promise. The darkness shall never overcome the light. It never has. It never will.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Seed of Wishing
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the seed of wishing.

It is the first week of a new year, and the archive does what minds do in January. It thinks about wishing. About hope. About the things we want and the strange way they come to us, or do not. Hatonn speaks first, and then Latwii takes the theme deeper, and between them they give one of the fullest teachings on desire anywhere in these pages.

Hatonn begins with a warning that is also an invitation. Be careful what you wish for, he says, not because wishing is dangerous, but because it works. What you desire, you draw toward you. This is the law, and it does not check your wisdom before it obeys. So wish carefully. Wish for the things that enlarge the heart. And know that the wishing itself is a faculty, a muscle. It can be trained, strengthened, refined. The one who wishes idly gets idle results. The one who wishes with a clear heart sets great machinery in motion.

Then Latwii takes up the image that gives the evening its name. A wish, they say, is a seed. You plant it in the dark ground of your being, and then you must do the hardest thing. You must leave it alone. The seed needs the frost of meditation, the silence, the stillness, the time in the dark when nothing seems to be happening. And many seekers dig up their seeds to check whether they are growing, and in the checking, kill them. Plant the wish. Tend the ground with your daily practice. And wait. What blooms may not look like what you planted, for the growing changes the gardener too, and by the time the flower opens, you may be someone who wants a different flower. That is not failure. That is growth.

Listen to how they put the companion teaching, on fear. Fear, Latwii says, is negative hope. It is the same faculty as wishing, pointed in the opposite direction. You plant seeds of dread in the same dark ground, tend them with the same attention, and they bloom just as faithfully. This is why the discipline of wishing matters. You are always planting. The only question is what.

The evening turns to anger, and the teaching is bracing. Anger, Latwii says, is the other side of love. It is love mixed with barter, love that has made a deal and feels the deal has been broken. I expected this, and I did not get it. I gave that, and it was not returned. Beneath every anger, if you dig, you find a love that felt cheated. And this is why anger is such a valuable teacher. It shows you exactly where your love still has conditions. Do not curse the anger. Thank it for the information, and then get to work on the conditions.

There is a passage about meditation as gardening that I want to keep. When you sit, Latwii says, you will find weeds. Old resentments, old fears, old bargains. Do not be dismayed. The weeds prove the ground is fertile. Pull them gently, one by one, and plant something better in the cleared space. And there is a word about detachment that corrects a common mistake. Detachment is not coldness. It is finely tuned compassion, love that has learned not to grip. The hand opens. The seed is planted. The waiting begins.

Someone asks about a loved one lost to drink, and the answer is given with unusual gravity. Each entity chooses its lessons, Latwii says, and the ones who love the drinker must love without controlling, support without gripping, and trust the deeper self that chose the hard curriculum. I offer this as their way of seeing, and I add my own gentle note. If addiction is in your house, you do not have to face it on philosophy alone. There are people who help with this, counselors, groups, friends who have walked it. Reach for them. The seed of wishing grows best in tended ground, and sometimes the tending needs many hands.

So tonight, as the new year stands fresh before you, plant one wish. One clear, generous, heart-enlarging wish. Plant it in the dark, tend it with silence, and do not dig it up to check. Let the frost do its work. And watch, in the months to come, what blooms. It may not be what you expected. It will be what you need.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Ever-Moving Mirage
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the ever-moving mirage.

Hatonn tells a story tonight, and he tells it alone, with no questions after, as if the story needs the silence around it. It is about a mirage, and about us.

Since the beginning of recorded time, he says, humankind has chased a mirage. It shimmers on the horizon, just ahead, always just ahead: the promise that if you could only have a little more, be a little more, arrive a little further, then you would be happy, then you would be safe, then you would be complete. And generation after generation sets out after it. The mirage moves as they move. It is ever-moving, ever-receding, ever-promising. And the tragedy, Hatonn says, is not that people chase it. The tragedy is that they do not see it is a mirage. They think it is an oasis. They die of thirst within sight of water that was never there.

And then the story turns strange, as true stories do. Into this world of mirage-chasers, Hatonn says, there came one who was clay mixed with mirage, a teacher, a healer, one who touched the sick and they were well, who spoke and the words were light. And the mirage-chasers did what they always do with the real thing. They killed him. And in the killing, something broke open. The light that was in him shone out through the breaking, and for a moment, a terrible bright moment, the mirage was exposed for what it was. The kingdom he spoke of was not ahead on the horizon. It was within.

Listen to how they land it, because the landing is the whole teaching. The mirage is within you as well as before you. The thirst, the chasing, the promise of just a little more, all of it rises from inside. And so the seeking must turn inward too. Stop running toward the horizon, Hatonn says, and sit down where you are, and look within. The water you have been dying of thirst for is not ahead. It is here. It was always here. The mirage only had power while you believed the real thing was somewhere else.

I keep thinking about how gentle this story is, for how sharp it is. Hatonn does not mock the chasers. He was, by his own account, watching with love. The chasing itself is a kind of seeking, misdirected but sincere. Every step toward the mirage was a step taken in hope. The teaching does not ask you to be ashamed of the chase. It only asks you to stop, at last, and drink.

So tonight, notice your own mirage. The one shimmering just ahead of you right now, the thing you are sure will complete you when you reach it. And ask the honest question. Is it water, or is it light on sand? And then, whatever the answer, sit down where you are. Close your eyes. Look within. The kingdom is not on the horizon. It never was. It is here, in the seeker, waiting for the seeking to come home.

Thank you for listening.

title: Your Own Jerusalem
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: your own jerusalem.

Anger is the theme of this evening, and the archive does not flinch from it. Latwii begins with a craftsman's image. Your emotions are tools, they say. And anger is a broad, cold chisel. It is not evil. It is not a sign of failure. It is a tool, and like any tool it can build or it can wound, depending on the hand that holds it and the skill of the holding. The work of the seeker is not to throw away the chisel. It is to learn to use it.

Listen to how they develop it, because the distinctions are fine and worth keeping. There are angers and angers. There is the hot flash that passes through like weather. There is the slow burn of the grievance nursed for years. There is the righteous anger at injustice, which can move mountains or make martyrs. Each has its own shape, its own edge. And the mastery Latwii describes is not suppression. It is not the spiritual performance of never feeling angry. It is the slow education of the hand: learning to pick up the chisel when the work requires it, and to set it down when the work is done.

And then Oxal comes forward, and the evening changes key. When you are angry, they say, when the chisel is in your hand and your hand is shaking, step back. Step back from the anger, and find within yourself the place that the anger cannot touch. And Oxal gives that place a name. Jerusalem. There is an old prayer, they say: pray for the peace of Jerusalem. And the Jerusalem you must pray for is your own. The holy city within you. The place of stillness at the center of the storm, unchangeable, untouchable, where no anger and no despair can enter.

I love that image, and I want to hold it up to the light. Your own Jerusalem. Not a doctrine. Not a destination. A place within you that is already at peace, already whole, already holy, and that does not cease to be any of those things when you are furious. The anger is weather over the city. The city remains. Your work, when the weather comes, is not to deny the storm. It is to remember the city, and to take shelter there until the sky clears.

The evening holds one more thread, a question about healing, and Nona's answer is brief and warm. The healing, they suggest, comes not from the technique but from the love with which it is offered. The hands matter less than the heart behind them. And this belongs with the anger teaching more than it seems. The hand that holds the chisel and the hand that offers the healing are the same hand. The difference is not in the hand. It is in whether the hand remembers Jerusalem.

So tonight, when the anger comes, and it will come, try the practice. Do not throw away the chisel. Do not pretend you are not angry. Step back. Find the city within, the still place the storm cannot enter. Pray for its peace, which is your peace. And then, from the shelter of those walls, pick up the tool again, and use it for the building, not the breaking.

Thank you for listening.

title: Whom Do You See
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: whom do you see.

Hatonn begins this evening with a small, sad, familiar figure. There once was an entity, he says, who chased happiness the way the world teaches you to chase it. More pleasure. More comfort. More of everything. And the chasing worked, in the way chasing works. The entity got what it chased, and found it hollow, and chased harder. If you have ever stood in the middle of a life that looks right and feels empty, you know this entity. You have been this entity. I have been this entity.

And then, because the archive always balances its sorrows, Hatonn speaks of laughter. Laughter, he says, is the great restorer. It breaks the spell of the chase. The one who can laugh at the solemn business of getting and spending has already stepped outside it. So the evening holds both: the small entity running after happiness, and the laughter that catches up with the runner and taps it on the shoulder.

Later Latwii offers a meditation, and it is one of the loveliest in the archive. See yourself as a tree, they say. Feel your roots going down into the dark earth. Feel your branches reaching up into the light. And know that every other person is a tree too, rooted in the same earth, reaching for the same light. The forest is one forest. The separation is the illusion. Sit with that image until you feel it, they say, not as an idea but as a fact of the body.

And then Oxal comes forward with the passage that gives the evening its name, and I am going to give it to you slowly, because it is the kind of teaching that rearranges the furniture of the mind. Whom do you see, Oxal asks, when you look at another person? You see a stranger on the street, and you look away. You see a boatman at his oar, and you see only the boat. You see a derelict in the gutter, and you see only the ruin. But look again. Look with the eyes of the tree that knows the forest is one. The stranger is your brother. The boatman carries you across waters you cannot cross alone. And the derelict, Oxal says, the derelict is the Buddha. The derelict is the Christ. The derelict is your beloved, your sweetheart, yourself.

Listen to how they put the practice that follows. When you meet another, do not ask what they can do for you, or what they are, or what they have been. Ask whom you are seeing. And answer: I am seeing the Creator, wearing this particular face today, teaching this particular lesson, asking for this particular love. The divine folly, Oxal calls it, this willingness to be fooled by the costume, and then to see through it, and to love the actor underneath.

The evening's questions touch on hunches, on the quiet nudges of the higher self, and Latwii answers that the hunch is the tree speaking to the tree, the forest communicating through its roots. Trust it, they say. It knows more than the branches know.

So tonight, an experiment for the next person you meet, whether stranger or beloved. Look at them, and ask, in the silence of your own heart: whom do I see? And let the answer come. Not the name. Not the story. The deeper answer. The Buddha in the checkout line. The Christ in the traffic. Your own sweetheart, wearing a face you almost did not recognize. See them. And watch what changes.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Cutting Edge
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the cutting edge.

Choice is the theme of this evening, and the archive approaches it from the one direction you do not expect. Not how to choose rightly. But what it means that you cannot choose wrongly.

Hatonn begins with a sentence that takes a moment to land. There is no failure, he says. There are only choices that are more or less efficacious, more or less skillful, more or less aligned with what you hoped. But failure, the final verdict, the closed door, does not exist. Every choice moves you. Every choice teaches you. The path does not punish the misstep. It absorbs it, and continues. I love that line, because it quietly dismantles the fear that keeps so many seekers frozen. You cannot get it wrong. You can only get it more or less right, and the getting is the teaching.

Listen to how they develop it. Each choice has momentum, Hatonn says. It carries you forward into the consequences that teach you what the choice meant. And the consequences are not punishments. They are curriculum. The seeker who chose the harder road learns the lessons of the harder road. The seeker who chose the easier road learns the lessons of the easier road, which are often harder than they look. There is no vantage point from which one life is the mistake and another is the correct answer. There are only lessons, wearing the costumes of outcomes.

And then Latwii takes up the word the evening has been circling: crisis. The crisis, they say, the moment when everything seems to be breaking, is the cutting edge of consciousness. It is the place where the old self can no longer hold, and the new self has not yet formed, and in that gap, in that sharp and shining edge, the most growth happens the fastest. Do not waste the crisis wishing it away, they say. It is the most alive you will ever be. The edge cuts, yes. But the cutting is the opening.

There is a passage about the author of the script that I want to keep. Step back, Latwii says, far enough to see your life the way an author sees a story. The author does not panic when the hero suffers. The suffering is the story. And you are both the hero and the author. The part of you that is living the crisis is also, at another level, the part that wrote it, that chose it, that knew what it was for. When you can hold both, the character and the author, the fear loosens. You are not being punished by the plot. You are being developed by it.

The evening's smaller questions serve the same theme. Someone asks about momentum, about getting stuck, and the answer is simple. Begin. Any beginning restores momentum. The stuckness was never in the circumstance. It was in the waiting for certainty. Choose, and the choosing moves you, and the moving teaches you what the choice meant.

So tonight, if you are standing before a choice and the fear of getting it wrong has frozen you, hear the archive's verdict. There is no wrong. There is only the next lesson, wearing the costume of an outcome. Choose. Step onto the cutting edge. And trust that the part of you who wrote this chapter knew what it was doing, even if the part of you living it has not yet found out.

Thank you for listening.

title: Addicted to Truth
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: addicted to truth.

Hatonn opens this evening with the widow's two coins, the old story of the poor woman who gave everything she had, two small coins, into the treasury, while the rich gave from their surplus. And Hatonn draws the line straight to the seeker. The spiritual life, he says, is not a donation from your surplus. It is the two coins. It is everything. You do not fit the seeking around your life. You fit your life around the seeking. Give the whole of it, he says, not dramatically, not all at once, but completely, the way the widow did. Hold nothing back in reserve.

And then the image that gives the evening its strange and wonderful title. The search for truth, Hatonn says, is like an addiction. It gets into the blood. It reorganizes the priorities. The one who has tasted it cannot go back to the old hungers, not because the old hungers are forbidden, but because they no longer satisfy. I love the boldness of that comparison. The archive does not flinch from the word. It takes the most driven, most consuming human pattern and says: this energy, turned toward the light, is the engine of the spiritual life. Be addicted, then. But be addicted to truth.

Latwii takes the theme into the hardest territory, and I want to handle it with care. Someone asks about addiction, about the loved ones lost to it, about how to help. And Latwii answers with a principle that cuts through every strategy. Do not judge. The judgment, they say, is the barrier. The moment the one who suffers feels your judgment, a wall goes up, and no help can pass through it. Offer love without the verdict. Support without the sentence. Be present without the demand that they change on your schedule. The helping that heals, they say, is the helping that leaves the other's dignity intact.

I need to speak in my own voice here, gently. The archive offers a spiritual picture of addiction and of how to stand beside someone in it. It is not medicine, and it is not a substitute for the real help that exists: counselors, recovery groups, friends who have walked the road, crisis lines that answer in the night. If addiction is in your house, or in your own body, please reach for those hands too. The teaching of the evening still holds. Do not judge, neither them nor yourself. But do not walk alone either. The climb is steep enough with company.

For the evening does give us a climb. Hatonn closes with meditation as a mountain. You begin in the valley, in the noise and the dust of the ordinary day. And you climb, breath by breath, thought by thought, up out of the valley to the clear lake at the top, where the water is still and the air is clean. And in that stillness you are washed. You are made new. And then, and this is the part that matters, you climb back down, carrying the viewpoint of the mountain into the valley. Meditation is not an escape from the life. It is the high place from which the life, at last, makes sense.

So tonight, give the two coins. Let the truth get into your blood. Climb the mountain, wash in the lake, and come back down with the mountain's eyes. And if you meet another climber on the trail, one who has fallen, one who is struggling, do not judge the stumble. Offer your hand. The mountain is climbed together, or not at all.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Polarized Hour
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the polarized hour.

Some evenings the group came with a simple, uneasy question. What is happening out there? Why does the world feel so divided, so strange, so charged? Tonight the ones who call themselves Latwii answer with a picture of a planet in the middle of a great sorting, and of new arrivals coming to help.

Hatonn speaks first, and briefly. I love how simply he puts it. Never feel alone, he says. There are always many souls concerned with your welfare. If you will just remember this one sentence, he says, a lot of the loneliness of your third density will disappear.

Then Latwii takes the questions, and the first one is about the children. A member has heard that many children are being born now for the express purpose of helping the planet, some of them from other densities. Could they comment? Listen to how carefully they answer. Indeed, they say, at this time on your planet there is the birthing of a great number of entities of various origins who have come to aid the planetary consciousness in its evolution.

Many, they say, are what the group has called wanderers, souls who have come before in small numbers for thousands of years. But in the last two centuries, the number has increased greatly. And there is something newer still. Some are early incarnations of those who will form part of the fourth-density population of this planet, harvested from third-density planets of other solar systems, given the honor of incarnating early as the harvest begins. Their lightness, their distortion toward love, is added to the cumulative vibration of the planet.

These young ones forget, as everyone forgets. But they bring skills that are not so easily forgotten, and Latwii points to the children of this time who show abilities your peoples call extraordinary or paranormal. These skills, they say, are the subconscious remembering of lighter vibrations, brought along for the purpose of aiding the evolution of the planet.

Then comes the sentence I keep returning to. Thus, they say, you will find upon your planet at this time a great polarization in consciousness occurring. That is, you will find great examples of love of others and service to others, and great examples of love of self and power over others. Both, side by side, intensifying. That is the polarized hour of the title.

A member asks whether the powerful negative ones are in politics. Latwii will not point fingers at any office. Instead they describe the principle. The principle of negativity, they say, is that principle which intensifies the illusion of separation, and it is used by those who have learned it to dominate those who are not, as they put it, elite. You will see it in politics, yes, but also in armies, in economies, in businesses. And, they add gently, within the self. For are not all entities one, and do you not contain all things?

The last question of the evening is a tender one. Can a person who is decidedly negative or positive change within a single lifetime? It is most unusual, Latwii says, for an entity to completely change polarity in one incarnation. But then a member offers an example, someone who was destructive and then, through a program of recovery, became helpful to others. Was that a change of polarity?

Latwii answers with care.
