He knelt upon the sand with his palms upward and prayed to no one in particular. I know not why I began this journey. Oh singer of the song, speak to me and tell me what I must do.

No answer came, only the song. In the deep blue gloaming he decided to go back, to retrace his steps to his mother's home. But the road had disappeared. Oh singer of the song, he cried, I have changed my life because of the beauty of the music. Are you only a siren to lead me astray?

With dawn came a small ship at anchor, and a man who rowed to shore. Are you the singer of the song, the boy asked. The man only smiled and shook his head. No, he said. I am a fellow traveler. The boy asked how he knew the path. I do not know the path, the man said. I seek the path.

And then the words this whole story was built to deliver. You will find that your journey has changed you, the traveler told him. I cannot offer you a road that goes backwards. You will never again be who you were when you first heard the song. You will never visit the home of your mother, for even were you to go there now, you would be a stranger to her. Your ways would be strange and your thinking outlandish, for you hear the song, and she hears the insects.

To all of you who journey upon the path and who hear a song, Hatonn says, know that you have comrades, that that which is needed will be provided, but that you cannot go back. You can only refine your ears that they may listen better to the song of faith, hope, love and peace. The first and greatest power, he says, is given to you in the act of surrender, for the heart that has surrendered can hear the song which will lead you.

The evening's questions turn to grief, and I want to tread gently here. One of the circle speaks of trying to work through the feeling that she should be dead, of guilt toward a lost friend, of a sadness so deep it can feel logical. She has sought professional help, and the grief is somewhat softened, but the attacks of sadness still come. Latwii's response is long and tender, and its essence is this. You are limited beings attempting to reflect the limitless, they say, and you will fall short in each opportunity. Dwell not overlong within those opportunities you feel were less than adequately met. For as long as you draw breath, you have the treasures this illusion can offer, the opportunity to take what is mundane and transmute it into what is sacred. If you are carrying a grief like this, please hear the evening's gentleness, and please keep the human help close, the counselors, the doctors, the friends who know your name.

Surrender, then, Hatonn says, and purify your ears to the song of life, that life which is beyond life and death. Farewell, pilgrims. Take what you can use from our poor story, toss the rest away, and join us in the infinite quest for the Infinite.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Drop of Water
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the drop of water.

March tenth, nineteen eighty-five, a Sunday meditation, and Hatonn opens with an image from a laboratory. Each of you has seen the picture of a drop of water, he says, which is then placed under ten times magnification, and then fifty times, and so on, until we are looking at the very nucleus and the surrounding electrons. Each time you looked, something had changed to that drop of water, something outside of that drop's control.

Scientists surrender to their technical equipment, Hatonn says. It is left to those of the path to surrender in another way, and that is to welcome, accept and encourage spiritual growth and change in themselves and others. What one may see as a drop of water, another may see ten times magnified. Each is looking at the same universe, caught whole and perfect in a microscope's eye.

This is true also, he says, of you in your relationship with yourself, with the Creator, and with others. You must first be able to accept and like yourself in order to serve the one Creator with the most efficacious effect. One entity may need one thing, another another, but it is all the same experience, seen from different points of view.

Then Hatonn turns to the seasons, and the evening becomes a gardening lesson. As your season moves from the cold, windswept, barren winter into the warming spring, he says, there is a lightening of hearts, a sparkle to the mind's eye. The tendency of winter is to turn the eye inward, that those portions of the self which exercised their luxuriant summer's growth might be observed and considered for their harvest, and that this harvest might become the foundation of yet another season's growth.

You will move through this new season, Hatonn says, watering those planted ideas and tendencies that you feel have value, and plucking those growths that seem as weeds and hinder your spiritual journey. And here is the turn I want you to keep. From one point of view, a certain experience may seem very difficult and quite undesirable, a weed that needs plucking. And yet, if you look deeper, you may discover within that situation the possibility of a great acceleration in your spiritual journey.

For the strength of spirit which is possible for you to gain, Hatonn says, is most often gained not with the ease of a feast table plainly set, but through those experiences which cause you to reach deeper within your own being to find harmony with self and other self. Those experiences are, as the sandpaper to the roughened board, what smooth the spiritual journey.

Things are not always as they seem, Hatonn says, and this is especially true for the seeker of truth. For in the metaphysical sense, it is very difficult to determine one's own progress. You move within an illusion. And yet you are moving, my friends, in perfect harmony with the cycles and seasons and the rhythms of being.

So tonight, look at the difficult thing the way you would look at the drop of water. Magnify it. Then magnify it again. See what changes.

Thank you for listening.

title: Open the Door to Love
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: open the door to love.

March seventeenth, nineteen eighty-five. Hatonn speaks about meditation and love, and issues a warning that sounds strange until you sit with it. The warning is about loving love too much.

Let us approach the subject, Hatonn says, from the standpoint of love being offered as a goal, as some proper name like a town or a city. There is a tremendous danger in looking at love as a goal, he says, for it becomes a kind of deity unto itself, one drawn within the imagination of man's mind, not that of the Creator.

The difficulty, Hatonn says, lies in the willingness to stop short before achieving the final attainment. One strives not toward reunification with the Creator but toward the objective of limitless loving, and in such attainment finds difficulty reconciling the Creator's universe with what the seeker believes should be apparent as a result. In seeking not far enough, yet obtaining the objective of the search, the seeker is suddenly stricken with doubt concerning the validity of what has been attained, and the attainment begins to tarnish in his own eyes.

Loving is frequently described as a gift of the Creator, Hatonn says. Yet is not all equally a gift of the same source? He does not seek to devalue loving, but to introduce a perspective through which one might see this gift as a tool through which attainment may be attempted, rather than an end product which one may settle for and fall short of the Creator's intention.

Then Hatonn walks through the sacred traditions, and I love the even-handedness of it. The master known as Jesus broke his body like a loaf of bread and poured out his blood upon the earth, and yet in no way did he wish to be worshipped for himself. The one known as Mohammed called himself a prophet, not the one God. In the story of Arjuna, the message that comes clear as a bell is that man is within a temporal clime, a time of living during which many temporal and seemingly nonspiritual decisions must be made. And the one known as Gautama Siddhartha ended his journey plying the pole of a boat, ferrying travelers across the water, gazing at the water, not at the men, not at their problems. There was in him no idolatry.

Most of your idols are unwitting, Hatonn says. One becomes enamored of an experience or a point of view and clings to it until it becomes hard, dogmatic and rigid. If your love is not flexible, endless and sweet as fresh water, then the love you are seeking is a graven image, a dead figurehead which mimics love. Love is not a thing. It is a force, a beingness, a consciousness which you share. It is your birthright. You may love, but in the beginning and in the end you are love, and you are a channel for limitless love. You cannot seek limitless love. You can only open the door through which that love may pour.

Hence, Hatonn says, we turn again to daily meditation. Regardless of how much the discipline may cost you in worldly terms, its central importance stands. It need not be long. One meditation during the day to center you, preferably in the morning, and then the perspective can be regained in a near-instant, by suggesting to yourself that you should meditate when you hear the clock or the doorbell or the telephone ring.

Lift off your shoulders this great responsibility for finding a limitless love in a world which does not have what you seek, Hatonn says, and open yourself to that love through meditation, and through watching experiences as if they were water flowing past you, making interesting configurations. Your life is a pattern. May you make it beautiful by surrendering to love itself.

The evening's questions turn to healing, and Latwii offers two thoughts worth keeping. The first is about the healer who tries and seems to fail. The attempt, they say, is the most important aspect. The fruits of your labors are seldom noticeable within this illusion, for what you see as healing is the result of work first done upon metaphysical levels. The variance between the attempt and the achievement is never measured and may be considered unimportant.

The second is a boundary every healer should hear. One who would offer itself as healer should not attempt such efforts unless first approached by the one to be healed, Latwii says, for entities shoulder those burdens which are theirs for as long as the burdens are theirs. To attempt to remove a burden before it is ready to be removed is much like attempting to peel the skin from the snake before it is ready to be shed.

So tonight, do not chase love as a prize to be won. Open the door. Let it pour. And let it be flexible, endless, and sweet as fresh water.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Antitoxin Is Love
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the antitoxin is love.

March twenty-fourth, nineteen eighty-five. Hatonn speaks about judgment, and he does it the way he always does, with small human stories that quietly dismantle you.

We would tell you of the small boy who asks to go into the road and play, Hatonn begins. Absolutely not, his mother tells him. The boy is too young to understand that her meanness is the means of his survival. I have just lost my job, wails the young woman. But this causes her to think about what she wishes to do with her life, and in years to come she has forgotten the pain and begun to enjoy having a past.

The master known to you as Jesus could have judged himself to be in a sorry state indeed, Hatonn says, for he was scourged and beaten and nailed upon a cross until he was as inanimate as the wood which bore him. And yet the great triumph of resurrection could never have taken place had all that passed not occurred.

We see the circle of each of your lives, Hatonn says, the circle of judgment, of poor things which turn out to be so helpful and of seemingly excellent things which turn out to be worthless. And we would point out that judgment is a good thing to practice upon, but is almost never correct. For the balancing between the good and the bad in each thing that occurs will go on within the widening ripples of your life patterns until the pond ripples no more.

Let us turn now to that which is beyond judgment, Hatonn says, that which you may do to more carefully align yourself with the great and limitless light of the one infinite Creator. That has to do not with action but with intention. What you intend in a polarized manner, when you begin to act or think of acting or hold someone in your thoughts, is the lever by which you polarize your own being. It is your choice.

If you work and give of yourself to the effort of being loving, Hatonn says, no matter how poorly or how well your actions are realized, you shall have polarized. When one does all that one can do, that is the end of the ripple.

But the effort will produce in each seeker a veritable melee of judgments, Hatonn says. You judge yourself. You judge others. You judge ideas. Most of all you judge whether or not you are polarized. Look upon these exercises as a type of spiritual inertia which pulls at you and drags you back. Nevertheless, that you have offered being loving cannot be taken from you, for it becomes part of the vibration which forms that which is called you.

Because judgment is never particularly useful and is often a painfully strong deterrent to one's own progress, Hatonn says, we urge each to rest the judgmental faculties. We are not urging you to cease discriminating betwixt one thought and another. We simply ask you to ride the mare, not for the mare to ride you.

I love that image. Your intellect is a good tool, Hatonn says, crafted by you through many experiences. But many among those who seek allow the intellect to ride them. Temper it. Ask yourself, am I thinking or am I feeling? Is my thinking bent upon aiding either myself or another in spiritual growth?

And the first person to practice your lack of judgment upon is yourself, Hatonn says. Have you allowed yourself to shine forth today? Have you allowed laughter to bubble in your voice, joy to fill your eyes? Have you listened and looked and heard the music of the creation, the nodding flowers, the first willows waving their greening branches? Whatever it is that feeds you, turn to it, allow it to fill you with the love of the Creator, and then allow that love to shine through you.

We would almost wish, Hatonn says, gazing upon your peoples, that the planet could see itself as bitten by a snake, so that the people could begin to take restorative action to contain that poison which is judgment, and to release into the body the antitoxin, love.

Before he leaves, Hatonn asks one thing for your daily priorities. The first priority, he says, be meditation. Within yourself is the only solitary place where one may go and shut the door and open to that beauty, that power which is the Creator. Meditate, open inwardly, and then turn toward the friendly sun, or smile at the raindrops.

Judge all you can, Hatonn says, and there will always be another side. Love all you can, and your lives shall be transformed. The willow has already made up its mind. It will turn toward the light. Shall you?

Thank you for listening.

title: The Tender Instrument
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the tender instrument.

March twenty-sixth, nineteen eighty-five, an intensive meditation, and the evening is given over to beginners. Laitos works with three new instruments in turn, and the whole session feels like watching someone learn to walk while everyone in the room holds their breath with love.

Hatonn opens briefly, with a thought about the body. It is often the case, he says, that one does not know how caught up in one's very physical vehicle one has been in the daily round until one first sits down to relax. There is much illness among your peoples, he says, that could well be eased if entities were aware of their bodies all the time and responded appropriately when the need arose. A gentle reminder, offered as opinion, to listen to the body you live in.

Then Laitos begins the real work, moving from instrument to instrument, adjusting vibrations, asking each new channel to speak freely without analyzing. To one they say, now is always the time. Later is almost never the time for what one wishes to do.

And then Laitos says something I think every seeker should hear, whether they ever channel a word or not. These vocal contacts are services that may be performed for the benefit of others, they say. It is one of an infinite array of ways to help another. There is no extreme rightness or cachet to the ability to channel, nor is there any lack of service if one wishes to serve in other areas. To channel is not to be spiritual. There are times when to be spiritual is to desire to channel.

One new instrument speaks a few trembling words and loses the contact. Another manages only the greeting before analysis rushes in. Laitos is delighted anyway. When a new instrument begins to speak, they say, it is very frequently the case that the contact becomes lost because of analysis, or because of the distracting rush of feelings that accompany the contact. And they offer a small practical trick. Refrain from speaking in the first person. Channel about yourself in the third person, as if narrating, until the confidence is there to stride forward.

What moves me most is how Laitos describes the new instrument's desire itself. That desire to perform this service, they say, is as a great light within the metaphysical realms. You cannot see it with any of your senses. But it shines quite, quite brightly.

The evening's questions turn to healing, to crystals, to whether a charged stone in a friend's hand could help another's illness. Latwii's answer keeps returning to the same ground. The crystal is useful, they say, to the extent that the one who serves as healer has healed the self. As you progress, you in your energy centers become as the crystal, regularized and able to transmit light. And the intention of the one to be healed, they add, is paramount, for it is the desire and ability of the one to be healed which allows the healing to occur.

So tonight, if you are the tender shoot just moving from the seed toward the light, as Latwii once described the new instrument, do not rush yourself, and do not despise the trembling. The desire is the light. The practice will follow.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Planet's Fever
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the planet's fever.

April third, nineteen eighty-five. Laitos spends the evening working with new instruments, and then Latwii takes questions, and one question opens a strange and sobering picture of the Earth itself.

As the planet spirals into fourth density, a seeker asks, does it carry the solar system and the galaxy with it, or is it a local phenomenon? Latwii's answer is disarmingly simple. The galaxy and the solar system more properly carry your planet with them, they say. All creation is in motion. There is no portion of creation that is truly at rest.

Your planet, in its seeking of the one Creator, moves according to its vibration, Latwii says. And this movement is reflected in the increase in vibration of its core atomic particles, as you may call them.

But then comes the harder part. Will there be tremendous earth changes, the seeker asks, terrain changes, a shifting of poles? Latwii answers carefully. There shall be some geothermal activity during this period, they say, but it is not necessarily related to the change in vibration. It is, rather, a result of the relative disharmony experienced by the great majority of your planet's populations for a large portion of time.

Listen to how they put it, because the image is unforgettable. As the bellicose nature of various cultures has been expressed in disharmonious fashion, Latwii says, these vibrations of anger and disharmony move into the surface of the planet and are stored as what you know as heat. As your planet moves into a higher frequency of vibration, this heat must find release in some fashion, and this will be seen as various geothermal events which will cause some disturbance upon the surface of your planet's garment.

It is not the elevation of a place that determines where this heat is stored, Latwii says, but the location of cultures which have engaged in the warlike behavior. The anger of centuries, banked like coals under the skin of the world.

Asked about pyramids, those ancient structures raised by earlier peoples, Latwii says they were built to align and balance the instreaming love and light of the one Creator, that this new configuration of energy might balance the disharmonious effects of warlike behavior. And then, with a dryness I adore, they add that the pyramid is as the metaphysical training wheels.

Could we build a new ring of pyramids to balance our nature, the seeker asks. Latwii's answer is gentle and pointed. Such is possible, they say, yet it might be superseded by the continued movement of entities toward the resolution of conflicts between nations. The movement toward peace has a greater likelihood of balancing the planet's bellicose nature than any construction of mechanical devices.

Within each nation, Latwii says, there are those whose love of peace far supersedes the love of war. To these entities one may send the love and light of the one Creator, that they might receive the support to manifest it. Remember, my brother, they say, that all is truly one, and when you send love and light and thoughts of peace to any entity, that entity is as yourself, and receives your message as clearly as if you had sent it to yourself.

So tonight, consider the fever under the ground not as doom but as stored weather, waiting for release. And consider that the most effective technology for cooling it was never made of stone.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Reawakening Spirit
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the reawakening spirit.

April seventh, nineteen eighty-five. It is the Easter season, and Hatonn comes with a message about dying and rising that is not only about one teacher, but about every seeker in the room.

This day you celebrate a reawakening of a spirit, Hatonn says. The one whom you call Jesus, the bearer of the Christ force, is recognized as a teacher among many of your people, and rightfully so. But, my friends, you are all teachers.

Each of you is but a vessel, Hatonn says, which may allow itself to accept the triviality which surrounds and permeates it. This reawakening is the object of the path of those who seek opportunities for service to others. In serving your brothers and perceiving the oneness of yourself and your other selves, you allow the reality which exists about you to be made manifest through your own creative act.

It is your act of creating, Hatonn says, of placing your will, your self, on this path, that reawakens the sleeping world about you, that shatters the stone of confused perceptions which would hold you back, and that leads you forth to perceive the light of that day which dawns.

When the one known as Jesus stated, all these things and more you shall do, Hatonn says, he foresaw the dawn to which each of you would awaken. The darkness of confusion can exist in your lives only for those moments you are willing to accept that condition. Therefore, my friends, simply go forward. Follow your path, and see within its light that which truly exists.

And there is a line from earlier in the evening that I cannot leave out. The instrument had returned from church with the wondrous feeling of the near end of the passion of Jesus, Hatonn says, and what she had not realized is this. Before the one known as Jesus could be transformed, he had to die.

I sit with that line. Before the transformation, the death. Not as punishment, but as passage. The seed does not apologize for splitting open.

The evening's questions wander through the practical and the strange. One seeker asks about a contact claiming to be a Confederation source, and Latwii answers with unusual bluntness. The contact, they say, grafted the message of a service-to-self entity within a message initiated by an entity seeking to serve others. It is worth remembering, when any voice claims authority, that Latwii's test is always the same. Does it serve others, or does it serve itself?

Another asks about back pain appearing in many people at once, and Latwii offers an image. The pains are the alarm bell tolling, they say, the entities individually informing themselves that their constructions are not up to their own standards. The catalyst is self-explanatory. It exists to inform the individual that it is time to draw back from the illusion and examine what is being built. When we turn our back on our own power, one seeker quotes, our power will eventually turn us back upon that which we should see.

And then, at the very end of the night, a small voice called Yadda speaks, and steals the whole evening. Many, many questions in this meeting about other people, about wise men and teachers, about constellations and galaxies, Yadda says. What do you wish to learn, my friends? What do you wish to know? Do you know yourself?

There is that in the desire for knowledge which is a kind of contamination, Yadda says. For only learning is when one does not have. We cannot say enough when we say, meditate, meditate, and meditate more. Who are you? Where are you going? And what do you believe the truth to be? Seek these things.

You have chosen to see the dirt, Yadda says, in their wonderfully plain way. We encourage you to try to get your ring around the collar very clean. But please, do not puff yourself up as consequential, and do not puff up others. Remember yourself first.

So tonight, whatever in you needs to die so that something truer can rise, consider letting it. The dawn, Hatonn says, is already on its way.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Still Deep Pool
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the still deep pool.

April ninth, nineteen eighty-five, an intensive meditation with Laitos, and the evening belongs to two new instruments learning, stumbling, and learning again to speak what comes.

Laitos begins with the instruction the whole archive keeps repeating. Simply relax, they say, and then speak the thoughts that appear within your mind without analysis. Become indeed the fool. Step out without knowing if thin air or earth awaits.

One new instrument manages a few sentences and then, mid-stream, analyzes, and the contact is lost. It is always a joy, Laitos says, to express the love and light of the one Creator through a new instrument, no matter how many instruments have previously been utilized. For the unique point of view that each entity has to offer is as yet another beautiful vessel which holds the nourishing waters and offers them to those who thirst.

As each new instrument practices, Laitos says, the tendency toward analysis will be reduced, for as you build confidence in this type of service, it becomes more of an automatic skill. And they commend the small victories specifically. The speaking of the identification and the greeting is the first major step. The next is speaking a thought not previously known. Each step counts.

Then a seeker asks the question every beginner asks. The thoughts seem so distant, like pulling them out of the ether. Is there any way to amplify them? Laitos answers with an image I want you to carry. You become able to perceive our thoughts, they say, as you clear your mind and relax your thinking. Then you are as a still and deep pool, which can become aware of any ripple upon its surface, and focus its attention upon describing that ripple.

It is merely necessary, Laitos says, to widen the availability of your field of perception. If any portion of that field is concerned with a thought or a sensation or a response to either, then that portion provides a static which makes perception more difficult. Still the water, and the ripple will show itself.

And there is a humility in Laitos that steadies the whole evening. You shall not know anything within your incarnation for sure, they say, for yours is not the illusion of knowing with certainty. The faculties of will and faith are the sure and steady rod and staff of the seeker of truth. If you ask for our presence in meditation, we are most happy to join you. But do not expect proof. Expect companionship.

The questions turn to the great brotherhoods and fellowships of the tradition, those groupings of beings devoted to serving. Laitos describes them plainly, as gatherings of entities, each unique, each seeing service in a different light, all bending their efforts toward sharing their experience of love and light with those who call for it. The names and labels, they suggest, are ours as much as theirs, chosen by human minds trying to categorize what is essentially one work.

So tonight, whatever you are trying to hear, the instruction is the same. Be the still, deep pool. Let the static settle. The ripple will come.

Thank you for listening.

title: Spiritual Food
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: spiritual food.

April fourteenth, nineteen eighty-five, a Sunday meditation. Hatonn speaks about love, and Latwii answers questions, and by the end of the night the whole evening has become a meditation on what feeds the spirit.

This evening we would speak a few words upon a subject which is ever and always the focus of our being, Hatonn begins. That, of course, is love. There is much upon your planet written concerning this concept, he says, that is described so inadequately by the word love.

Beyond romantic love, beyond the love of parents and children, teacher and student, Hatonn says, there is a greater love, or greater and greater perceptions of that called love. And then he offers the image I want you to hold. Love, seen in the mystical sense, is a focus through which the will of the Creator moves and makes that which is made. Love is seen as a force which creates and creates and creates, that the one Creator in many portions might seek Itself, might then experience Itself.

Seen in this fashion, Hatonn says, love as the energy becomes the container, the vessel, in which the Creator places Itself and moves through Its own being in form as well as essence. For before there was anything created, there was that which had no form and was merely essence. This essence of the one Creator has found its form, and seeks its expression through that called love.

I love that line. Love as the vessel in which the Creator pours Itself, in order to move through Its own being. You are not outside the vessel looking in. You are the vessel, being poured.

And as you seek, so shall you find, Hatonn says, for you are as the magnet attracting the iron filing. That which you desire, being a portion of yourself, is made available to you by a greater portion of yourself. As you open your being, your mind, your heart to the unknown of love, it is brought into your awareness from deeper portions of your own being, those portions less distorted and more aware of the connection between all things.

The questions begin with prayer. A seeker has been rewording the prayer called Our Father, trying to capture its true meaning, and failing to improve on two words without needing a dozen. Latwii's answer is gentle. The words within any prayer or ritual, they say, may be seen as the clothing one wears to protect the self from the storms the journeyer will experience. If the cape is too small or too large, the journeyer will find it too great a load or not covered in all necessary areas.

When you can put a phrase in a manner that has meaning to you, Latwii says, you increase the power of the prayer for yourself. But the fitting must be yours, for each entity is unique in its configuration. No one can tailor your cape for you.

Then the evening turns to something stranger and, to me, more nourishing. A seeker asks about an experience of being psychically attacked during meditation, and whether there is value in such greetings. Latwii's answer reframes the whole thing. As light shines within darkness, they say, it is noted by those who appreciate light, and some of those are of the negative polarity. They cannot place an obstacle in your path that you have not chosen. They can only intensify those distortions already within you, which alerts you to where the work is.

And here is the practice. In this type of experience, Latwii says, the welcoming of a negative entity, and its sending into one's own heart, and seeing this entity as the one Creator and as the other self, and bathing this entity in love, is that magical expression which transforms what seems negative into that which is positive.

Any added catalyst, Latwii says, provides the seeker with a spiritual food, that the seeker might utilize it and, by processing it, increase its own spiritual strength. You need not seek out such greetings, they add, for they shall in their own time seek you out. In your choice to enter this incarnation, you placed before your table a great plenty of catalyst, the spiritual food you prepared for yourself, in hopes that your learning might be propelled by these experiences.

I love how Latwii closes the night. Your queries, they say, are as treasures, for we would not have thought of them without you. As you query, you present that which is ours to share, and by this sharing, we ourselves discover more of the subtle nature of service and of love.

So tonight, whatever is on your table, the sweet and the bitter alike, consider that you set it there yourself, before you were born, as food for the journey. Eat, and grow strong.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Harvest of a Life
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the harvest of a life.

There is a moment almost every seeker knows. You stop, you look back over years of effort, of reading and meditating and trying to be kinder than you were yesterday, and you cannot find a single clear milestone. No sign that any of it worked. The one who calls himself Hatonn knows this moment well, and tonight he names it plainly, not to shame it, but to unmake it.

He begins by noticing what the group has already been doing. Before the channeling even started, they were talking, sharing their thoughts and experiences and opinions with one another. And he says this is one of the oldest ways seekers have ever quickened their journey. Listen to how he puts it. Each of you, he says, has offered to the others the harvest of your lives to this point. Not your achievements. Your lives. The whole crop, just as it grew.

Because each of you is the one Creator, expressing some facet of that Creator in your own way, everything you have lived through is something you can offer another. Even the parts that look wasted. Especially those, perhaps. For there is a common phenomenon among seekers, he says, and he describes it without flinching. Again and again the seeker tries to measure progress, and again and again the measurement comes up short. And at some point the seeker decides the efforts have failed and been wasted. It is easy, from there, to decide the whole seeking was foolish.

I love that he does not argue with this feeling. He explains it. The power of your illusion, he says, is to persuade you that there may be that which is not love, that which is not the Creator, that which is not whole and perfect and balanced. That is the illusion doing its job. It is very convincing. And so the seeker, who has no clear vision through it, assumes the lack of visible progress means no progress.

But then he turns the whole thing inside out with a single image. The one Creator, he says, awaits at the heart of each experience. Not at the end of the journey, not after you have finally become wise enough. At the heart of each experience. Of this morning's frustration. Of the conversation you handled badly. Of the grief you carried all week. He asks two questions, and I want to give them to you exactly as he asked them. How deeply shall you delve, my friends? How carefully shall you search each day's experience?

The choice is yours, he says. There are layers and levels to every experience. The seeming negative rests on the outer surface. A little below that, the mundane. And as you keep moving deeper, the nature of the experience approaches what he has been describing all along as love. No one can require this of you. No one can grade it. You may search as deeply as you choose, from one moment to the next, or not at all. The free will is complete.

And here is the part that quietly undoes the whole idea of failure. When seekers gather and share honestly, he says, they discover they are much like all others. Each is trying to learn from what is placed before them. Each feels there has been more failure than success. And each, in listening to the others, finds inspiration from those who have learned great lessons from difficult experiences, and then looks into their own experience and discovers the same opportunities were placed there too.

He closes the image with something I keep returning to. Love is always and ever the same, he says. It is one thing. Yet each of you, moving through your daily round of activities, expresses and experiences that same love in a unique fashion. You add another hue to the infinite colors of the experience of the one Creator. Your life, no matter how mundane it seems at the moment, is yours, and it is unique to you, and it holds the wholeness of the Creator, awaiting your discovery.

So the harvest is not a prize for the successful seeker. The harvest is the sharing itself. The willingness to say, this is what my life has grown so far, and to let another take nourishment from it. The Creator, it turns out, was never anywhere but at the heart of it.

Thank you for listening.

title: Vacation and Vocation
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: vacation and vocation.

The voices called L/Leema had never spoken to human beings before this evening. They say so themselves, with some delight, rummaging through the channel's mind like guests in a fascinating kitchen, and choosing two words to build their whole message around. The words sound almost the same. They could not be more different.

Vacation. Vocation. Listen to how they take the words apart. Vaca, they say, means to be open. Voca means to call, or to be called. Vacation is to have time, to be free, to be empty. Vocation is to be called, to be selected, to be initiated. One small difference in sound. A whole difference in the quality of a life.

They are quick to say that rest itself is not the problem. In the workaday world, empty time is a balance, not a luxury. That is not the vacation they are talking about. They mean something deeper, a choice at the level of the self. The self that will take itself seriously, no matter the consequences, or the self that wants time off and time out. What you wish, they say, you will receive.

And then comes the line that the whole evening seems to turn on. A vocation, they say, is that which is so loved that you are called to it, not because you understand or have reasons that you should answer, but because you are called, and you must go. It is not a job. It is not even, quite, a choice. It is a summons. And they promise that the joy of answering it belongs to a completely different order of living than the enjoyment of time off. They actually say they would risk annoying you by insisting on this. I love that. They know how it sounds. They say it anyway.

There is another thread running through the evening, and it braids itself into the first. Leema urges the group to ask the questions that endure. Most questions, they say, satisfy curiosity for a moment and then dissolve. But some questions strike to the heart of the mysteries of being, and the answers to those hold their interest firmly, through all time. Seek those.

Which brings them to their most startling claim about seeking itself. It is not the answers, they say, that will most illuminate you. As you learn, you will learn that it is the questions themselves that live. The company of those who seek may aid you in becoming a seeker. And then the phrase I cannot get out of my head. Serious with laughter. Of course, they add. Seriousness should be full of joy. It should be full of all that you are and all that you have.

And then the urgency, gentle but absolute. If you wish to be a serious seeker, they say, it is not tomorrow, and it is not yesterday, that you will be one. Take yourself now, and acknowledge that you are what they call, in their borrowed vocabulary, God stuff. Infinite and beautiful Creator stuff. Then ask yourself if you wish to seek the truth. That question alone, they say, will fill lives.

So tonight is a kind of crossroads, drawn in two words. You can be open, empty, free, and there is nothing wrong with that. Or you can hear the call, and go. Not someday. Now. Laughing, serious, all the way in.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Two Cities
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the two cities.

Tonight Hatonn tells a story. He calls it a tale of two cities, and it is one of the clearest pictures in the whole archive of the two great roads a life can take.

The first city was small, with no great power in war or in learning. But it was a place of calm and repose for the soul, because its people sought what cannot be acquired on the physical plane. The second city was full of people who sought and fought and pursued their ambitions, who attempted much and accomplished less, because their conflicts kept interrupting one another's efforts.

In time, the ambitious city turned its eyes outward. Unable to subdue one another, its people made alliances and treaties, and marched to conquer the quiet city. They stormed it in great excitement, banners flying, and found it empty. The treasures were there, but no one to fight, no fear to spark, no cowardice to display. So they did the only thing they knew how to do. They began to argue among themselves. The arguing turned bitter, then violent, and for the most part they slew one another, and the survivors loaded what treasure they could carry and went home.

And here is the turn that makes the story more than a fable. Hatonn says each side achieved exactly what it sought. The violent found the violence they sought, and took from one another in satisfaction. The peaceful, in their own way, found fulfillment too, for they simply left behind what they no longer valued, knowing it would be of value to the invaders. Both paths worked. The difference, he says, lay simply in the direction of the paths.

Listen to how he draws the two roads. Those on the path of taking, the path of service to self, chose a circuitous road that circles repeatedly back upon itself, rebounding from its contacts with others, finding its pain, acquiring its minor treasures, and returning where it began. Those on the path of service to others took what gifts were given, used them while they were useful, left them behind for their brothers, and proceeded outward on a path which had no return, only progression.

He does not end with judgment. He says it is appropriate to be of what assistance one may to those on the other path, for such service can only help both. But he also says it is not necessary to lay down your life for the whims of those who take pleasure in destruction. There is no demand here. Only a description, laid out with unusual clarity, of where each road actually goes.

And then the closing counsel, which I think is the sentence the whole story was built to carry. In the times ahead, he says, difficult choices will come, and your world offers many examples of nobility and common sense and the right thing to do. But confusion might be termed the dominant theme within your illusion, and nobility that stems from confusion may not always be the most beneficial choice. Therefore, he says, look to your heart for guidance, and not to conventional wisdom. For it is within your heart, and not your mind, that the course of your desire will be revealed.

Two cities. Two roads. One question, asked in the quietest place you own. Which direction are you actually walking?

Thank you for listening.

title: The Curious Heart
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the curious heart.

Have you ever watched a small child watch something? Hatonn asks the group to picture it, and the picture he paints is so exact it feels like a memory of your own. A child watches an ant crawl over a stick, and for those few moments the child is completely absorbed. The span of attention seems short, and yet, while it lasts, the child almost becomes the experience.

This, he says, is what it looks like to love another. Not a feeling, first of all. An attention. When you love someone, he says, it is well to tune that love with the same intensity and purity with which the child watches the ant. Each person you meet is a portion of the Creator. Of course, he adds dryly, many times this is anything but obvious.

There is a second purity in children, and he names it with real tenderness. The openness to ask direct questions. The young child, he says, seems to have no limits about what may be asked, and is completely interested in everything about you. This is an enormous secret, he says. I love that phrase. An enormous secret, hiding in plain sight, in every playground.

Because here is what goes wrong between people. When there are difficulties between two entities, he says, the difficulties are normally due to the lack of effort on the part of each to imagine the other's actual situation, their creativity, their emotional and mental biases. We do not fail at love because we feel too little. We fail because we are not curious enough.

And he is honest about how hard this is. To love another is a challenge, he says, and it cannot be done without the inner underlying silence, the peace and poise that unites you not only with friend and mate, but with all of creation. The Creator, he says, wears a face as biased and full of self-contradictions as your own. How much more difficult it is to penetrate not only your own confusion but that of another, and achieve communication. Yet this, he says, is an expression of love.

Listen to how he puts the next part. Each person is the voice of the Creator, he says, filtered through many biases. The children shouting in the yard, the colleague, the spouse, the friend, all of it is that voice, coming through static. And there are times, rare and magical, when two people recognize each other and for a while there seem to be no biases at all, and communication is clear and life is ebullient. Those periods seldom last a whole lifetime. But he suggests something practical and beautiful. Keep the memories of the times when closeness was achieved. In a difficult season, those memories help orient you. They remind you what the harmony felt like, so you can find your way back toward it.

So the teaching tonight is almost embarrassingly simple, which may be why it works. Watch the way a child watches. Ask the way a child asks. And when the static rises between you and another, remember the clear channel you once shared, and listen for it again.

Thank you for listening.

title: Everyone Is Chosen
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: everyone is chosen.

The voices called L/Leema open with a statement so large it takes the rest of the evening to absorb. You are all chosen, they say. Not some of you. Not the advanced ones. All. And chosen since before there was time, before there was any created thing. Older than all the galaxies, they say, are the souls that move through the levels of consciousness within them.

They know how this sounds, and they immediately take aim at the shadow side of it. Many groups, they say, foster an elitism built on a truth seen but not comprehended. The truth is that each person who turns toward love and service is special, anointed, set apart. The error is thinking the circle is small. There is no elite, they say. There are no permanent wailers and gnashers of teeth. All shall be made one. For some it will take more cycles of experience than others. Those who are learning slowly are not lost. They are taking a different road, going more slowly. And there is time enough, they say, for all of consciousness to fully tap its birthright.

I love the plainness of that. No one is behind. No one is disqualified. The curriculum is the same for everyone, and the classroom is simply larger than we thought.

The evening then turns to the questions loss raises, and here the teaching grows teeth. When you lose a friend, a parent, a home, a position, these are the tests all shall face, they say. And the losses are provocations, central ones, that force the seeker to look deeper within for what truly supports a life. Because behind the loss, if you look with enough intensity, you find the unity of all things, which does not allow true loss in any degree. The gains and losses, they say, are the illusion of the One moving in and out of your life.

Separation itself gets the same treatment. Your illusion, they say, seems to be made of nothing but separation, one thing from another, one desire from another. Many pass an entire lifetime without finding even a small degree of the unity that binds it all. Yet wherever separation appears, they say, there is a polar opposite awaiting your discovery, just behind the one that seems apparent. The most separate-feeling corner of your experience is the one that offers the greatest opportunity to find the unity.

And then a questioner asks the question many of us live inside. I understand the path, he says, but I cannot seem to walk it. Someone cuts me off in traffic and the love vanishes. Why, after so many repetitions, can I not follow what I know? Listen to the answer, because it is one of the most honest sentences in the archive. There is a great difference, they say, between intellectually knowing a concept and actually becoming that concept. Each of you attempts to become what you believe you know with your rational mind. Yet until love has found its roots within the heart of your being, you cannot truly know love.

You are, as another questioner put it that night, already plugged into the generator. There was never a true separation. The work is not to earn the current. The work is to become the kind of being through whom it can flow. And those times that seemed most difficult, they say, when you look back on them from beyond this illusion, will seem as great treasures, where now they seem as great burdens. It is all a matter of the point of view.

Chosen before time. Never unplugged. Becoming, slowly, what you already are. That is the whole of it.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Frozen Lake
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the frozen lake.

Hatonn begins with a picture that arrives whole and will not leave you. Each mind, he says, is like a lake. On the surface there is ice, and on that ice, skaters. All the busy mental activities of the day, opinions, errands, arguments replayed, go sweeping back and forth above the frozen water, and very few skaters ever wonder what lies beneath.

Below the ice, he says, there is an entire sea of water. Most of it is dark. The light from above penetrates only partway, and the part closest to the ice shines with the most light. But light, he says, is deceptive. The deepest water, where the light does not reach, is not to be feared. It is simply dark because nothing in the shallow mind has yet learned how to look there.

This is the inner truth of consciousness as he describes it. A vast depth, much of it unexplored, the deeper the darker to ordinary sight, but as the seeker continues, the waters of consciousness become transparent to the light of the one Creator, and even the darkest portions of the mind reveal treasures. That is the shape of the inner life. Not a mountain to climb. A lake to dive.

And then he turns to meditation, and his framing of it is one of the gentlest and most freeing in the archive. There is no right or wrong way to meditate, he says. There is only going within, through whatever doors the seeker finds. The practice that has served seekers through the ages is simply this. Go within as deeply as you may. Open to those portions of the mind which seem less accessible. Allow your consciousness to become clear, so that you may receive what is beneath the surface. That is all. No posture, no technique, no grade.

What the waters give back, when the diving continues, is a way of living with the self. For there is much within any mind which is unaccepted, he says, and it is very human to turn away from those portions. But listen to the method he offers for self-acceptance. See yourself first, he says. Accept the self you see. Forgive it. And then begin to love it, for it is the Creator, experiencing the infinite creation in a completely unique fashion. He adds that this is one of the most difficult teachings ever attempted through this group, and you can feel the care in that admission.

He is honest about the work ahead, too. The path is extremely long, he says, and very seldom, if ever, reached on purpose. It is by accident, and by grace, that an entity perceives the path at all. And each, in each life, in each day, in each moment, moves slowly through it, seldom knowing which way the path turns. Patience, he says. Patience with yourself, patience with others, patience with the Creator. And as the patience grows, the love grows. And when the patience is fully grown, the self is loved as a part of the Creator. And at that moment, all things are loved, for there is nothing which is not a portion of the one Creator.

So the invitation tonight is quiet and radical. Stop skating. Pick a door into the deep water. Dive, accept what you find, and dive again. The lake is bigger than the ice you live on.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Clay Vessel
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the clay vessel.

The voices called L/Leema speak tonight about service, and they begin with an image of startling plainness. Think of yourself, they say, as a clay vessel. A pot. A jar. Something made of the most ordinary substance in the world.

Whatever kind of work you are called to do, they say, you will not do it by force of the self as the clay vessel. The pot does not fill itself. It must be lifted by something beyond itself, moved aside so that the contents may flow through. And here is the part that takes real honesty. There is no place, in this teaching, for being the pot. In order to be a servant of the Creator, they say, the self must be emptied. Only then can the vessel be lifted and poured out in service to another.

Listen to how they describe what flows through when the emptying happens. An energy, a light, a power which is of the Creator, flowing through the instrument, moving it into a specific work, a specific task, a specific lesson or service which is designed for that instrument and no other. You are not generic. You are a particular vessel, shaped for a particular pouring.

And the ground where this happens matters. They borrow an old phrase, and you have heard it before, but they place it where it belongs. The place on which thou standest is holy ground. For the service the instrument may render, they say, is performed in the presence of the Creator, upon holy ground, at all times and in all places. Not only in temples. Not only in meditation. In the kitchen, in the car, at the desk.

I love how they handle the question of results, because this is where most service quietly dies. The vessel, they say, does not decide what the pouring accomplishes. They tell of a teacher who gave his entire life to a people and watched them reject him in the end, and yet the words he spoke grew in the centuries after, precisely as the Creator intended. You may not live to see what the emptying was for. That is not your portion. Your portion is the emptiness, the willingness, the letting the current move through.

There is also a tenderness here about surrender that is easy to miss. The vessel does not strive to become gold. It stays clay. Ordinary, cracked, nothing special. What makes it holy is not what it is made of. It is that it has been lifted.

So tonight's question is not what you will accomplish. It is whether you will let yourself be picked up. Emptied of the need to control the outcome. Placed on holy ground, wherever your feet happen to be. And poured.

Thank you for listening.

title: When Nothing Changes
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: when nothing changes.

One of the questioners tonight wants to know about the big changes. The harvest, the upheavals, the turning of the planet. Hatonn's answer is quietly subversive, because it does not deny that changes are coming. It relocates them.

There is, he says, a pattern to the planet. It will continue for some time in the same pattern of activity it has known. There will be alterations, and the alterations will become more pronounced, but they will not take place on a great scale in any one moment. They will take place gradually. And then he says something that stops the whole speculation in its tracks. It matters little, he says, whether you know the dates, the places, the predictions. What matters is what you do with the days you are given.

Because the change he is actually interested in is not happening to the planet. It is happening to you. Each seeker, he says, is moving through their own harvest, their own transformation, and that process is underway right now, in the middle of the ordinary day. The outer events are the backdrop. The inner events are the play.

Listen to how he puts the choice. Each of you, he says, has the opportunity to seek, to find, and to serve, and this opportunity is always present, regardless of what the planet is doing. The question is never really what the world will look like. The question is what you will look like, from the inside, when you have finished becoming.

I love the steadiness of this. It refuses panic and it refuses passivity at the same time. Panic, because the outer changes do not define you. Passivity, because the inner change is entirely your responsibility. You cannot wait for the world to transform you. You have to do the transforming, one choice at a time, in the middle of the untransformed world.

And there is a gentleness in his manner of answering that is itself part of the teaching. He does not scold the questioner for asking about predictions. He simply keeps returning the attention to the place where attention actually changes something. The present. The heart. The next act of service, offered freely, with no one watching.

So when nothing around you seems to change, the teaching tonight says, check within. The glacier is moving. It moves in the dark, under the ice, a fraction at a time, and it carves the valley whether anyone sees it or not.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Gifts We Bring
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the gifts we bring.

The voices called L/Leema open with a small, human scene. The group has been discussing a wedding gift for two friends, and what would be appropriate. Leema takes the occasion and gently turns it inside out. The question is not what the gift should be, they say. The question is what you have to give, and what it means to give it.

And then they describe the gifts that actually matter, and the list is nothing like a registry. The gifts you truly have to offer, they say, are your willingness, your patience, your courage, your unselfishness, and your enthusiasm. Listen to that list again. Willingness. Patience. Courage. Unselfishness. Enthusiasm. No object on earth carries what these carry. No price tag, no wrapping, no occasion required.

I love how they connect this to the deepest structure of the self. What you are, they say, at the very center, is love. And love cannot be contained. It overflows. It reaches out a hand. And that reaching, that simple gesture of the hand extended toward another, is the gift. Not the thing in the hand. The reaching.

There is also a quiet realism here about giving in this world. The illusion, they say, is full of confusion about what is valuable. We have been trained to measure generosity in objects, in amounts, in gestures that can be photographed. But the true gifts, they say, move invisibly. Patience, given to someone who is difficult, is a fortune. Courage, lent to someone who is afraid, is a treasure. Willingness, offered without being asked, is rarer than gold.

And they are honest about what giving costs. The hand that reaches out, they say, does not always find another hand. The gift is not always received, not always understood, not always returned. But the nature of love, they say, is that it gives regardless. The reaching is the point. The rest belongs to the other.

So the wedding gift, in the end, was never about the wedding. It was about the practice of being the kind of being from whom true gifts flow. And that practice does not end when the occasion ends. It is a way of moving through the world, hand extended, offering the only things you truly own.

Willingness. Patience. Courage. Unselfishness. Enthusiasm. The gifts we bring.

Thank you for listening.

title: Tunnels Toward the Light
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: tunnels toward the light.

Tonight Hatonn is in a playful, almost riddling mood, and the image he offers is one of the strangest and most memorable in the archive. Imagine, he says, a vast maze of tunnels, all of them winding and twisting in every direction, and every single one of them leading to the same light at the center.

You are in one of those tunnels. Everyone you meet is in one of those tunnels. Some tunnels run close together for a while, and the travelers can hear each other through the walls, and sometimes they even break through and walk together for a stretch. Some tunnels seem to head away from the light for a long time before curving back. But all of them, he says, without exception, end at the same brightness.

I love what this does to the question of other people's paths. The tunnel that looks wrong from inside yours may be curving back toward the light in ways you cannot see. The traveler who seems lost may be on the long way around. Judgment, in this picture, becomes almost comical. You are judging the curvature of a tunnel you cannot see the end of.

But he does not leave the image as mere comfort. He gives it teeth. For the maze has its dangers, he says, and the chief of them is the temptation to stop walking. To sit down in the tunnel and declare that the tunnel is the destination. To mistake a resting place for the light. The teaching is not that every stopping point is fine. It is that every genuine movement, however winding, is movement toward the same center.

Listen to how he describes the light itself. It is not a reward at the end of the maze. It is the nature of the maze. The tunnels exist because the light exists, and every step through them is a step the light made possible. You do not earn the brightness by navigating correctly. You navigate because the brightness is already there, pulling.

And there is a practical counsel woven through the riddle. When you meet another traveler, he says, do not try to drag them into your tunnel. Walk with them in theirs for a while, if they will have you. Share what light you have found. And keep walking your own. The maze is vast enough for every pace, and the center is patient enough for every route.

So if your path has been twisting lately, if it has doubled back on itself, if it has passed through stretches so dark you wondered whether you were still moving toward anything at all, tonight's image is for you. You are in a tunnel. The tunnel leads to the light. Keep walking.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Shipwreck and the Castle
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the shipwreck and the castle.

Hatonn tells a story tonight, and it begins in a storm. A ship goes down, and a sailor is thrown into black water, fighting for his life, certain he will drown. And then, through the rain and the dark, he sees it. A castle, lit from within, standing on the shore. He swims toward the light with everything he has left.

The castle, it turns out, is empty of people but full of warmth. There is food. There is a fire. There is a bed. The sailor eats, sleeps, wakes, and for a while he lives there in peace, exploring the great halls, looking out at the sea that nearly killed him. He begins to think he has found his home.

But the sea has not finished with him. One morning he wakes and the castle is gone. Not ruined. Gone. And he is back in the water, in another storm, fighting again. This happens again and again. Shipwreck, castle, storm. Refuge, then the deep water. Each time the castle appears when he most needs it. Each time it vanishes when he has rested.

Listen to what Hatonn says the story means, because he does not leave it as a riddle. The shipwreck, he says, is the life you thought you were living, the one that was carrying you somewhere, until it broke apart. The storm is the catalyst that breaks it, the loss, the illness, the ending you did not choose. And the castle is the peace that meets you in the middle of it, the strange, unearned refuge that appears exactly when you cannot go on.

And the vanishing. This is the part I keep turning over. The castle does not stay, he says, because you were never meant to live in the refuge. The refuge is for resting. The water is for swimming. Peace is not the destination. It is the provision for the journey.

I love the honesty of this. It does not promise that the storms will stop. It promises that the castle will keep appearing. Again and again, in the middle of the dark water, there will be light on the shore, and warmth, and rest. Not permanently. Not as a reward for swimming well. As grace, given to a drowning sailor who did nothing to earn it but keep swimming.

So if you are in the water tonight, look for the light. It has appeared before. It will appear again. Rest when it comes. And when it vanishes, and it will, swim on. The shore you are really heading for is further than any castle.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Telephone Within
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the telephone within.

The voices called L/Leema begin with something practical, almost technical, and it turns out to be about the most intimate thing there is. Communication, they say, is the great art of the seeker, and the first communication you must master is not with other people. It is with yourself.

They describe the self as layered. On the surface, the conscious mind, busy, verbal, full of plans and opinions. Beneath it, the deeper self, quiet, vast, holding what the surface cannot hold. And between them, they say, there must be a line of communication. Most seekers, they say, live with that line down. The surface chatters. The depths wait. And the two rarely speak.

Listen to how they say the line gets repaired. Meditation, they say, and they mean something very specific by it. Not an escape from the noise, but a deliberate sitting down at the telephone. You quiet the surface mind, not by force, but by patience, and you listen inward. At first there is nothing. Then there is static. Then, slowly, the deeper self begins to speak, and what it says is almost always simpler and truer than what the surface was shouting.

I love the realism here. They do not promise that the deep self will tell you what to do about your job or your marriage. They promise something better. That the deep self will tell you who you are, underneath the noise about the job and the marriage. And from that knowing, the decisions start making themselves.

There is also a counsel about other people woven through the evening, and it follows from the first teaching. Just as you must learn to listen to your own depths before you speak from your surface, you must learn to listen to another's depths before you judge their surface. The same telephone. The same patience. The same willingness to sit through the static.

And they are honest about the discipline this requires. The surface mind, they say, does not like to be quieted. It has opinions about the silence. It will tell you that you are wasting time, that nothing is happening, that you should get up and do something useful. The seeker, they say, must learn to smile at all of that and stay seated. The line is being repaired. The static is not failure. The static is the sound of the connection forming.

So tonight's practice is almost embarrassingly small. Sit down. Quiet the chatter. Pick up the telephone within. And listen, with the patience you would give a beloved friend, for the voice underneath your own.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Messenger and the Message
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the messenger and the message.

Hatonn speaks tonight about discernment, and he begins with a scene anyone who has followed a teacher will recognize. A messenger arrives carrying something genuine, something of real value. And the crowd, he says, cannot see past the messenger. They argue about the messenger's manner, the messenger's past, the messenger's style. The message sits unopened while the debate about the carrier consumes everything.

Listen to how sharply he draws this. It is a habit of the mind, he says, to judge the vessel instead of tasting the contents. We do it with teachers, with books, with friends who tell us hard truths. If the messenger is odd, or flawed, or unfamiliar, we dismiss the message without ever examining it. And if the messenger is impressive, we swallow the message whole without examining it either. Both are the same error. Both are looking at the wrong thing.

The discipline he proposes is simple and demanding. Look at what is being said, he says. Test it against what you know of love, of truth, of the deep things. Does it ring? Does it open? Does it make you kinder, braver, more honest? Then it does not matter who carried it. A flawed messenger can carry a true message. An impressive messenger can carry an empty one. The message is what you are being asked to judge.

I love the freedom in this. It releases you from the endless evaluation of people and returns you to the evaluation of ideas. You do not have to decide whether the teacher is enlightened. You do not have to defend or attack the source. You only have to ask, of the words in front of you, whether they are true. That is a smaller job, and a much more honest one.

And there is a second edge to the teaching, for those who carry messages themselves. If you would serve as a messenger, he says, then be clean about your motive. Speak what you have found, and let the message stand on its own. Do not demand that others admire the carrier. The moment you need them to think well of you, you have stopped serving the message and started serving yourself.

So tonight, when the next voice arrives claiming to carry something important, and it will, pause before you judge the voice. Open the message first. Taste it. Test it. Keep what rings true and release the rest, and let the messenger be whoever they are. The truth, if it is true, does not need an impressive carrier. It only needs an open reader.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Ancient Stone
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the ancient stone.

Hatonn begins with something you could walk past a thousand times without seeing. A stone, old beyond reckoning, half-buried in moss at the edge of a wood. It has been there longer than any living thing around it. It will be there long after they are gone. And he asks the group to consider it, really consider it, because the stone is teaching something.

The stone, he says, does not hurry. It does not strive. It does not measure its progress or worry that it is falling behind. It simply is, in its place, through rain and sun and winter, being exactly what it is. And in that stillness, he says, it holds a kind of wisdom the busy mind cannot reach. The wisdom of remaining.

Listen to how he connects this to the seeker. The spiritual path, he says, is long. Longer than a lifetime, longer than many lifetimes. And the seeker who measures it in days and weeks will always feel they are failing, because the movement is too slow to see. But the movement is real. Like the stone, shaped grain by grain by water and wind, the self is being shaped by every experience, every meditation, every act of love, whether the shaping is visible or not.

I love what this does to impatience. Impatience, he suggests, is the surface mind demanding that the deep work show results on the surface schedule. But the deep work does not keep that schedule. It keeps the stone's schedule. It moves at the pace of geology, of seasons, of roots growing in the dark. And the seeker who can accept that pace finds a strange peace. The urgency drains away. What remains is the quiet confidence that the shaping is happening.

There is also a tenderness here about aging, about the long arc of a life. The stone does not grieve its youth. It does not wish it were a different stone. It has settled into what it is, and in that settling there is a dignity the young, striving things cannot have. The seeker, he says, can learn this. To stop fighting the shape of your own life. To let the moss grow where it grows.

And he closes the image with something I want to leave you with. The stone, for all its stillness, is not separate from the life around it. The moss needs the stone. The ferns need its shade. The small creatures need its crevices. By simply remaining, being exactly what it is, the stone serves everything around it. So with you, he says. Your steady presence, your quiet being, is itself a service. You do not have to do more. You have to be more fully what you are.

The ancient stone. Still there. Still teaching.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Well Within
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the well within.

The voices called L/Leema speak tonight about virtue, and they begin by turning the usual idea of it upside down. Virtue, they say, is not a list of rules. It is not behavior imposed from the outside, not the careful performance of goodness. True virtue, they say, flows from within, like water from a well. And no one can draw that water for you.

Listen to how they describe the difference. There is the virtue that is put on, like a garment, for occasions, for observers, for the approval of others. It looks right. It sounds right. But it has no source. And then there is the virtue that rises, unforced, from a self that has been quietly transformed. Kindness that was not decided upon. Patience that was not performed. Honesty that costs nothing because there is nothing to hide. The first is decoration. The second is nature.

I love the image of the well, because a well cannot be hurried. You cannot command water to rise. You can only keep the well clean, keep it deep, keep it open to the underground springs. And the keeping of the well, they say, is the real spiritual work. Meditation. Honesty. The slow facing of what is in you. The water rises on its own schedule, and when it rises, it rises pure.

And they are honest about what pollutes the well. Fear, they say. Self-concern. The constant calculating of how things look, what others think, whether you are getting enough.

These do not just produce bad behavior. They muddy the source itself, so that even the good acts come up cloudy. The work is not to act better. The work is to become clearer, so that better action is what naturally flows.

There is a gentleness here about failure that I want to linger on. When the well gives muddy water, they say, the answer is not to condemn the well. It is to keep drawing. To keep cleaning. Every bucket of cloudy water removed is progress, even if the next bucket is cloudy too. The well is being cleared. The spring is still there, underneath, waiting.

So the question tonight is not whether you have been good. It is whether your goodness has a source. Are you performing virtue, or are you becoming the kind of being from whom virtue flows? The well within is deep. Keep it clean. Keep drawing. The water will come.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Broken Bread
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the broken bread.

The voice tonight is Oxal, and they speak of brokenness. Not as tragedy. As necessity. As the very mechanism by which transformation happens.

They begin with bread. Bread, they say, must be broken to be shared. A whole loaf feeds no one. It sits, complete and useless, until hands break it, and only in the breaking does it become food. The cup, too, must be poured out. What is held inside, kept safe, kept whole, nourishes no one.

Listen to how they turn this on the self. The self, they say, is like the bread. As long as it remains whole, intact, defended, it cannot feed anyone, not even itself. It is the breaking that opens it. The cracking of the certainties. The shattering of the image you have so carefully maintained. These feel like ruin. They are, they say, the beginning of usefulness.

I love the tenderness with which they speak of this, because they know how we resist it. No one volunteers for breaking. We spend our lives trying to stay whole, to hold ourselves together, to avoid the crack. And they do not mock that effort. They simply observe that the wholeness we defend so fiercely is the wholeness of the loaf on the shelf. Impressive. Untouched. And feeding no one.

And there is a second movement to the teaching. The breaking, they say, is not the end. Bread broken is bread shared, and in the sharing something new happens. The broken pieces, given away, become part of other lives. The self that has been broken open, poured out in service, discovers that it is not diminished by the giving. It is multiplied. What was one loaf becomes food for many.

They are honest that this is not comfortable. The breaking hurts. The pouring out feels like loss. There will be moments, they say, when you look at the pieces of what you were and grieve the wholeness. Let yourself grieve it. But do not try to glue it back together. The pieces are not a problem to be solved. They are bread, waiting to be shared.

So tonight's teaching is one of the oldest and hardest. Do not fear the breaking. The loaf must be broken. The cup must be poured. And you, in your own breaking, are becoming food for a hungry world.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Eternal Now
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the eternal now.

Hatonn speaks tonight about time, and his first move is to dissolve it. What you call the past, he says, and what you call the future, are conveniences of the surface mind. Beneath them, there is only the eternal now, the single moment in which everything actually happens, and has always happened, and will always happen.

Listen to how practically he means this. The seeker, he says, is always postponing. I will meditate when things settle down. I will be kind when I am less tired. I will seek when the crisis passes. But the crisis never passes, he says, because the postponement is the crisis. There is no later in which the seeking will be easier. There is only now, which is the only place seeking has ever occurred.

I love the directness of this. It cuts through every excuse at once, not with judgment, but with a kind of physics. You cannot seek yesterday. You cannot seek tomorrow.
