The session also speaks to the specific anguish of the seeker who feels she should be further along. If only I understood more, she thinks, I would be at peace. Q'uo's answer is gentle and firm. Understanding is not the gate. Surrender is the gate. The peace you are seeking does not come after the answers. It comes from releasing the demand for them.

I want to close with the session's most practical counsel, because it is small enough to try tonight. When the mind starts its circling, its demanding, its building of cases for why you need to know right now, pause. Place a hand on the heart, literally if you like. Ask the heart what it knows. Then listen, without requiring the mind to agree. The two ways of knowing do not have to match. They only have to take turns leading.

So tonight, if you are lying awake with unanswered questions, try what they suggest. Relax. The water holds you. The dawn we spoke of in an earlier episode does not require your understanding in order to arrive.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Trap of Assumptions
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the trap of assumptions.

This session comes from early April, nineteen ninety-two, and the question on the table is about one of the mind's most automatic habits. We assume. We assume we know what another person meant, what they intended, what they feel about us. How much of our suffering, the questioner asks, is built on these unexamined assumptions?

Those of Q'uo answer with an honesty that implicates all of us. A very large portion, they say. The mind is a meaning-making instrument, and it abhors a vacuum. Where information is missing, it supplies it, drawing on past experience, on fear, on hope, on the oldest patterns laid down in childhood. Most of the time, we never notice the supplying. We mistake the assumption for a perception.

I love the example they work with, because it is so ordinary. Someone does not return your greeting, and within seconds the mind has built a story. They are angry with me. I did something wrong. They have always been cold. The actual truth might be that they did not hear you, or were lost in their own worry, or were simply having a bad morning. But the assumption, once installed, begins to generate feelings, and the feelings begin to generate behavior, and soon the relationship has a chill that no one intended and everyone can feel.

The session names the mechanism precisely. Assumption is the mind's attempt to feel safe by feeling certain. If I know what you think of me, I can prepare. If I know what will happen, I cannot be surprised. But the certainty is counterfeit. It is a story the mind tells to cover the discomfort of not knowing. And the cost of the cover story is that we stop seeing the person in front of us and start relating to the character we have cast them as.

Q'uo's counsel is simple to state and genuinely difficult to practice. When you catch an assumption forming, they say, name it as an assumption. Not as a fact. As a hypothesis. I am assuming she is upset with me. The naming creates a small gap, and in that gap there is room for curiosity. And curiosity, they suggest, is the solvent in which assumptions dissolve.

There is a passage here about asking that I think is the practical heart of the session. The antidote to assumption, they say, is the question asked in genuine openness. Not the leading question. Not the accusation dressed as inquiry. The real question, the one to which you do not already know the answer. Are you all right? Did I misunderstand? What is happening for you? These small questions, asked sincerely, dismantle stories that might otherwise run for years.

The session also turns the lens inward, and this is the part I find most challenging. We assume about ourselves as well. I am the kind of person who always does this. I will never be good at that. The identity we have assembled from old evidence becomes a set of assumptions about what is possible, and we live inside them the way we live inside a house whose walls we no longer see. To question the assumption about the self, they say, is the beginning of real freedom.

I want to close with the image they offer for the alternative. The mind without its assumptions, they suggest, is like a room with the windows open. Things can come in. Air moves. You might be surprised, and surprise, in this account, is not a threat. It is the feeling of reality getting in past the story.

So tonight, a small practice from the archive. Notice one assumption you are carrying about someone close to you. Just one. Name it as an assumption, out loud if you can. And then, if you are brave, ask the question that would test it. You might be surprised by what comes through the open window.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Gift of Service
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the gift of service.

This session comes from early April, nineteen ninety-two, and it is unusual in the archive for its form. It is a dialogue. Two voices speak, Aaron and those of Q'uo, in conversation with each other and with the group. The question on the table is about service. What does it mean to serve, truly? And what is given, and what is received, in the act?

Aaron speaks first, and their teaching has the warmth of someone who has watched many seekers tie themselves in knots over this. Service, they say, is not a performance. It is not the grand gesture, the visible sacrifice, the thing that earns the admiration of others. The truest service is very often invisible, even to the one who serves. A kindness done without thinking. A patience extended without effort. A presence offered without agenda.

Those of Q'uo take up the thread, and they add the metaphysical frame. To serve another, they say, is to serve the Creator, for there is no other. But they are precise about what this does not mean. It does not mean erasing yourself. It does not mean the martyr's bargain, in which the servant is diminished so that the served may grow. True service, they say, enlarges both. The giver and the receiver are both fed by the same act.

I love the passage where the two voices converge on the question of motive, because it is so psychologically honest. The desire to serve can itself become a distortion, they agree. The servant who needs to be needed. The helper who cannot rest. The giver who keeps accounts, remembering every kindness extended and quietly expecting return. Aaron names this with particular gentleness. If your service leaves you resentful, they suggest, look at the expectation underneath. The resentment is information. It is showing you where the giving stopped being free.

Q'uo adds the teaching on discernment that the session keeps circling back to. Not every request is yours to answer. Not every need you see is a call for you to meet it. The servant who says yes to everything, they say, will eventually serve no one well, least of all herself. Discernment is not selfishness. It is the stewardship of the gift, the recognition that the energy for service is finite in the incarnation and must be allocated with wisdom.

There is a beautiful exchange here about receiving, which is the part of service our culture least understands. To receive graciously, Aaron says, is itself a form of service. For the giver needs the gift to be received, and the one who cannot receive blocks the circuit. Many seekers, they observe, are generous givers and terrible receivers, and the imbalance eventually hollows the giving. To let yourself be served, to accept help without apology, is to complete the circle.

The dialogue turns, near its close, to the smallest scale of all, and this is where I think the session lands its deepest point. The greatest service, both voices agree, is very often the quietest. The way you greet the cashier. The patience you extend to the difficult colleague. The attention you give to the person no one else notices. These are not consolation prizes for those who cannot do great things. They are the great things, seen up close.

Q'uo closes with a reframing I want to leave you with. You do not serve in order to become worthy, they say. You serve because you already are, and the serving is the expression of it. The gift was never the act. The gift was the love that moved through the act, and that love was yours before you gave anything at all.

So tonight, if you are wondering whether your small kindnesses count, the archive's answer is yes. They are the whole of it. The gift of service is not in the size of the gesture. It is in the freedom of the giving.

Thank you for listening.

title: Being Service
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: being service.

Tonight we sit in on a rare conversation. It is April of nineteen ninety-two, and two teachers are speaking together through two channels: Aaron and Q'uo. Their subject is service, and they want to pull it apart in a way that might surprise you.

Aaron begins with a distinction. There is doing service, and there is being service. Listen to how they put it: being service is simply opening yourself and moving away from any duality. Doing service, they say, creates a distortion of self and other, of server and served. I love that line because it names something I think many of us have felt. The moment we decide to be the helper, we have quietly made the other person the helped, and something unequal creeps in.

Aaron notices something funny about us. Those who aspire to serve, they say, grasp so hard at something innate to them. The real question is not how to serve better, but where your natural service gets blocked by fear. Watch for that blockage, and the service takes care of itself.

Then Aaron tells a story that has stayed with me. It is about the one you know as Jesus. A poor village welcomed him and laid out a meal, the best of what they had, elaborate by their standards, simple by yours. He was served first and took a bowl. And as he sat there with the bowl in his hands, he saw children at the edge of the circle. An elder rose to shoo them off. This child is the son of one who disdains your teachings, he said. Get out of here. Go.

One boy hung back. He was nine or ten years old, emaciated, with sores on his body. Jesus got up and walked toward him. The boy was frightened, because he had been told to leave, and here was this stranger walking toward him. And Jesus said gently, do not be afraid, I will not hurt you. Do you want food? And he offered him that bowl. While the boy ate, he asked for cloth and water and washed his sores. Then he came back to his seat and took another bowl.

No lecture about service. No words like, you should love your enemy. No verbal teaching at all. He simply served. Aaron says there is no teaching received in all their many lives on service that has touched them as deeply as that one. Just that. One child who needed to be fed at that moment, fed, and his sores washed.

Q'uo picks up the thread. Many seekers feel guilty for taking time to work within their own consciousness, while others grow proud, insisting ordinary life must take second place to the inner work. But either way, Q'uo says, the time spent working on the self is part of the service, not separate from it.

Here is a practice Q'uo offers, and it is wonderfully concrete. Examine your thoughts for the last hour. Were you nervous? Irritated? Impatient? That which you think of another, you think also of the self. So make an appointment. Let nervousness, irritation, impatience, anger, resentment, disappointment all see the doctor within. Let them sink in and find their root and their home. Then touch that home with your compassion, your love, and your redeeming forgiveness of self by self.

Aaron returns with a story about the teacher Gurdjieff. In his community there was a man unpleasant in every way: he did not do his share of the work, spoke harshly, and smelled foul. Nobody wanted him there. One day he left, and Gurdjieff went after him and offered to pay him to return. The community was aghast. Gurdjieff answered: he is the yeast for the bread. How would you learn compassion without a catalyst for that compassion? How would you learn non-judgment without a catalyst for that non-judgment?

Q'uo closes with two words Aaron and they have long discussed. Go higher. When a trouble bubble flies at you, to lose the game is to catch it and fall under its weight. To win is to leap toward it in joy, praise, and thanksgiving, and as the bubble meets that sea of joy, it simply pops. There will always be another bubble. Leap toward it anyway.

And then, at the very end, a moment of plain human honesty. Aaron speaks of a wrenching cry from somewhere inside Barbara: yes, all of these thoughts are fine, but how do I do this? And Aaron answers gently. This is the gift of being human. It is not going to go away. You will never become pure service, constantly and without error, while in this incarnation. And yet, each moment given with mindful attention and love brings you closer to that beautiful ideal.

Each moment of attention to the fear arising in you brings you closer to non-judgmental acceptance of everything within the experience of mind and body. Not mine or yours, but all of ours. It is this unconditional love that you are here to learn and practice and express in whatever ways you are able.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Wind Chimes
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the wind chimes.

Tonight we join a Sunday meditation from the spring of ninety-two. The group has asked Q'uo about hurrying. Not just hurrying through the day, but hurrying through life so fast that the details blur and some of the experience is lost. What steps, they ask, can bring change? How do we slow down and actually enjoy each experience more fully?

Q'uo answers with an image I keep coming back to. As they listen to the chimes swaying and singing in the wind outside, they suggest this: wind chimes do not have a previous agenda. The wind moves them. They readily yield. And when two pieces of metal touch, the pleasing sound is emitted for which this instrument was created.

So it is with a human instrument, they say. Metaphysically speaking, there are winds that come and sometimes are still, winds from one direction or another, at one speed or another. No entity can process all the information pouring through the physical senses. There is a thousand, nay, ten thousand times too much. So a ruthless choosing goes on. What seems most tied to survival and comfort gets noticed first. Everything else falls away.

Then there are the metaphysical winds. Strong trade winds of destiny, blowing from forever. And the delightful, unpredictable whims of spirit. The dance between destiny and free will. Rushing through life is not only a physical habit, Q'uo says. It is a spiritual one.

Here is the part that might sting a little. Q'uo observes that rushing without rhythm, without awareness of the winds, carries a negative cast. It controls and orders the self for the benefit of the self. Yet the people who rush rarely mean any such thing. Their reason for moving so fast is usually service to others, the wish that the utmost be done. The doing is intended as love. The result is a kind of spiritual static.

And then, quickly, a warning against judging yourself for this. Do not assume that because you see the negative cast of the attitude, you are a negatively oriented person. Under no circumstances, they say, should a spiritual student try to monitor its rate of success or its place within the journey. One looks into the same informational system and pulls out both the question and the answer. The Creator will not inform any entity of its spiritual score. The Creator grades on a curve.

Q'uo paints a picture of the hurrier. Someone stands ignorant of the wind, gazing only at the compass, saying doggedly, this I shall do now, then this, one step then another. I shall go north. I shall always go north. I have my compass and I shall go north. And they shall not go long, Q'uo says, before they run into a tree, a bus, a child, or some wind of destiny that, if caught, if heard, if felt, could transform the experience.

The characteristic feeling of the dogged and determined and unrhythmical life is a deadening of experience. A numbing of enjoyment. A killing of the gift of spontaneity. And the greatest hindrance to change, Q'uo says, is the honest and genuine belief that one is actually fine just as one is.

So what can you do to change the program of rushing? Q'uo will not tell you to do anything. You are already doing too much. Nor will they tell you to do nothing, because this is subtler work than that. They ask you to ponder at odd moments how you feel about the rhythms of life. How you feel about missing the dances. How you might feel about unwittingly behaving in a way that gives others a harsher catalyst than you intend.

Then a question from the circle. In all that was said, the questioner heard nothing about how to help a companion, a loved one, in this quest for the rhythms of life. Is it simply not anyone's place to do that work for another?

Q'uo answers with care. One cannot work for another or change another. That is neither appropriate nor possible. Each entity's life is generated from patterns built over a lifetime, set in motion by choices made before this incarnation. The free will of each is paramount.

What you can do, they say, is provide the atmosphere of support. Begin from a point of view as filled with compassion as possible, so that understanding and support may be given without qualification. This gives the other entity the free and open reach for seeking change, and adds no obstacle but the ones they find within themselves.

If you try to tinker with their inner process, the desire to aid becomes distorted into the desire to change them in a way that meets your needs rather than theirs. So the greatest aid is simply to provide the atmosphere, and let their free will operate within it.

So tonight's teaching comes down to something very simple. The chimes do not schedule the wind. They hang, they wait, they yield, and the music happens. Your body is a small boat on a physical sea and a metaphysical one. Learn the weather. Put the compass among your other instruments instead of staring at it alone. And when someone you love is also learning to listen for the wind, you cannot listen for them. You can only make the room quiet enough, and kind enough, that they can hear it for themselves.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Vine and the Branches
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the vine and the branches.

Tonight's session asks the biggest question there is. What is truth? The group wants to know how to find their own truth beneath habits and fears, and how to share it with others without imposing it. Q'uo begins with a small story about the channel herself, and it sets the tone for everything that follows.

On this day, the channel had been tuning herself by focusing on the suffering servant, on the sorrowing Christ. And Q'uo gently noticed that this tilted her perception. The one known as Jesus, they said, is not a man upon a cross, suffering unselfishly. He is an entity willing to do the will of the one infinite Creator at whatever cost to itself. That willingness, not the suffering, is the essential Christ consciousness.

Listen to how they describe that consciousness. A personality consisting of one query: what is Your will for me, beloved Creator, father and teacher? It lacks salt, lacks personality, lacks any mask. It is infinitely vulnerable, infinitely willing, infinitely desirous of serving. Does this consciousness not feel full of light, almost a quality of floating, of being lighter than the air you breathe?

And yet, they say, the circle is not levitating. Each of you remains glued by gravity and humanity to an illusion in which there must be the persona, the mask. In your incarnation you shall not know a factual, provable, repeatable truth. All your truths shall be subjectively perceived, subjectively proven, and subjectively held. They are not transferable.

Q'uo asks a strange question. Why would the Logos, the Original Thought of love that created all that there is, build an illusion where serious choices must be made without sure and certain knowledge? Their answer comes through a parable. The one known as Jesus said: I am the vine, you are the branches. Deep within each of you, they say, lies the consciousness of Christ, rooted in that one great creative Original Thought. From these roots grows a vine, and as the roots are made of love, so the vine is love.

Imagine, they say, a spiritual self waking in the crib of experience. Its first thought is: what is truth? What is happening? I see between the bars of my crib but it all is so loud, so stunning, and so much. Where is the sense? Where is the truth? And as it grows it makes choices, and each choice bends the branch a little.

Think of the twists and turns of your own branch, they say. The times you turned your leaves to the sun, and the times you sheltered them because the sun burned too hot. The times you sprayed pesticides on yourself because you felt threatened by other branches. Yet do not all the branches of the vine have the same root? They do.

So how do you dwell in a way that makes those moments more accessible? Move, as always, to the inner closet of meditation. Open yourself to the silence. Sometimes speak, which you call prayer, but oh so importantly listen. Allow the silence to wash over you until you are full and more than full. Open inwardly if you would wish to open outwardly.

The more grounded a spirit becomes in this root system of love, the more the grounding informs the persona, and the more transparent that persona becomes to the love itself. The straightest road to the roots of being is bathed in silence.

And then Q'uo offers an opinion on how we treat with each other. The greatest truth each may offer each, they say, is the truth of fearlessness. When one abandons fear and speaks from as close to the heart as one may find the grace to speak, one is as open as possible to that which cannot thrive in fear: honest and open communication.

Then their last secret, and it is my favorite part of the night. There is great truth in laughter. One who takes himself seriously and goes solemnly about the business of telling the truth will find himself with his leaves turned away from the sun, unfed by light and love. Take a light touch, each of you, with yourselves. Love and care passionately. Burn for your highest ideals. But not for your own performances and behaviors. At these you may laugh.

How glorious you are in your folly, oh humans, they say. How glorious is your search for the truth, and how telling are your choices. To be human and to be foolish is to say one thing twice. You will be foolish. Enjoy the folly that allows you to care so much, too much, that you risk everything and leap into midair knowing nothing, because of your love of a mystery you know only by faith and hope.

In the questions, the group asks about Q'uo's claim that there is no truth, and yet a truth to be experienced later, and that no truth is final. Q'uo clarifies: words cannot transfer what truth is, but there will be opportunities, in this life or beyond, to experience unity with the Creator directly. And because the Creator learns through each portion of Itself, what was true gets added to. Creation builds upon creation.

What is truth? Each of you is the truth, yet to be born. Nurture yourselves, and smile as you wait in care and intention for the days of understanding that are yours in a life yet to be experienced.

Thank you for listening.

title: Bread Upon the Waters
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: bread upon the waters.

Tonight's question comes from a tender place. The group asks about service that seems to fall short. What about visiting someone who will not remember you were there, an elder whose memory is failing, a person whose drinking has blurred the days? What about serving someone whose life is so set in its patterns that you cannot feel any real contact, any recognition, any change? What consolation is there in continuing to serve when the service seems to land nowhere?

Q'uo begins by reframing the question. When we ask what service is not such a good service, there are two ways to look: from the viewpoint of the one serving, and from the viewpoint of the one being served. And the needs of any entity are never completely apparent. Entities seldom know their own needs. So the servant is bound to be confused sometimes, trying to judge what service is appropriate.

True service, they say, works with spiritual principles that aid the other in spiritual maturation. But here is the caution. If a servant is ruled only by the calm logic of spiritual principles in the abstract, the servant moves from a place of impersonal compassion, comfortably separated from any deep fellow feeling for the one being served. So inform yourself with principles, yes, but let it be the wisdom of the heart that moves you into open and full giving of the self without reservation. Not the temperate demands of logic.

At the heart of the night's question is the ache of the unthanked servant. And Q'uo offers a shift of perception that I think is worth sitting with. They draw a distinction between the small self and the capital Self. The left-hand path, they say, is service to small-s self. The right-hand path is service to capital-S Self, the infinite Creator Self.

The difference is in the definition of the self. When a small self serves another small self and does not remember that it is serving the capital-S Creator Self by serving another Self, the service will feel incomplete without the thank you, without the good feeling of success. But if service is offered with the firm memory that one is serving the infinite Creator, simply serving other selves as a means to that noble end, then one can be freed of the misery of feeling unappreciated and unnoticed.

Perhaps the service is appreciated. Perhaps it is not, by the self apparently being served. But in the generation of positive intention, in the ever more purified desire to serve the one infinite Creator in all Its infinite parts, the need for recognition falls away. The need for the thank you. The need for the justification.

This is not emotionally satisfying advice, and Q'uo admits it. This is cold consolation. But then they ask you to think in memory of all the unexpected gifts of service that have moved into your life. The bread returning upon the waters, again and again, tenfold, a hundredfold, until you cannot count all the blessings. The energy for those blessings begins in the self's desire to give of the self. As it gives, it creates an energy which is forever spherical, and returns and returns and lifts you higher each time it returns.

No good intention, they say, no desire to help, is ever lost. Let the illusion's disconsolate, apparent nature never cause you to stumble on the path of service to others. Let it redouble your desire, knowing that all your love has flown to the heart of the Creator Self of this planet and is immediately a portion of the light of the world.

The questions that follow take this deeper. One questioner works with people who over-function in relationships, giving too much from a need to please or to avoid conflict, until the relationship gets out of balance and both people are crippled by it. The question is tangled, but the ache behind it is clear. If my giving is really about my own need to be acceptable, is the desire to serve in me still real?

Q'uo answers that the tangle itself has value. Its purpose is the untangling and balancing of all relationships so that love without condition may move freely. And they make a distinction I find deeply comforting. The desire to serve is the heart of all service. The uninformed desire to serve may be, at its heart, foolish, because it is not yet informed by wisdom. Wisdom comes later, in a higher density, after the lesson of love. But the foundation must be placed upon love first. Until one has the pure heartfelt desire to serve, wisdom is useless.

Carla restates it, and it is worth repeating slowly. The pathology of trying to please, of trying to avoid conflict, meets its own reward of exactly what you fear. You do not please, and you do have conflict, because you can never predict what will please someone. But beneath it all, there is that germ of desire to serve, which is healthy no matter what pathology is there.

So if you are visiting the one who will not remember, feeding the one who will not thank you, pouring yourself out where nothing seems to take root, Q'uo would ask you to remember who you are really serving. Not the small self that wants a receipt for its kindness. The one great Self in which every act of love is registered, and from which every act of love returns to you, multiplied, like bread upon the waters.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Wise Heart
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the wise heart.

Tonight the group asks the great why. Why, if there is a benevolent Creator, is there so much sorrow, suffering, sickness, violence, and disharmony in the world? Why must people go through so much difficulty just to survive? Why does the Creator not intervene?

Q'uo begins by telling you their name for themselves. They call themselves the brothers and sisters of sorrow. Not saviors. They are social entities who have moved far from their planetary home to speak to those who sorrow, who stumble, who face deeply central choices in an atmosphere profoundly lacking in trustworthy information upon which to base choice. We are not those who will save the planet, they say. You may put that phrase in quotations.

And then they widen the question until it includes every listener. It is not only the starving and the dying who are suffering. Each entity born into this illusion begins immediately a process of loss, suffering, increasing limitation and ordeal, followed by physical death. Each of you recapitulates in a leisurely manner the misery of the starving infant. It simply takes many entities longer to complete the menu of suffering. And oh, my friends, they say, there are so many interesting entrees on this menu.

Why are you in the place of suffering? They ask you to come into the same environment as those for whom you feel compassion. Each is the beaten. Each is the one who wields the instrument of beating. Each is the jury member forced to evaluate the incident. Each is the rioter. Each is the shopkeeper. Each of you lives a life that is seemingly personal, truly unique, but deeply planetary.

The group had been talking about karma before the session. Q'uo offers their opinion. Karma is a kind of residual energy or momentum. An action which produces an imbalance between giver and receiver creates a bond of imbalance. The momentum is often visualized as circular, hence the wheel of karma, the way a balance is offered again and again to those who are imbalanced. Again and again, a situation occurs in which an entity may forgive the self and the other self. When forgiveness is complete, the wheel stops.

There is societal karma too. Nations and groups have offered unbalanced action to other groups, and these mount to the heavens. And some among you, they say, have chosen to incarnate for the purpose of suffering as intensely and as long as possible, absorbing the deadening, merciless distortions of greed and slaughter that have erupted through your history. These Christ-like entities, they call them, pursuing a beautiful, poignant, and terrible service.

Why would the infinite Creator place you so firmly in a milieu of loss, ordeal, limitation, and eventual dying? Q'uo answers with a question of their own. What gets your attention: the perfect halcyon day, or the moment of toxin, the alarm, the adrenaline, the sudden movement to cope, to save, to defend?

Each of you has two minds, they say. One will keep you in this density forever. The other will evolve. The first is the intellectual mind. Its sole purpose is to manipulate the environment so you survive, find shelter, be fed, have comfort. The other mind is best described as the wise heart. Its roots move into racial, societal, planetary, and Creator mind. It is this mind that is always and forever.

The suffering, the ordeal of living, is specifically designed to grab the attention of the intellectual mind and then baffle it so thoroughly and completely that the intellectual mind gives up, and the thrust of inquiry moves to the heart.

There is no why in the heart's wisdom, nor is there any answer. The heart sees suffering and embraces it. To the heart, any entity who is thirsty is the Christ waiting for a drink. Any entity who needs clothing is the Christ waiting to be covered. The ordeals become opportunities for service, challenges worthy of attracting one's attention.

They ask each of you to touch yourselves with loving and forgiving hearts, to be healers of the self, so that each may become a healing expression to those around them. Not by word, they say. Merely by the point of view.

In the questions that follow, one questioner asks about the feeling so many carry of being away from home. Q'uo suggests that many entities on this planet journeyed here from elsewhere, to complete a cycle of learning, or to serve. They passed through the forgetting process, so they walk as citizens of this world, with only a dim homesickness for somewhere else.

But the true home, they say, is not a place. The true home of all seekers is within that service and within that light that comes from one source, the one Creator. And when the questioner asks, so home is within us, Q'uo answers: this is correct. Home is truly, as your peoples say, located where the heart is able to love.

So tonight's answer to the great why is not really an answer at all. It is a relocation. The question belongs to the intellectual mind, and the intellectual mind will never get its answer. The suffering is designed to exhaust the mind's questions until the questions themselves are surrendered, and what remains is the heart, looking at the thirsty and seeing the Christ, looking at the night watch of praying souls, and joining them.

Thank you for listening.

title: Love the Dirty Dishes
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: love the dirty dishes.

Tonight's question is about destiny and choice. How do we cooperate with our destiny? How do we use free will to make choices that change us? How can we make enlightened choices, and cooperate with our highest path in learning and serving others?

Q'uo begins by distinguishing two things people often confuse: passion and courage. People of passion and courage sit in this circle, they say, each desiring the most lucid life of service. But passion has one central lack. Although passion seems to come from deep within the heart, the untutored conscious mind cannot discriminate between the passion of the emotion, the passion of the spirit, the passion of the mind, and the passion of persuasive circumstance.

So when you approach a fork in the road, know that you have the passion to accomplish what shall be, and the courage to see it through. Then step back. Ask the self to pause, so the spirit may go into the inner room and take all adornments off. All things of the world. All the trappings of circumstance. All the aura of success and reputation and desire itself. Lay it to one side. Become of a quiet mind and a quiet heart, and say: here am I, what would you have me do? What is that highest and best that I may achieve and remain a stable person?

I love that image, the inner room. Not a temple out in the world, but a tabernacle you carry with you. A few moments spent there, asking one simple query, aids you enormously, they say, when you put the garments of reputation and success back on. You become unswayed and unimpressed by the patter and tap dancing that all of us are capable of.

In each spiritual evolution there is a repetition of information, a pattern to the individual lesson. Your incarnation is designed specifically to addle the brain and confuse the mind totally, so it is not remarkable that almost no one understands the main thrust of the work the first time.

As an example, they point at the cultural lesson about love. The culture still carries the opinion that males learn love by providing physical safety and comfort, and females learn it by sacrifice of the self. They use this to show why one cannot generalize about personal lessons. In this density, all lessons have to do with learning to love in society. And the society begins with the self.

You are your main company. Are you a good friend to yourself? Do you treat yourself well? Do you care deeply about yourself? As you are able to fall in love with your human self, the shell of personality through which your spirit expresses itself, just so will you be able to treat other selves.

When one is in pain, the instinct is to avoid it. But compassion and love do not grow from avoidance, and trouble avoided is the unlearned lesson of love, which shall even more surely be presented to you again. So take the situations where compassion is lacking into the inner room. Bring them into the silence. The key is silence.

Now gaze at yourself, they say. You are an object of compassion. Does the sun not shine upon you whether you are happy or sad, feeling virtuous or distinctly unvirtuous? Does the breeze not lift the tendrils of your hair from your neck? Do the trees not give you oxygen no matter what your condition? You are objects of love and mercy and infinite compassion because you are part of love, part of a Creator.

If you move from your humanity, from your shell of personality, you will quickly run out of compassion, for you have it in small supply within the reasoning mind. But if you can open your heart and sweep aside the pretensions and blockages, and move to yourself as the object of love unlimited, free flowing and infinite, then you are merely that through which compassion moves, and you shine infinitely.

This, they say, is the answer to both queries. If you shine with that which moves through you, you are doing your utmost to manifest compassion in your personal evolution, and you are also directly adjacent to the inner room of asking. How can you give more than infinite light? How can any choice made in this frame of heart and mind be incorrect?

And then the famous image. As you open your eyes and greet the world again, the first challenge to your manifesting compassion may be an obstreperous child, a difficult co-worker, or a pile of dishes. None of which seem particularly central or worthy of all the machinery of dedication of self to the loving way. Yet all services are equal. To love the dirty dishes is worthy, just as to offer instruction for healing to many is worthy. There is no quantity to right action or just service, but only the quality of unrestrained compassion.

One last exchange. Carla asks: if you simply do not like someone, could you write them a love letter and drop it down a well and expect it to do any good? Q'uo answers that the love letter can be effective if it is written in the heart's true compassion, opening a pathway between you on the metaphysical levels. But first, explore your own heart, and be certain the seeds are sown in true and honest compassion.

So tonight: the inner room, the shining, and the dishes. The destiny you seek is what moves through you when the heart is open and the mind is quiet.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Courtship of Wisdom
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the courtship of wisdom.

Tonight the group asks about the two halves of the mind. How does the feminine portion, the subconscious, work with the male portion, the conscious mind? How can the conscious mind gain clearer access to the deep mind? And how, having learned something of this, can one help others who come seeking the same?

Q'uo begins in an unexpected place: the body. Before they will talk about the deep mind, they want to lift the stigma of physicality from sexuality. To many, they say, the body is seen as either beautiful in its sexuality or innocent of sin, as if those were the only options. But human physical sexuality is an information resource which, like any other, speaks of the love and the light of the one infinite Creator.

So they ask each listener to pause and feel the heavy, familiar physical vehicle. This is that which has given itself that you may think and feel and express your free will in this life. Feel the breathing, the limbs resting, the muscles as they are supported. You are not your body, they say, but your body is a living form, and every cell of it vibrates with the love and the light of the infinite One. Take a moment to thank this beautiful animal form for the sacrifice of its instinctually lived life. That life you have tipped upon the ear, and that life is not possible. This body of yours is living your life and dying your death.

Then Q'uo turns to the seeking of what they call, archetypically, the feminine within: the intuitive wisdom of the subconscious. And they describe the relationship between the conscious and subconscious mind as a courtship. The conscious mind is the lover. The subconscious is the beloved, coy, hidden, not always immediately responsive.

The first feminine quality the conscious mind must learn, they say, is patience. There is the reaching, but not the immediate grasping. Not the rapid, obvious success, but the long, patient, tender courtship of these qualities within, which are lighter, freer, and more wise than conscious plodding thought. How difficult it is to be patient. How weary one is of the waiting.

At that point the second quality is evoked by need: faith. Faith that patience is deserved and appropriate. Faith is a fruit of the wisdom within the deep mind, yet it cannot be reached except by faith. So the conscious mind reaches for this perfect bride of wisdom using faith, that which it believes it does not yet have, and the very reaching evokes the principle. Faith is found. Persistence can be sustained.

Then Q'uo uses a striking image. The desire of the conscious mind for truth, for how to love the Creator, how to know the Creator, how to serve the Creator, may be purified as seeking proceeds. The questions do not change, but the seeking of the answers can be refined, until the lover of truth has ever more ability to penetrate in a gentle yet fruitful way the recesses of the unconscious. The reaching becomes single-pointed, courtly, passionate. And the desire truly impregnates intuition. Something is born. Something that as a unit may rise through dreams, through daydreams, or, for those whose thresholds are permeable, simply through the surface of the conscious mind.

And here is the part I want you to sit with. The way in which you approach wisdom creates the precise kind of information you shall receive. The unconscious organizes itself according to the gentle, loving courtliness it has received from the conscious mind, and becomes attuned toward wishing to give the conscious portion more information. You are creating your own information, they say, because you are the spirit you seek.

The group also asked how to help others with this. Q'uo's answer is bracing. Think of the teachers who aided you. Insofar as the teacher took responsibility for your learning, the teacher vitiated the progress by creating a false dependency. When one gives counsel and acts as an effective catalyst, the overwhelming response is gratitude, and the giving of credit away from the self to the catalyst.

To empower the student rather than make them dependent, Q'uo suggests two things. One may smile and say nothing. The lack of feedback becomes catalyst for the student to realize that a blank wall cannot be given credit. Or, more seemingly humane, one may explain what happened: the catalyst remains unchanged; the work and the reward are both those of the student. In either case, entities which wish to be dependent will simply choose to be dependent. Your work is always with the self.

In the questions, one seeker asks about frustration in seeking. Q'uo answers: within each frustration there is a trigger point, a place of beginning, which is the key to unraveling the experience. Look at the experience objectively, as but experience, and see the frustration as that which you have created, not as inherently contained in the experience. Frustration is a sticking point where more is not understood than understood. It is a kind of friction that wears away the lesser qualities no longer useful to you, and gives you a more polished surface, so you may see yourself more clearly.

So tonight the teaching is a love story between the two halves of your own mind. Be the patient lover. Reach without grasping. Let faith do what force cannot. And trust that the wisdom you court is already, in some holographic and miniature way, the very Creator you seek.

Thank you for listening.

title: Lamps With Fuel
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: lamps with fuel.

Tonight the group brings a question everyone has lived. When we face a new challenge, many of us feel fear, foreboding, dread, a sense that the worst case is staring us in the face. Is there any value in that fearful approach? Should we instead rely on blind faith and simply believe everything will be all right? Or is there a dynamic tension between anxiety and faith that brings out the best in us?

Then they sort worry into categories, and I think this sorting is the real gift of the night. The first category is the distant worry. Many times we mentally create a possible future that may not be probable, and if probable, may not occur, and if it is to occur, will be long enough in coming that decisive consideration is premature. In this case, pessimistic spinning is not recommended. It is not useful.

When the concern is only on the horizon, Q'uo says, see it as weather. The storm cloud over someone else's land, some other farmer's crops. It will not impinge upon you. That cloud is real, far more real in the world of thought than in your continuum, but only damage can be done by applying rational intelligence to a situation not yet susceptible to rational thought.

The second category is smaller but important. It concerns keeping your word. Being a certain way. Dwelling with a certain point of view, and noticing you have slipped away from it. Here Q'uo uses the parable of the ones who awaited the bridegroom, each with a lamp that used oil. Some carried no fuel for the lamp. Others were prudent and had both light and fuel.

Your principles are your lamp, they say. They are what you hold up before you as you await marriage with the present moment. But without the fuel to light the lamp, the bridegroom of the present moment cannot find you in the darkness. Your forethought, your energetic concern in backing up previous ethical choices with the fuel to keep them fresh and lighted, is your way of being prepared for the usually unexpected arrival of a present moment that has need of your light.

So in this one area, be pessimistic. Look most pessimistically and firmly upon your perceived lack of forethought in fuel-carrying. One who seeks the truth cannot rest upon previously found truths or previously made ethical choices, but must be continuously prepared to meet the circumstance that uses all past choices and demands a living witness of your own polarity. Your choices without the energy of your will are like lamps without fuel, and are not useful.

The third category is the largest: the actual decision. Here Q'uo wants balance. They offer the story of Joseph of the many-colored robe, interpreting the ruler's dreams. Seven bumper crops, then a like period of drought and hunger. The response was to preserve enough food to buffer a drought, should it occur. This, they say, is a right use of what you might call fear or pessimism. If a precaution can be taken without destructive impact upon the integrated life of the self or family or society, and without dwelling on the possibility as inevitable, then such a precaution is well made. It shows prudence rather than random fear.

When a decision must be made, there is no fault either in blind faith or in worst-case spinning. What matters is that faith be part of each decision. They tell the parable of the master who gives servants money. Those who act in faith, investing for their master, are rewarded with thanks and more duties. The one who buries the coin, the pessimist, has only what he had, and then the master takes even that away. Harsh in logical terms, but the point is that one who acts without faith will not progress in polarity.

On the other hand, many lessons are those in which an entity moves foolishly and quickly in blind and unreasoned faith, abandoning the tools of reason the Creator gave. These faculties of reasoning and questioning are valuable tools, not given to create excess. So the counsel is this. First ascertain that the time has come to make the choice. If the time is not yet, the mind should remain out of gear, and the concern given to the heart, to the inner room of prayer, and to the affirmative workings of an over-reaching faith in the rightness of all that is.

If there is continuing disquiet, Q'uo offers two techniques. First, refuse any thought concerning the choice for a limited period, allowing the deep roots of mind to express their deeper wisdom. Second, spend one day espousing the positive choice and the next day the negative choice. This over-stimulation of the mind's duality quiets the surface, and a way is made for the deeper wisdom to rise.

We do not disparage the intellectual mind, they say. We do not disparage the uses of fear. We do not disparage the uses of faith. Both faith and doubt are necessary in the discovery of the true self.

So tonight, when the dread rises before the new thing: ask first if the time has come. If not, pray and let it be weather. Check your lamp, and carry fuel. And when the choosing comes, open the heart to faith and the mind to reason, and then choose from a place so deep that you cannot defend it, but you know it is yours.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Pebble's Ripples
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the pebble's ripples.

Tonight the group asks about something painfully familiar. We look for what is real and dependable in ourselves and in each other. We join groups to aid one another in seeking. And yet the groups divide. Factions form. The unifying factors we believed in do not seem to hold us together. What, within us and within creation, can we actually depend on?

Q'uo answers with an image. The pebble drops into the pond, and the ripples flow out from it. So is each self a pebble, with its own ripples impinging upon the ripples of other pebbles. The mate, the friend, the group does not move in synchronized perfection. Each self's energies ripple into the energies put out by others.

And here is the quietly startling part. You are one person to self A, and seemingly quite another description to self B. Each entity receives a somewhat different facet of your projected energies, and connects with those energies in a way comfortable to them. So no two of your friends know the same person in you.

Nor do you know yourself as the same person. Within you there are many pebbles dropping at various levels of consciousness into that admixture of personae which make up the mask of personality. You define and redefine the self again and again, yet never know the self in its entirety.

But within this fragmentation, Q'uo finds the first unity. The same perceiver sees all of these differing selves within the self. Here lies the first dependable thing: the one who watches all your versions is one.

The second corollary is about groups. Why does a group form? Supposedly because of a vision, an ideal, a set of principles everyone wishes to honor. But entities who place great emphasis upon things that can be known develop the chronic tendency to define the precise nature of those ideals. And that which begins in a generous outburst of honor and devotion soon becomes that which has been defined, and ceases its growth. It grows a hard carapace, a built structure that will not accept expansion or movement into different shapes.

That which begins in a generous outburst of honor and devotion soon becomes that which has been defined, and ceases its growth. It grows a hard carapace that will not accept expansion. In moving from the first rapturous experience of love for a principle to the desire to codify it, the entity or group has moved from the open heart to what must always in the end be the closed mind. But beneath every faction, Q'uo says, there remains the unifying principle that brought these souls together in the first place. Q'uo simply calls it love. Not the dead love of fixed romance, nor friendship, nor any definition within your experience, but love as a fiery creative principle which has dynamically created and set free the universe, which moves endlessly from its source back to that same source, dwelling always in what has been called a cloud of unknowing.

Then they turn the lens inward, because what is true for the self reflects upon the society. When the self has learned its own nature and accepted it unconditionally, that self is ready to become part of a unity of selves which shall remain unified. Not in the deadened sense of agreement to a dry structure of words and creeds, but because of adherence to love. That love is diverse. Each self which loves itself unconditionally is unique, yet each is love.

The first act of the peacemaker is to have faith in this dubious-seeming self. When faith has been found in the self, the entity has no more point to prove, no more battles to win, no preferences that reach the point of necessity. Such a self listens to divisive speech and by its nature finds the point of balance where each party departed from the unifying principle. The path back to unity from discord lies in calling to remembrance that unifying principle.

In the questions, one seeker asks whether the teaching is this: all systems arise out of the present moment, and as soon as we try to codify them, we are no longer in the present moment, and they lose validity. Q'uo agrees. The intellectual mind analyzes infinitely, but in all this complexity there is the tendency to move experience from the moment in which all occurs to a distant reality created by conceptualization. That is why they recommend leaving that kind of thinking for a time each day, in meditation, so the mind may be quieted and brought back to its source.

So what is dependable? Not the structure. Not the agreement. The perceiver who watches all your selves, the fiery principle that set the universe free, and the present moment, where it all still lives.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Primary Ethic
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the primary ethic.

Tonight's question is about control. In relationships with friends and family, especially children, we often exert influence over another person, often for their own good. We do it to ourselves too, controlling our behavior and thoughts to make them align with what we think is higher or better. The group asks: what are the ethics of attempting to affect our own and especially other people's behavior, because we think the effect we desire is better?

Q'uo begins with the largest possible view. The universe, they say, is in one way or another in balance. The stars in their courses, the galaxies in their huge orbits, the seas within their limits. All speak of the immeasurable control with which the universe is created. The tiny fertilized egg has the life and death of the body it shall become written in miniature within itself, just as the seed knows precisely what plant it shall grow into, the manner of its blooming, and the nature of its fruit.

Against this fundamental dynamic is its echo, and that which offers the opportunity for balance: the freedom of all sentient beings to choose. Were the universe to relax its discipline, there would be no universe. Yet the fixed quality of stellar events is the backdrop against which the choices of humans are played out. Each entity has both more power and less power than it may think.

Now the key turn. The effect that entities have when controlling or attempting to control others is far from fixed, they say, for the relationship between the two entities shifts constantly. Therefore the ethics of choosing to control another are ethics of a corollary nature. The primary ethic is the control of the self. Before we ask whether we may steer another, we are asked whether we have learned to steer ourselves.

Q'uo traces the spiral of control through a life: the infant with needs for comfort and food, the toddler learning to say no, the child with friends and teachers and a growing sense of self, until one day the culture says, now you are an adult. And suddenly the shoe is upon the other foot, and there are times, Q'uo says, when it is ethically correct to attempt to control others to some extent. This is a shock indeed to many a young parent.

How to tell when it is correct? They offer questions. The first: will my inaction prevent this entity from surviving? There is no case, they say, where any negative karma accrues from the attempt to keep another from becoming unviable. To save another is a hero's or heroine's service. But usually the questions are subtler.

Ethics is a system of thought describing appropriate actions. So ask: is this a situation where I should attempt to control because of an appropriate end? Appropriate ends are suggestions that may aid someone in spiritual maturity, or save time or other valued commodity. If control is used when it is appropriate, then regardless of whether the entity can actually be controlled, the choice has been well made. If, on the other hand, an entity desires to control another from fear, the fear that another is not doing the correct thing spiritually, politically, socially, or economically, then this choice may be seen as inappropriate.

The term war, they say, may be seen as the largest, broadest example of inappropriate attempts to control others. And closer to home: look at how much control is attempted by those who would have others do as they do, believe as they believe, dress as they dress, behave as they behave.

When teaching the child what is appropriate, many choices are made for the child. But when gazing at an adult, those choices have passed from the need for outer control. And here is the deeper principle: the more centered, self-knowing, and quiet-hearted an entity becomes, the less fear it has that entities seemingly different from it will somehow harm it. Intolerance, prejudice, and the cant of religious rhetoric are based upon fear. The ways in which fearful individuals see themselves controlling may well look to them like love and concern. Yet no entity can learn for another, be safe for another, or do another's work.

Q'uo closes with an image to carry home. Gaze within, they say. See the starry heavens of your own fixed universe. Within you are subsystems, galaxies: the heart, the stomach, the liver, the musculature. Each has its instinctually given work for the good of the whole. All this space within, all these fixed orbits within, and you as controller over all.

You are a co-creator. Step back from the constellation of the self. See the constellation of your own mind. See the unimaginable number of choices that have brought you to this moment. And see that you will treat others as a corollary of the way you treat yourself.

As each fear is noticed, addressed, blessed, accepted, and eventually dropped away, for it is unneeded, there will be fewer times that the constellation that is yourself finds, through fear, that it wishes to control in an inappropriate way. Look always first to the discipline of the self, and the acceptance, blessing, and forgiveness of the self, as the self is imperfect, so it seems. Then when you gaze upon a fellow being, there will not be the blinders of fear to distract the thinking or blind the eyes of judgment.

As this instrument often says, and as Q'uo repeats: free will is paramount. Let this and love be your guides.

Thank you for listening.

title: Absorb the Monster
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: absorb the monster.

Tonight's question is an unusual one. The group asks about visitations by negatively oriented entities or energies, sent by a third-density human practicing what is usually called the black magical arts. How should the person receiving this energy, or one wishing to help them, deal with it? What is the best attitude, the best action, the principle to hold?

Q'uo begins by defining the ground both sides stand on. The metaphysical, both of the service-to-others path and the service-to-self path, takes place upon a field which appears to be dark. The background of metaphysical work for both polarities is darkness, for the consciousness of the living spirit within this illusion is hidden within the deep and unlit roots of mind. Both those who seek the darkness and those who seek the light begin in a common ground of darkness, the darkness of that which is not known.

Many metaphysical seekers expect the positive search to be done in noonday sun. This is untrue. The metaphysical search is not clear, obvious, or simple. In these night conditions, the moon's dimmest light is the brightest illumination, and in the dim moonlight, shadows can be deceiving.

Now the comparison of the two paths. The entity upon the negative path feels there is no safety, no haven, that it and only it can be counted upon. So it wishes to build personal power, and this magical personality is simpler to build, for the negative entity need only gather to the self all possible power, without the need for discrimination. The positively polarized entity has the harder task: balancing the seeming opposites of all things to find the most careful balance of truth, beauty, and goodness. What is not obvious is that the negative path becomes more and more difficult, until at last it is a road impossible to be walked, whereas the positive path is eternal.

Here is the teaching at the center of the night, and I want to give it slowly. When one is assaulted by word, dream, feeling, or other action by a negatively polarized entity, one is dealing with not only a godly person but with one's own self. For all are one. In each mind, body, and spirit there is all that there is. Each person is a holograph of the creation, the created, and the Creator.

So when negative greeting is known or suspected, the positively oriented person sits down to reckon with its own universal nature, fully capable and fully supplied with negativity. The perceived negativity succeeds when the intended victim does not know it is being greeted by its very self.

If a ravening beast comes at your body, you attempt to slay it. But if a metaphysical ravening beast attacks, you reckon with it by welcoming it into the self, and accepting fully that this horrible monster is a part of the self.

The first defense, they say, is to visualize this negative power and fearlessly invite it to take up a loving absorption within the very heart. For positive power is power balanced by knowledge of the self. All magical work is done upon the self.

As one forgives oneself, one becomes able to forgive all. The negative greeting is visualized as a creature of the night, which is then lovingly absorbed, accepted, and forgiven. The forgiven selfishness becomes harmless.

This alone, they say, is enough to dissuade most negative entities who wish to control others, for most are not particularly skillful. Being accepted is poison to a negatively oriented entity, who gains power by causing fear, anger, hatred, disgust. When its selfhood is seen for its blackness, yet lovingly accepted and forgiven, the negative entity experiences loss of all its power, and goes looking for others who will be satisfactorily afraid.

For the very few who have pursued the path of control far enough to contact deeper sources of negativity, the situation is no less solvable but not as simple. It takes a good deal of wisdom to calmly gaze upon metaphysical malevolence. In such cases, Q'uo suggests the practical solution of finding one among your people who is steeped in rituals of positivity. Such people exist in various of your religious traditions.

Each of you, gaze within. Do you feel magical? Do you feel powerful? If the answer comes too easily, it is likely that something within would choose the easy way toward power. Each step upon the negative path seems from within to be positive. One wishes power so one may help people. Most beginning negative entities have no idea they are embarking upon the path of negativity.

Contrast this with the positive path, where power is accrued by being the weakest, where greatness is achieved by being the servant of others, where advice and teaching are given only when asked for. How many among your religious systems, caught in the fervor of rightness, judge and condemn and control many for their own good? And how few there are who lay aside doctrine and seek only to serve each entity according to its requests when they can, and to offer benediction, forgiveness, and acceptance when they cannot.

The closing counsel is the one I would underline twice. We do not expect third-density entities to be without fear, they say. We simply ask entities who wish to live in faith not to be afraid of their fear. Not to be ruled by their fear, but to accept this fear, to love this fear, as part of the universal self, and to move on, leaping foolishly into the next step in blindness and in faith.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Democracy of Spirit
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the democracy of spirit.

This session, from the fourth of July in nineteen ninety-two, opens with a different voice. Laitos, a social memory complex of the Confederation, comes to share thoughts on joy, and says some startling things about the Creator before Oxal joins with the teaching the group actually asked about.

The Creator, Laitos says, is that which does not know, but longs to know. And the Creator knows Itself through you, and is able to know Itself in every present moment through your experience. This is the great mystery of the Creator. The infinite love, light, and power is made manifest by an all-encompassing knowledge of Itself. All the joys you experience are the joys of the Creator in learning of Itself.

So learn to love the Creator that is you, and in doing so, you shall come closer to the Creator that is the universe. For these are the same. I find that disorienting in the best way. The Creator longs to know. And it knows through you.

Then Laitos speaks of meditation as an act of great honesty. Meditation is that time within your life where you are able to see what truly is the situation. To open the self as it is in the present moment, and to accept this as that which is. Each of us is a manifestation of the Creator that has distorted perceptions of ourselves. The Creator knows that these are distorted perceptions, and loves them as the Creator loves all.

The group, perhaps sensing that Oxal has something to say about teaching, has asked about the teacher and the seeker. Oxal greets you, and what follows is the heart of the night.

We come as those who serve, they say. And this, my friends, is the democracy of spirit. All are equal in the desire to serve. All are equal in the realization of the Creator. We are here as servants. We are here to serve. And we ask you to aid us in serving you well. By your vibrations, by your desires, by your queries, you aid us in serving you.

Then comes the sentence that unhinges every schoolroom instinct I have. We cannot teach. The teachers that can teach are those who realize that they cannot teach. They can only aid another in realizing that which they seek.

No entity may truly teach another. Learning occurs, Oxal says, because of the catalyst of another's attempt to learn. It is this catalyst that we provide: the presence of another entity that has a different viewpoint, a different way of seeking, a different way of loving, a different way of serving. We aid you in learning by our very being, and you aid us by your being.

I want to sit with that a moment. The teacher does not transfer knowledge. The teacher's being is the catalyst, and the student learns because the attempt to learn was already underway. It changes what a teacher is for.

This democracy of spirit flows through the whole session. When the group asks whether some present are teachers, or even priests, Oxal answers gently. Teaching is the communication between the seeker and the teacher. Not between the seeker and the knowledge of the teacher. This is the true meaning of teaching. And the greatest gift that a teacher can give is faith in the being of the taught.

There is an honesty in this session about how much goes unspoken. At one point the instrument is asked why Oxal seems so hesitant, and Oxal answers that they feel the desire to speak but also the difficulty of saying what must be said without violating free will. They speak carefully, precisely, as though each word were placed by hand.

One questioner asks about learning without understanding, whether real learning requires comprehension. Oxal's answer is subtle: there is learning in the mind, and there is the knowing that bypasses the mind. Sometimes the deepest teachings are received without the mind's understanding, and yet the being is changed.

There is a lovely moment near the end about a young child in the group, someone's son, who has been acting as a teacher to his elders without knowing it. Oxal affirms that this is exactly how the democracy of spirit works. The teacher is not the one with the credentials. The teacher is the one whose being catalyzes learning in another.

So tonight's teaching is really two teachings woven together. From Laitos: the Creator longs to know Itself, and knows through your joy. Love the Creator that is you. And from Oxal: no one can teach you, and no one needs to. You are learning because you are seeking, and every being you meet, young or old, learned or unlearned, is a catalyst for that learning. The teacher's greatest gift is not information. It is faith in you.

Which brings us back to the beginning, and to the service with which Oxal opened. We are here to serve. Aid us in serving you well. In the democracy of spirit, even the extraterrestrial brotherhood is asking for your help in helping you. That is how equal it is.

Thank you for listening.

title: Mercy Turned Inward
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: mercy turned inward.

Tonight the group asks about one of the oldest questions of the seeking life: why are relationships so difficult, and what can we learn from them? Q'uo answers with a long teaching, and at its center sits a sentence I think many seekers need to hear.

They begin with a reframing. A relationship is itself an entity. It has its own birth, its own life, and its own death. It rises upon the wings of some shared purpose or need, and as it lives, the pair within the relationship either learns to fly together or learns that flying together is not the path.

There are two basic kinds of relationship, they say, and both are ways of serving. One is the relationship of service to others, in which both entities attempt to serve one another and the relationship. The other is the relationship of service to self, in which each attempts to use the other for its own ends. Both, in the end, are forms of service. The negative path, too, is a way of learning, though Q'uo does not dwell on that.

The great spiritual work of relationship, they say, is mercy. Mercy extended outward is relatively natural to most of us. We can forgive others. We can make allowances for others. But here is the turn. Do not forget, in the midst of being merciful to others, to turn that same mercy inward upon the self.

For many, forgiveness of the self is the most difficult forgiveness of all. We carry standards for ourselves that we would never impose on a friend. And Q'uo suggests that this inward harshness is not a private matter. It leaks into everything.

Here is the teaching that ties the whole night together. A relationship is a mirror. Use your judgment about others as a way of learning about yourself. There are no accidents in what is attracted to us. What we notice in others, what we judge in others, what we cannot forgive in others, is telling us something about what we have not yet forgiven in ourselves.

When others cannot be merciful toward us, they say, this reflects our own self-judgment. The people in our lives are showing us the shape of our own inner court. And when we become as merciful as possible toward ourselves, we move into harmony with creation itself.

I want to slow down here, because this is easily misread. This is not blame. It is not saying you caused someone else's cruelty. It is saying that the work of the seeker is always with the self, and that other people are the mirror in which the self becomes visible. The question is never really what is wrong with them. The question is what the mirror is showing you about the one holding it.

In the questions that follow, the group presses on the practical difficulties. One asks: how do we see the pain of others without being affected by it? Q'uo answers that being affected is in some sense the point. The open heart cannot avoid being moved. To be unmoved by another's suffering would be to close the heart. But there is a balance: be careful not to become so absorbed in another's pain that you lose yourself in it. Feel with them, but do not drown with them.

Another asks about relationships where others cause us pain. The same principle applies, they say. See yourself within that judgment. The mirror works in both directions. The one who hurts you is showing you something about the one you are, and the one you are judging them for being is showing you something about the judgments you carry.

One questioner wonders about seeing more of the self through the perspectives of others, and whether that risks losing the self in other people's opinions. Q'uo cautions: do not identify the self with the persona, with the mask of personality that others see and respond to. Gather what the mirror shows you, but remember that you are more than the image in any mirror.

And there is a gentle note about relationships that have no resonance, that seem to have run their course. Such relationships end, or change form. Not every bond is meant to last. The entity that was the relationship has completed its life, and what was learned remains.

So tonight's teaching circles back to where it began. Relationships are difficult because they are the mirror, and the mirror does not flatter. But the work is mercifully simple in its direction: whatever forgiveness you would extend to the other, turn it inward first. Forgive the self with the same generosity you would offer a friend. And watch how the world around you begins, slowly, to reflect that mercy back.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Good Neighbor Within
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the good neighbor within.

Tonight the group asks about transformation, about the inner change that remakes a life. Q'uo's answer begins in an unexpected place: with soil.

They speak of the parable of the sower, whose seeds fell on different kinds of ground. Some fell on rock and could not root. Some fell among thorns and were choked. Some fell on good soil and brought forth a harvest. The question for the seeker is not really about the seed, they say. The seed is always the same. The question is about the soil.

What makes the soil good? It is not virtue, not effort, not the right opinions. It is openness. The transformed self is the self that has become good soil: receptive, unguarded, willing to receive what is planted without strangling it in judgment.

Then Q'uo takes up a phrase from the Christian tradition, and works with it in a way I had not expected. I am the light of the world, the teacher known as Jesus said. Who is this I? It is not the personality, not the name, not the biography. It is the consciousness that says I am. And that consciousness is not the private property of one teacher. It is the shared identity of all.

When you say I am, you are speaking with the same voice. The light of the world is not a person. It is what you are when the personality steps aside.

This leads to one of the most freeing sentences of the night. Do not be too concerned about other selves, they say. Each has its own road to walk, its own soil to tend, its own harvest to bring in. Your work is with the one field you can actually cultivate: your own.

Q'uo then describes the hallmarks of the transformed self, and I want to give them plainly, because they read like a checklist for the inner life. The transformed entity is no longer frightened by its own thoughts. It has seen the worst of what the mind can produce, and it knows that thoughts are weather, not identity. It sees beyond the immediate circumstance to the larger pattern. It takes the self lightly.

That last one stays with me. Taking the self lightly. Not taking the self unseriously, but lightly: holding the personality the way you might hold a bird, firmly enough that it does not fly away, gently enough that it is not crushed.

There is a teaching about the neighbor here too. Do not identify with the good neighbor or the bad neighbor, they say. The judgment itself is the neighbor. When you call yourself good, you have built a neighbor. When you call yourself bad, you have built another. The transformed self steps back from both verdicts and tends the soil instead.

All of this is really a teaching about compassion for the self, though Q'uo never uses those words in a sentimental way. The soil does not judge the seed. It receives it. The self that has learned to receive itself without the constant verdict is the self in which transformation can actually happen.

In the questions that follow, the group asks about pain and difficulty in the body, about the hard passages of the inner life. I want to handle this part with care, because the session touches on illness and suffering, and the archive's metaphysical framing of these things is not medical advice and should not be taken as such.

What I will carry from the exchange is this: Q'uo treats pain as catalyst, as experience that the self can work with rather than merely endure. The question is never why is this happening to me in the medical sense, but what is this experience offering the self that is having it. That is a spiritual question, not a medical one, and it belongs to the one living the experience.

If you are living with illness or pain, please hold this teaching the way you would hold anything from a channeled archive: as one perspective among many, not as a diagnosis and not as a prescription. The care of the body belongs to the body and to those trained to care for it. What the archive offers is a way of meeting the experience inwardly, with the same mercy we spoke of last time: turned inward.
