If you are learning lessons of love, Q'uo said in closing, your first lesson is to love, accept, and forgive yourself. You are loved so very much by the infinite One, they said. You are precious. You are unique. Your nexus of experiences is irreplaceable. Feel that jewel within yourself grow and glow — and let it be your rudder on the uncharted sea. The angst is not a sign you are off course. It is the weight that keeps you upright while you sail.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Way of Leaning
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the way of leaning.

In January of nineteen ninety-three, the group returned to the subject of attitude — but from the other side. If our experiences shape our attitude, they asked, can we shape it back? Can we sow the seeds of a wider, lighter perspective and go through our days with less turmoil — or is that a figment of the imagination, and should we simply ride the ups and downs as they come?

Q'uo turned the question around first. The experiences of an incarnation affect your attitude, they said, and are designed to do that — so no one begins with a blank slate. Before birth, you and your higher self laid out a destiny: a plate of human experience, lessons of loving, chosen not from mischief but from the ambition of a seeker who wishes to stretch and grow while serving the infinite One. You gave your future self, they said, what you felt was the very best possible. The eyes, as they noted, can be larger than the stomach — the plate may have been loaded generously. But there is nothing wicked in the lessons flying toward you in the gale of experience. When difficulties seem overwhelming, it is easier to malign destiny than to do the laborious work of digesting the catalyst.

And what is an attitude, exactly? Q'uo offered the etymology: the word means the way of leaning or tending. To take an attitude in dance is to turn the foot sideways and raise it, instead of lifting it straight — it is the slant you put on the straightforward march of events. And yes, they said, that slant has a great deal to do with how rough the march feels.

They added a humbling footnote: the consideration of an attitude is a luxury. It belongs to those with a full stomach, a warm shelter, comrades in arms. Those simply trying to survive know only the background attitude of the desire for life. But for those with the luxury of the inward turn, much of what feels like a conscious choice of attitude is really ripeness — the greater part of the work on a lesson was done beforehand, so that when the catalyst arrives it is recognized, and can be respected. It is the old lesson unlearned that ambushes us — the novelty catching us flat-footed, with the sinking feeling of: oh no, here we go again.

That oh-no moment is so precisely observed it almost hurts. The new lesson we can meet with curiosity; it is the repeat that freezes us. Q'uo is saying the freeze itself is the signal — the sign that here, exactly here, is the work we came to do.

Look at the fear in that turn of thought, they said, and see its dulling, freezing, darkening effect. The first adjustment is simply to accept difficult material. In another density you may work on accepting it with total and unconditional love; in this one, for the choice of the light, it is enough to say yes to whatever the incarnation brings. To refuse the material, they pointed out, is really to say to life itself: I do not believe there is a reason for this suffering. I do not believe I am a loved child in my Father's care. And yet we say we believe exactly that — until the day's events put it to the test.

Here Q'uo aimed the teaching where the question was really pointing. You cannot expect any attitude to buffer you from feeling emotions, they said plainly. If you focus on events, you are lost in meaningless detail. Focus instead on the emotions — and notice what the emotional body does with pain: it resists, tightens, says no in a speechless, silent way. The work of the attitude is to hold, love, and forgive that knotted self. A good attitude cannot make you not angry. But it can kick in like an afterburner and say: I accept myself angry as well as calm.

In that self-acceptance, they said, lies the compassion the lesson was meant to teach. The events do not teach; our reactions do not fully teach; what teaches is how we deal with our unredeemed emotions. And the tools are smaller than you would think. The attitude can be steadied by daily silent meditation — but much of the day is active, with no time to reseat the consciousness. For those hours, Q'uo said, one small word is enough. Love. Or, as this instrument prays, Jesus. Or any short expression of truth. One word, to feed the flame of balance within.

A song on the lips helps, they added. Joking with yourself helps — it almost always does. And the attempts to soften another's pain, when someone comes to you for aid, have a profound effect on you. Rejoice in the outworking of destiny, they said. Let your attitude be that all is well, even as you pick yourself up again and yet again — dust yourself off, as the instrument's song goes, and start all over again. The crux of a good attitude is that moment of recognition and forgiveness of the self by the self.

So the answer to the group's question is yes — and no. Yes, the slant of your leaning shapes everything. No, you cannot force it, and you were never meant to. Say yes to what comes. Forgive the knotted self. Keep one small word in your pocket for the hours when meditation is impossible. And trust that the puzzles simplify exactly to the extent that you cease judging yourself for finding them puzzling.

Thank you for listening.

title: Wise as Serpents
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: wise as serpents.

In January of nineteen ninety-three, a seeker named V wrote in from San Diego with a question about discernment. She had been working with a channeled source called Metatron, studying a book called The Keys of Enoch, and spending time with groups of those who believe they are wanderers from other worlds. She wanted to know what Q'uo thought — which of these were genuine, which were trustworthy, which she should follow. Q'uo's answer was not the verdict she was expecting. It was better.

We have no authority over you, they began. We are prone to error. And then the foundation stone: there is no final authority anywhere. No hand or word holds a master's authority over servants of the infinite One, for the infinite One has established that in all manifested creation there be no final, provable answers. As entities discover what seem to be definitive answers, the frontier of knowledge is pushed back — and beyond it lies still an infinite mystery. In the end, they said, the only authority is the student. Each spiritual seeker, having its own universe, must and shall evaluate for itself all that enters the net of awareness.

This is not a license for gullibility, and Q'uo did not offer it as one. They encouraged the hungry to seek widely — to read, to gather tools, to sit with entities visible and invisible — and to enjoy all of it. But not simply to accept it. Even the most inaccurate contact, they said, is attempting to serve the Creator in its fashion, and even fear-driven material gathers seekers into a circle of seeking, where each consciousness aids each other. There is good in the gathering, even when the information is faulty. The question is never only is this true — it is also: what is this doing to me?

For that second question they offered a practical instrument: notice which energy center the material activates. Information fixated on survival, on who will make it and who will not, stirs the red ray of instinct. Information about groupings — who belongs, who is chosen, who should be avoided — moves in the yellow. Teachings about a special messiah or a chosen few: ask yourself whether the pull you feel is red, orange, or yellow — or whether anything in you is opening at the heart. Material that truly serves, they suggested, tends to activate the green ray of the open heart, or the blue of clear communication — and it is within the student alone that the indigo is kindled. The teaching does not open you. You open you.

I find this more useful than any blacklist could ever be. It moves the question from the source to the self — from is this teacher legitimate to what is happening in my own body as I listen. The body, it turns out, is the most honest reviewer. It cannot be flattered, and it cannot be fooled for long.

Q'uo closed with the old saying of the teacher known as Jesus: be wise as serpents, and innocent as doves. The serpent is wise in two ways, they explained. First, in the story your culture tells — the serpent's gift was the knowledge of good and evil, which is to say, the personal ability to judge what is good for you. That judgment is strictly personal, they stressed, and must never be offered dogmatically to others. Second, the serpent is wise in the field: when a possible enemy comes within hearing, it quietly removes itself. Discernment, and distance when needed. Both are wisdom.

And the dove? The innocence of the open, loving heart, they said, can see beauty in almost any situation — for as it speaks to itself, it hears the outer world. Two people in identical circumstances: one finds only signs of doom, the other finds much to be merry about and much to give thanks for. The difference is not in the circumstance. It is in the aperture of the heart.

They ended with unusual tenderness toward the fear that drives so much seeking. There is, they said, a wonderful urgency to this present moment — for these are the last minutes of each incarnation. There may be millions of those minutes, but they can be counted. The fear of annihilation stands stark before every seeker, with no evidential answer. The more compassionate response, they suggested, is not to solve the quandary but to inhabit it: to appreciate and attempt to fully inhabit each moment, each minute and hour, one at a time — so that whatever the outer circumstances, the inner journey shall be as full of light and blessing as the experiencer can hold.

So no, Q'uo would not rate V's sources. They gave her something harder and more durable instead: her own sovereignty. Read everything. Trust the resonance in your own centers. Withdraw quietly from what contracts you. And keep the heart open enough to find beauty anyway. Wise as the serpent. Innocent as the dove. It is still, all these years later, the whole of discernment in a single breath.

Thank you for listening.

title: Smile at the Ego
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: smile at the ego.

The tenth of the Aaron-Quo dialogues, in mid-January of nineteen ninety-three, took up a question that had been rising from many hearts: how do I live more lovingly for others, and still live with respect for myself? How do we serve without being used up — without giving away all our time and treasure and having nothing left for our own work? Aaron began, characteristically, by questioning the question's key word.

Let us speak about the word codependence, they said. All beings are, in fact, codependent. The word has picked up bad connotations — but codependence in itself is simply a statement of your non-separation, your inter-being. You breathe the air the trees make; the water in your body will return to the soil. What is negative is not the connection but the fear inside it: codependence as separation — acts and words based on the illusion that you are separate, laced with resentment, or with the quiet encouragement of another's unwholesome patterns as a protection for the self.

They told a story. A mother they had spoken with wanted, more than anything, to write. She had a small child who whined and pulled at her constantly — behavior she had, without knowing it, taught the child. She insisted she wanted the child to be independent so she could have her work back — and yet surreptitiously encouraged the dependence. Why? Because at a deeper level, the writing terrified her. The child's demands were protecting her from facing her own fear. That, Aaron said, is unwholesome codependence: not the caring, but the bargain underneath the caring.

When you see such a pattern repeating in your own life, they suggested a question: what does the continuation of this pattern protect me from? In what way am I encouraging it? At first it seems impossible to change — to simply say no. And here is the subtlety most of us miss: many do get as far as saying no, but the no comes out in anger. No! Sit down! I have had enough! That anger feels like strength, but it is still the fear talking. The no you think you are saying to the other's demands is really a no you have not yet said to your own fear.

That distinction lands like a small explosion, quietly. How many of my own firm boundaries have been exactly that — fear dressed up as clarity? Aaron is asking for something much harder than a louder no. They are asking for a truer one.

Q'uo added the other half of the mechanism: the need to be needed. You are entities who wish to be of service, they said — and so you need others in order to serve. That flavor of need played its part in your choosing each other, before birth and within the illusion. Two beings, each needing to be needed, form a loving symbiosis — until the press of time and complexity crushes it, and symbiosis curdles into codependence. The fear has many flavors, they said: running out of time, not being appreciated, abandonment. The content changes with the month. The tendency to react to your own fear does not.

Aaron's remedy begins with a change of pronoun. Watch yourself tending another's needs, they said, and notice the inner monologue: how much more time must I give? When do I get to do what I want? Now listen for the delusion inside it — the idea that service to the loved one and care for the self are two separate accounts. When you see that your service to your loved one is truly also meeting your needs — that your needs intermesh — then you are seeing clearly. The discipline that helps is not I will do this for him, or for her. It is: I will do this for us. With for us, they said, there is no resentment. As I serve you, I serve myself. As I help you find healing, I find healing.

And the ego? It does not die easily, Aaron said. It screams. It kicks. They pictured the mother again — the baby eased and sleeping in her arms — and underneath, the small voice: but I did not finish my chapter. Then the guilt, the squirming. Can we learn to smile at that voice? they asked. As she cared for her baby's cry of pain, can we offer compassion to our own cry of pain — hear it for what it is, the ego making a last-ditch effort to assert itself — and then bask in the deeper level of being, where the heart knows: I have just done exactly what I needed to do?

This is the practice of faith, they said — which grows, watched in this way, from blind faith to verified faith. You begin to know, intuitively, that you are moving deeper into connection — not getting rid of ego, but allowing ego to dissolve in the light of ultimate reality. And the reminder for the hard moments is the simplest sentence of the session: this is why I am here.

So the question the group brought — how to love others without losing yourself — resolves the way so many of these dialogues resolve: there was never a self to lose, only a fear to befriend. All beings are codependent. The only choice is whether the connection runs on fear or on love. And when the small voice starts its kicking and screaming, smile at it. It is only the ego, asking — in the only way it knows how — to be loved too.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Way No Is Said
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the way no is said.

The eleventh of the Aaron-Quo dialogues, on the eighteenth of January, nineteen ninety-three, stayed with the question of compassion — but moved it from theory into the kitchen and the driveway. Aaron wanted real-life examples, they said, so the group could pinpoint exactly where distortion creeps in. What follows is one of the most practical teachings in the whole series: a story about two partners, a chronic lateness, and the art of the loving no.

Call them A and B, Aaron said — they would not assign the roles to one sex or the other. A is always ready on time. B is always late. At first A is angry: the hosts are perturbed, and A feels blamed for B's fault. Slowly, A begins to see through the fear underneath the anger. A sees B's fear of fast motion, B's ambivalence about social situations — and A makes peace. A gets ready on time, and then sits and reads a book, waiting without quarrel. Compassion, so far, so good.

But then the pattern shifts. Left without the familiar friction, B gets later. B starts picking arguments on the way out the door — Did you lock the door? You were ready all this time, why didn't you check? — and A feels the anger rising again. Where does A say no? How does A say no? If there are two cars, it is simple: I am leaving at eight, see you there. But suppose there is only one car, and calling a cab would start a feud. What then?

Here is Aaron's answer, and it is worth memorizing: it is not the action of saying no, but the way no is said, that is most important. If A gets in the car and drives off in anger, that is provocation, whatever the words. But if A says, an hour beforehand, with no anger in the voice: I understand you need a lot of time; we need to leave in an hour; at eight I will be driving out of the driveway, and I hope you are in the car with me — here is money for a cab if you need it — then the no is clean. The line, Aaron said, is drawn not in the act but in the intention behind the act.

And then they asked the harder question: what if B is threatened by even that gentle no, and turns hostile? Can A have compassion for the hostility it has provoked? In loving, nonviolent movement with another, Aaron said, there must be a willingness to suffer the anger of another while asking them to consider your viewpoint. The soul speaks its truth — about lateness, or drinking, or rage — not in hostility, but with the deepest compassion for the other's pain. Nevertheless it speaks: this cannot continue.

I want to pause on that willingness, because it is the part everyone skips. We imagine that if we say it nicely enough, no one will be upset — that a perfectly phrased boundary produces a perfectly calm response. Aaron says otherwise: the other may rage, and your work is to allow the rage without personalizing it. If B calls you names and you can see the fear inside the names, why would you need to ask whether the names are true?

Before any of this, though, Aaron insisted on an audit of intention. Look deeply into your own heart, they said, and ask: is there any desire in my no to seek revenge for past humiliation — to create discomfort in the other as payback? It cannot be one hundred percent pure, they admitted. Nothing human is. But see if it is largely pure. Having uncovered the subtle, unskillful intentions, you are far less likely to act on them — and the choice that follows will carry a greater purity.

Q'uo set the same teaching in a larger frame. Remember, they said, that you are not B's teacher, if you are A. You are each other's teachers. You joined together recognizing the possibility of mutual service — and you are always precisely where you need to be. If the situation makes you squirm, ask: how did I get here? What learning might be in it for me? Distortions are not bad, they said — merely uncomfortable. And they may be the very catalyst for learning.

Fear itself, Aaron added, can be redeemed in this work. When conflict brings hatred and bitterness, you are not paying attention. But fear and frustration do not have to become hatred — they can become catalysts for deeper compassion. Let fear be a warning signal, a red light flashing: pay attention. And as you pay closer attention, finding compassion for the places in yourself that feel threatened, you move into deeper compassion for B — and into the intuitive wisdom of the open heart, which knows, without being taught, how to say no to what is unwholesome.

So the teaching of the morning is a single skill, practiced for a lifetime: the no that is not a weapon. Say it early. Say it without anger. Mean it without revenge. Allow the storm it may summon, and do not mistake the storm for failure. Somewhere on the other side of that clean, kind refusal, both A and B get to meet the people they actually are — and begin, at last, to help each other become them.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Nurturer Within
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the nurturer within.

The twelfth of the Aaron-Quo dialogues, later that same January day in nineteen ninety-three, turned from the mechanics of saying no to something quieter: the inner figure who makes any of it possible. Q'uo called it the nurturer — the part of you intimately connected with home, which accompanies you through the incarnation and offers, by its very being, the context in which you can see your right relationship to your suffering self.

The image they gave is almost embarrassingly tender, and I think that is the point. When the moment of suffering comes, Q'uo said, your nurturing part can say within you: I hold you with deepest love, and rock you in the cradle of my love. The parent does not only hold the quiet, good child — the nurturer goes for the bandage and the cleansing cloth, gives you a pat, and sends you back to play. Can you refrain from self-judgment, they asked, when you are out of tune with yourself — and instead allow the nurturer within to cradle you in your distress, spots and stains and dust and all?

Aaron set beside this their most clarifying distinction: the difference between pain and suffering. Pain is the arising sensation — physical or emotional — and it is not pleasant, but it is not the problem. Suffering begins when you get stuck in the illusion and start grasping at changing what is. It is not the discomfort of what arises that causes your suffering, they said. It is your aversion to what arises.

You are asked, they said, to live with one foot in the illusion and one foot in ultimate reality — to straddle the threshold like actors in a play. Like actors, you must play the role as if it matters; you must involve yourself in the illusion, or there is no learning, and you might as well not have incarnated. And yet you must keep the actor's awareness: the knowledge that you are playing to an audience, that there is a true self behind the role. Dismiss the ego self as mere illusion and you gain the comfort of the spiritual plane — but you lose the learning, and you smuggle duality back in through the stage door, because disassociation is itself a separate self protecting itself.

That is a demanding image to live inside — both feet required, neither allowed to do the whole job. I notice how often I try to pick one: to be only the actor, drowning in the drama, or only the audience, floating above it in cool detachment. Aaron says the learning lives in the straddle, in the discomfort of holding both at once.

With practice, they said, the wall between the two begins to dissolve — the infinite wall that seems to divide day from night, fear from love, separation from connection. You learn to be in the discomforting situation without struggling: resolving what can be resolved, allowing the rest, watching with the wisdom of the higher self. You find you can smile at the ego that keeps re-emerging. The frantic kicking and screaming — what about me, will I be nurtured — simply winds down. And then, as Q'uo had promised, you begin to embrace this human incarnation rather than condemn it: the actor on the stage, sometimes caught in the illusion, doing its brave best.

Q'uo then offered three forms of clear communication for the suffering that arises between people. The first: sit down with your B and speak in sentences that begin with I — picturing the messy, confused feelings exactly as they are, and then asking B to offer its own unapologized-for I in return. Egos, they said, are useful things — they keep the vehicle warm and fed and deliver you to each spiritually vital experience. They are to be honored, yours and everyone's.

The second: if B cannot or will not speak, have the conversation with yourself — say all the I-statements to the self, let the suffering be fully expressed, and respect it there. Then turn back to B with the face of one who suffers and is willing to abide its own ego self. It is lonelier, they admitted, but it clears the back-pressure out of the relationship, leaving B free to deal with its own ego without being asked to redeem yours.

The third is not a technique at all. It is the realization that communion is constant — that prayer without ceasing is not an activity but your nature. Your very nature, Q'uo said, is an unceasing hymn of love. You are one with the infinite Creator; you have never left home. The illusion is being visited — usefully, vitally — but underneath the visit, the connection never lapsed. None of these three modes offers a solution, they added, but then, the solution would be momentary anyway. Experience moves on.

Aaron's parting image stays with me: you are spiritual warriors, and with every small step upon this magnificent path, unseen multitudes bow to your courage and strew flowers before you. They may not cover all the jagged rocks — but they are there. Can you open your eyes, they asked, and begin to see yourselves as we see you? Held. Rocked. Accompanied. Never, for one moment, walking the king's highway alone.

Thank you for listening.

title: Sit by My Fire
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: sit by my fire.

The thirteenth and last of the Aaron-Quo dialogues, on the nineteenth of January, nineteen ninety-three, set aside codependence and turned to the thing underneath it: compassion — not for others, but for the self. The being that keeps sliding back into fear. The one that knows better and does it anyway. Aaron began with a story about a Tibetan saint, and it is the story I have been waiting three sessions to tell you.

Milarepa sat at the mouth of his cave, meditating, when the demons came — demons of anger, of rage, of fear, of greed. They were hideous: exuding a foul smell, dangling bloody knives, their bodies made of decaying flesh, bones rattling with a hideous sound. Milarepa took one look at them and said: Come in. Come sit by my fire. Are you not afraid of us, they asked. No, he replied. Your hideous appearance only reminds me to be aware, to have mercy. Come, sit by my fire.

That, Aaron said, is the whole of the practice. One does not stay undefended — one simply notes the arising of defense each time it appears, the arising of fear, and says: oh, you again. Here is fear. Come, sit by my fire. Your relationships will continue to inspire fear and the desire to defend. You do not move past that need by denying it, or wishing it away, or judging it and saying I should know better by now. You transcend the need to defend by embracing the ego self — comforting it, noticing the fear, inviting it to the fire. You cannot transcend what you do not accept. To transcend ego, you must accept ego.

There is a vast difference, they said, between the experience of fear and the reactivity to fear. Watch the process closely: first the perceived threat, then the fear itself, then the need to defend — the aversion, the urge to fling the fear onto another as anger or blame. The need to defend is not the fear. It is the reaction to the fear. And it is the reaction, not the fear, that pulls you into the old unwholesome patterns. Learn to experience the fear without the reactivity — to say, here is fear, sit by my fire, but I will not be reactive to you — and the fear stops being a summons to defend and becomes a reminder for compassion.

I keep testing this against my own worst moments, and it holds. The fear was never the disgrace; the disgrace, if there was one, was the flailing. And even the flailing — Aaron would say — deserves the fire too. Nothing in this teaching is refused a seat.

Aaron named the illusion that makes compassion for the self so difficult: the belief that your reactivity against another is about the other. It is not, they said — and they made it an unqualified statement: all of your judgment against another is judgment against faults perceived or manifest in yourself. You may judge another's impatience while showing none yourself — but somewhere in your heart the impatience is arising, and it is that inner arising you cannot stand. Can you see what a gift these discomforting emotions are? They are the constant catalyst reminding you: have mercy.

This is why the spiritual body came here at all, they explained. It is easy for the spirit to know its own perfection — but if it never meets imperfection, where is its opportunity to practice non-judgment, to practice unconditional love toward what was previously judged and found wanting? So it moves into the house of the physical, joins with the emotional and mental bodies — and learns, lifetime after lifetime, to love what it once condemned. The earthsuit is not a punishment. It is a curriculum.

Q'uo offered a visualization for the same truth: the house of your spiritual self. Above the ground floor door you have hung a sign reading I have my rights — the ethic of freedom your culture prizes highest. But climb the stairs, they said, and the upper story bears a different legend: the earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof. Sit there a while, in the awareness that you are in the Creator and the Creator in you. And when you come back down to everyday experience, you will find the sign above your front door has changed. It reads: I am worthy.

You are worthy to receive all good things, they said — and if you do not receive a good thing, you are still worthy. It is only your feelings, bruised and battered by rude experience, that communicate unworthiness. That is a false communication. Do not accept it. Know your worthiness, your loveliness, and feel compassion rising naturally within the portion of you that remains upstairs.

Aaron left the group with homework, and I will leave it with you. Watch the arising of fear. Note the tension in the belly, the throat. See the need to defend arise separately from the fear itself. And when the small ego self starts its kicking and screaming — when some part of you would rather blame than grow — smile at it. Oh, you again, they said. Come and sit by my fire. The more you fear that small self, the more solid it becomes. The more you welcome it, the more the heart opens — and the divinity that was straining to express itself, all along, finally gets its seat by the flames.

Thank you for listening.

title: Dynamic Peace
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: dynamic peace.

In February of nineteen ninety-three, the group asked Q'uo about one of the permanent tensions of the spiritual life: how do we balance accepting what the universe has given us with actively working to change it? When is the right move surrender — and when is it right to take the catalyst in hand and steer? Q'uo answered with a method. Not a rule, but a practice, in three movements.

Everything rests, they said, on a prior decision: do you trust the life pattern or not? If you can find a faith in the overall plan of this incarnation — that it yields lessons in love and opportunities for service — then much of the fog around any particular choice simply lifts. The outer picture, day to day, loses its power to shake your basic steadfastness. Without that trust, every decision is argued on quicksand. With it, the ground holds.

The first movement is surrender. When a difficult choice faces you, sit with the situation and ask only that light be given — no more direction than that. Become very quiet inside. Ask freedom from the timetable. Bathe in the feelings and shapes of the situation until the situation itself is clarified: what is actually happening here, seen accurately by the heart? Q'uo would not name a time limit — sometimes a tangled situation clarifies in an instant; sometimes a seemingly simple either-or reveals unsuspected layers. The waiting is the work.

The second movement is active. Turn now to the intelligence of the mind and heart, and trace, for each option, the spiritual shape of the road it opens. Not the surface qualities — do not seek contentment, they warned, for the seeker's path is often uncomfortable. Ask instead: which alternative tends more toward my learning of love, and toward my opportunity to be of service? You are looking, they said, for the highest proportion of helpful catalyst, and of openings to offer your gifts on others' behalf.

The third movement is surrender again. Return to the contemplative mind and give the still, small voice its place — which is always with you, in you, of you. You are not exterior to your situation, they reminded the group. You offered this situation to yourself, and now you have received it. There is a short prayer this instrument knew, Q'uo said, and it belongs here: God, grant me the ability to see the difference between that which I can change and that which I need to accept.

I admire the symmetry of it — stillness, effort, stillness — like breathing. We tend to do it backwards: agonize first, act in a panic, and then try to meditate the regret away. Q'uo's order insists that clarity is not found but allowed, then tested, then allowed again.

And how do you know the process has worked? By a feeling Q'uo described with two words I keep returning to: a purified, dynamic peace. When one option lets the whole of the heart rest in that emotion — not excitement, not relief, but a peace with energy in it — the decision is made. The emotions are treacherous at face value, they admitted, but refined, they contain enormous stores of wisdom. If no option brings that peace, the conservative counsel is to stay precisely as you are — keep doing the work before you, and wait for the inner insight that renders the whole entity, soul and body, peaceful and relieved.

To act before that clarification, they said, is not a catastrophe — you have not lost your way. You have only chosen the more crooked and bumpy detour, the road with heavier catalyst. Free will, they added dryly, seems just a joke, and a cruel one, when you are staring at your limits. But move inward to the point of present infinity — see the starry heavens instead of the two inches in front of your nose — and you give yourself room in which the decision can become obvious.

One more counsel, for the decisions that involve other people. There is not a decision you can make that holds for any other person besides the self, Q'uo said. If others seem entangled in the choice, the decision is not yet mature. Strip away, one by one, everything you do not control — and decide only among what is yours alone. As each seeker is responsible for the self, decisions are better made focusing on the direct and simple situation: your learning, your service, your road.

So the balance the group asked about is not a compromise between passivity and control. It is a rhythm: be still until the picture clarifies, engage fully in weighing the roads of love, and be still again until peace — dynamic, purified peace — signs the decision. Any road is good, Q'uo said, as long as the light is shining through you. The thirst for that light is itself the beginning of the deepest service.

Thank you for listening.

title: Gems in the Rock
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: gems in the rock.

On the fourteenth of February, nineteen ninety-three, the group asked Q'uo for something audacious: a definition of life — simple enough to be understood at our level, and true enough to cover all creation. They added two riders: why does the rainbow seem upside down, with the violet at the bottom — and how does the death of one of us, especially a child, affect the karma of those left behind? Q'uo took up all three, and then Hatonn came to close the evening with one of the most beloved images in the archive.

A definition of life, Q'uo said, tripping over the nouns and verbs of your illusion, as they cheerfully put it. The most comprehensive definition is this: life is manifestation. To put it another way, life is movement. All that is, is alive — all was created by a single Thought, whose character is the infinite Creator's, and the only name we have for it, however inadequate, is love. A love, they added, as terrible as it is wonderful — loving destruction as passionately as creation, embracing the whole process, every phase of the movement equally lovely.

For human life specifically: a life is joined when the vibratory nexus of what you call the soul enters and mingles with a physical vehicle in a permanent bonding. Body and spirit, enmeshed, harmonizing into a living being. And a life ends when the movement of the spirit ceases and separates from that nexus — sometimes before the body's death, sometimes at it, sometimes clinging after, unwilling to move on. Nothing in this picture, they noted, is ever lost: no iota of beingness, no learning, no loving, no giving ever ceases or comes to an end. The mystery gives all life, and absorbs all spent life, with no loss of coherence or energy.

The rainbow question drew an answer about the tree of life. Consider a tree, they said: roots gathering nourishment below, leaves turning to the sun above. Now consider the tree of life, whose roots are in the Logos — the light descending through the trunk, becoming most articulated where it grows conscious of itself, in third density, turning toward the light not by instinct but by free will. That light comes from the center of love and moves outward into every vibration of the universe — which means its frame of reference is not yours. What you experience is the final fruit of love's long travel into manifestation. You see, feel, and think by reflection, as in a mirror — and in a mirror, everything appears upside down. The rainbow is not wrong. You are looking at it from inside the reflection.

I love the gentleness of that — the universe is not mislabeled; we are simply standing on the far side of the glass.

On karma, Q'uo corrected the most common misperception directly: karma is not a ledger. It is not metaphysical bookkeeping, debits and credits to be balanced. Karma, in their considered opinion, is the energy of action — an action accelerates an energy within the centers of the being and sets body, mind, and spirit moving together. That acceleration is what each came into incarnation to experience. The unskillful life and the sage's life are both, equally, a witness to the light — and no one runs out of chances to learn a given lesson of love.

And here is the sentence I would carry out of the session like a lantern: what matters, metaphysically speaking, is not whether one chooses more correctly or skillfully. What matters is the purity and genuine authenticity of the desire to express as a channel of the love and the light of the infinite One. The report card, they said, is not graded on your abilities as a choice-maker. It is graded on your desire to love and serve. In every present moment — under every circumstance — there is a whole and equal opportunity to choose life: not the life that comes and goes, but the life that is one, infinite, and eternal.

Then Hatonn came forward, and the evening turned from definition to benediction. How delicate, how fleeting, they said, is your evanescent life within this beautiful illusion. Be of good cheer and merriment, my brothers, and share love with yourself and with each other — for that is your nature. And then the image: you are gems embedded in the living rock — the rock of flesh and bone, of thought and the brain's intellect. Within the rock the gem lies whole, complete, fully functional. It is simply not seen. Then someone mines it, chips away what seems to be dross, facets it according to its makeup — and lo, it becomes obviously radiant.

Know, Hatonn said, that as you feel the losses and limitations of life, dross is being melted away. Know that this takes many lifetimes. Know that you are as you are — perfect, entire, whole, and invisible, most of all to yourself. You see the rock. Breathe in, breathe out love — and though your vision of yourself will always be clouded, to the world you shall become, more and more, a light that lightens the consciousness of your beloved planet.

Forgive yourself, Hatonn said in parting, for being born into rock — with the gem tucked safely within, forever. You were never the rock. You were never the dross. You were the gem all along, waiting for the patient hands of your own lifetimes to cut the facets and let the light out.

Thank you for listening.

title: An Accurate Measure
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: an accurate measure.

We begin on a late winter Sunday, in nineteen ninety three, with a question about moderation. One seeker wants to know how to pace her body so her work does not wound her. Another wants to know how to walk the spiritual path without turning it into a race against herself. Q'uo answers both with one word. Accuracy.

Q'uo starts in the Garden of Eden, where all was plain and pure vibration, and where the first pair of humans chose to know good and evil and therefore to die. I have always found this a strange reading of the old myth. They do not call it a tragedy. They call it the founding condition of this whole density, a world built of dynamic opposites, where every living thing must choose, again and again, between reaching for radiance and clutching at life while pushing death away. The fall was a choice to live and die, and everything since has been the curriculum.

And here is Q'uo's surprise. The first pair were immoderate. And immoderance, looked at honestly, is how most of the best things get done. Look back over this life at the most fruitful choices ever made, they say, and notice that in retrospect nearly all of them were immoderate, full of passion, deeply and strongly felt. So the first point is this. The essence of this density is dynamic balance between two extremes, and progress is aided by full-hearted action that moves the seeker toward becoming a transparent conduit for love and light. That is the line that stays with me. Become a transparent conduit. Not a lukewarm one. A transparent one.

Then what is moderation? Q'uo defines it as activity in which there is an awareness of the limitations that pertain to that activity. For the very strong, a moderate exercise might be the careful, evenly paced climb of a great mountain. For the physically limited, moderation might be a short walk through a field or two. The climber and the ambler have nothing in common about their rightness. Moderation is judged only by the one entity who knows its own capacities and its rate of learning. That was the answer for the seeker worried about her injuries. The activities that broke her are not immoderate in themselves. What matters is the accuracy of the self-estimate.

What goes wrong, Q'uo says, is the refusal to make that estimate accurately. Entities avoid the true sense of what they can bear. The ones who break themselves are those who do not want to look at their limits, and the result is a cycle of being able to do less and less, until at last the seeker is forced to reckon with the failure. So the goal is not to hold back from the edge, but to move to the limit of what this particular instrument can bear without injury, taking small but frequent steps toward more discernment, more compassion, more transparency.

Then Q'uo names the voice that argues against accuracy. It is the old temptation in the garden, and it lives deep in every sea of consciousness. It is the energy of spiritual greed, and it says, eat of this, you will not die. The body says I can do anything. The ego says there is no cost. And so the seeker puts the gas pedal to the floor and hits the curve, and the crash does kill something, and there is an overwhelming sense of loss. Every one of us has heard that voice. It sounds like freedom. It is not freedom.

But there is one place where Q'uo says moderation is not suggested at all. That is in moral and ethical judgment. When the sense of right and wrong wakes up inside you, they say, heed it without moderation. Let your yes be yes and your no be no. The importance of respecting that ethical impulse cannot be overestimated. It is the foundation stone of the whole world of spiritual principle. Yet even then, in applying the principle, moderation returns as a central concern, except when something like martyrdom is necessary to witness to the principle, and even there what is required is an accurate sense of one's destiny.

The practical tool Q'uo offers is almost embarrassingly simple. The clock. Set the beginning and the end of the activity. But any tool must be used by the self, and the self must first come into accurate awareness of its capacities. That search, they insist, takes the light touch. There is humor inherent in limitation, standing starkly beside the joy of utter intoxication, and one wishes to move somewhere between that intoxication and a refusal to use any capacity at all. That image, of steering between drunkenness and dormancy with humor, feels like the truest sentence in the whole session.

Q'uo closes with a word about fear, and it ties the whole thing together. The fearful instrument worries about getting the channeling wrong. The fearless one misjudges the body's limits. In each seeker there are times when the answers seem very, very important. And yet there need be no fear concerning the gathering of information about the matter, whatever it may be. Let moderation be not the result of fear, but the embracing of freedom.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Silver Cord
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the silver cord. Early March, nineteen ninety three, and a question arrives from a seeker trained in medicine, who wants to know where the illusion ends and reality begins. Where is the juncture between this three-dimensional life and whatever is real? Q'uo's answer is careful, almost reluctant, and then it turns into one of their most quietly beautiful descriptions of what a human being actually is.

They begin by gently correcting the direction of the question. The true juncture of illusion and reality, they say, is within the spiritual complex only, and it is that direct linkage through the shuttle of intelligent energy to intelligent infinity. To move into intelligent infinity is to enter reality, and it is also to cease being aware of the self or anything whatsoever. There is unlimited intelligence there, but only one thought, the Logos of love. All other states whatsoever are illusory. That is a staggering sentence to sit with. Everything we call real is a dream, and the one reality is the one we cannot be conscious inside of.

But Q'uo knows what the questioner was really reaching for, and they move there next. The juncture between our space and time awareness and the inner planes, the levels of awareness that hold the light bodies which govern the physical vehicle. The physical body, they say, is partially a creature of the illusion itself. It carries the resources, physical and mental, of the creature that is your vehicle. But over it there is an overshadowing influence of the infinite and eternal creature which is your consciousness, connected to this incarnation's vehicle by an inextricable connection popularly known as the silver cord.

And then they describe the aura, the thing the questioner asked about, as a blending. It shows the natural health or discomfort of the physical and mental state, blended with the complex additions of resources and biases the consciousness brought into this incarnation. So the aura, seen by those with clear inner sight, displays not only the state of the entity but, to a variable degree, the native density of the wanderer, and overtones of vibration belonging not to one lifetime but to the continuing pattern of the being through many incarnations. When you look at a person, if you could truly see, you would see every life they have ever lived, shining through.

The connection is not broken except through death. It may release slightly before physical death or shortly after, but it simply withdraws from a vehicle that can no longer be used. I find that image consoling. Nothing is ripped away. The cord withdraws the way a hand withdraws from a glove it can no longer wear.

The rest of the session turns to healers, and it carries the same gentleness. Q'uo notes that when medical people study the body's medicine, they are trained in exactitude, in tremendous respect for detail. When a spiritual person turns to healing, that same entity moves as a poet or a dancer, expressing in generalities of grace and rhythm and aesthetic beauty. These two approaches, they say, can harmonize into one broad holistic way of viewing health concerns. The physical body is the child of the form-maker body, which is the creature of the infinite and eternal consciousness that says I am.

Disease, then, may be approached through allopathic measures, Q'uo says, or through laughter, meditation, visualization, fasting, and prayer. All disciplines can work together harmoniously and cooperatively, not one being greater than the other, but all used as appropriate. I want to be clear about how this series holds such words. Q'uo speaks of their own opinions, and asks that we each use our discrimination. These are reflections on healing, not medical instructions, and they sit alongside, never above, the care of a real physician.

A physician in the circle asks how those trained in medicine might merge their training with metaphysical belief. Q'uo's answer is simple. The tools aiding healers the most, besides being expert at their fields, include the glad awareness of a higher power and a recognition of the value of the patient's vital energy and will to live. Happy is the doctor, they say, whose patient has a destiny still upon this plane. Happy is the doctor whose patient has some awareness of this destiny. Those who believe rigorously in any one regimen, whether chemicals or visualizations, find that such dependence is not always rewarded.

Then Q'uo adds something that widens the whole conversation. They have noticed, they say, that physicians like the questioner are inspired to ask queries of sources like this group because they already carry the vision of a great universal healing center, a combination of all the various modes of healing, so that entities with disease may through more than one kind of doctoring receive a more complete healing. And the closing thought of the session is the one I carry away. Above all things, for the greatest health of all, turn always toward the infinite one in praise, in prayer, in silence, and in thanksgiving.

Thank you for listening.

title: Ownership Falls Away
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: ownership falls away.

Mid March, nineteen ninety three, and the question is about spiritual pride. What is it, how does it work in groups and in individuals, and what can a seeker do to get back to humility, that great ally? Q'uo's answer is longer than you might expect, because they are dissolving the question itself as they answer it. Humility, they say, is a kind of pride.

They start by defending an accurate estimate of the self. To look at yourself and fairly assess your assets, to know what you can and cannot do in a given situation, is a work of lucid observation. It is not pride. The balanced seeker moves upon the seat of knowledge of the self, and that seat serves it well as it does the tightrope walk through all the situations of the day. Pride begins somewhere else entirely.

They reach for two old stories. The Buddha, who found that being a prince, being loved and loving, filled him not with fullness but with the observation that all of it was prideful folly, until at last he was content as a ferryman rowing others across the river. And the rich young man of the western tradition, who had kept every commandment and asked what more he could do, and was told to sell all he had. That parable has made comfortable people nervous ever since, Q'uo notes dryly. But it is not about money. It is about one's relationship to that which comes and goes. It is not a crime to conserve wealth and use it prudently. The question is whether you are a steward of it or whether you are grabbing and owning it. The same question holds for the body itself. Care for it, yes. But ask what takes precedence, the body or the soul.

And then comes the sentence the whole session turns on. Spiritual pride, they say, is about ascribing ownership of absolutely anything at all to anyone except the infinite Creator. If everything is made of the love of the infinite Creator, then each seeker is of love, made of love, made for love, made by love, made to love. To love is the infinity of a verb. We are not nouns, not persons or objects, but energetic words which activate and enable love to be expressed and received, from love to love for love's sake. Where, in that, fits any individual expression that could own anything?

So what gets us off the merry-go-round between pride and humility? Not humility, because to be conscious of being humble is a prideful consciousness. True humility is of the one who, without thinking either well or ill of the self, has the impulse to serve under any conditions whatsoever. While one seeker is trying to be humble, the truly humble entity has already found a way to be of service, perhaps by listening to the conversation of the one who is seeking to be humble. I read that and laughed at myself, because I have been that second seeker so many times, polishing my humility while someone else was quietly doing the dishes.

They name the pitfalls plainly. The first is to worry about spiritual pride at all, that taking of the spiritual temperature. The second is the opportunity, in communicating with others, to defend or to impress. The impulse to defend, to have another think well of who you are, is fear-driven and is pride. The desire to impress is a special kind of defense, an offensive defense, the move to bedazzle others with the qualities you yourself consider impressive. It is never necessary, they say, that others grasp who you are or what you are doing. It is acceptable to be misunderstood. Release ownership of who you are.

And how do you release it? Seek simply to know your identity in love. Turn from any other consideration as frequently as possible and spend precious moments with the love that you are, with the love that you then may share. Seek to put your life in the Creator's hands, and the Creator's life will be in your hands. You will become the perfect mirror, transparent to the light and the love of the infinite one.

There is a small coda in the questions worth keeping. A seeker asks about the voice that pops up again and again to call her prideful, even after she has turned away from it. Q'uo's answer is full of lightness of touch. All learning requires a certain amount of failure. They paint the picture of a kitten that almost landed on its feet, stumbles, regains balance, looks puzzled at the situation, and moves on to tackle the ball of yarn again. Release over-concern for any area of learning, they say, lest the concern become over-exercised and cause a blocking caution that inhibits further progress. Watch the process with perspective and humor. There is much humor in each learning process. There is. There truly is.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Walled Light
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the walled light.

Late March, nineteen ninety three, and a new series of dialogues opens between Aaron and Q'uo, on the simplest and hardest question in the archive. How do we open the heart? Aaron begins by correcting the question itself. The heart never closes, they say. You may build a wall around it, but it never closes.

I want to sit with that a moment, because it changes everything. When you think of the heart as closing, you are captured in the distortion that you are totally separate from your deepest reality, the divine within you. The heart is the center of that divinity. So the real question is not how to open what cannot close, but how to express the divinity that is always there. The light always shines. The wall is only the fear you have built around it.

Aaron offers the working image. Think of the heart as a place of the purest light, truly reflecting the divine light. When you wall that light in out of fear, you have not turned it off. Constant awareness of the presence of that light becomes the tool. Here is the light. Pay attention. It is harder to see today because there is fear. Focus on it. Let it blossom. As you move back into that clarity, the wall dissolves by itself. There is no self taking down the wall. There has simply been awareness.

Q'uo follows with a model of the energy centers, and what is striking is where they start. They do not start with the heart. They start below it, because seekers so often dream and reach with the upper centers while leaving the lower ones unexamined. The red center is the vitality of mind, body, and spirit working together. The orange is self to self and self to other. The yellow is the self in relation to groups, the family, the nation. Then the green, the heart, the first energy that needs no instreaming but that of the one infinite Creator. You cannot clear the heart by refusing the ground floor.

They give two images for the self, and I love the strangeness of them. The first is a prince or princess in royal robes, seated on a huge lumbering beautifully decorated elephant. That is the seeker working at the brow while leaving the earthbound parts unaccepted. The second is to think of yourself as the elephant. This large, physically awkward animal contains a subjective beauty which has nothing to do with form. The form must be there within this illusion so that the spirit may learn and serve. One tool, then, is to reckon with the outer elephant without becoming discouraged, disgusted, or exhausted. O ponderous pachyderms, proceed, Q'uo says at one point, and I will never forget that line. Find a laugh in your heart. Smile at your beloved elephant that gives its life that you might learn better to be.

Aaron offers their own image, and it has become one of the most repeated images in the whole archive. You are angels in earthsuits. Both are real. Without the body and the emotions, the angel would be deprived of the catalysts that incarnation so readily offers. Without the angel, the earthsuit is sterile. It is far easier to focus on the angelness and look with disdain on the earthsuit, to grasp at graduating from this plane rather than being on this plane and trusting that this is where you need to be. The angel's wings can get a bit tarnished. Its feet get caught in the mud. And if the angel does not set foot on earth, where is it going to learn these lessons of love, of faith, of compassion?

There is a hard passage here for the old souls among the seekers, and I think it lands honestly. Those who see the light most clearly are often the most impatient with their human manifestations, asking perfection of themselves, and that very impatience cuts them off from compassion for this human. Aaron's image for the way back is actors in a play. Read your lines with convincing honesty, because the audience, which is also you, cannot learn if the actor treats the play as frivolous. Yet the actor cannot forget it is an actor. That is the balance. Put your whole heart into the illusion while remembering the spirit body, the reality of who you are.

The session ends with a practice, and it is worth trying tonight. Find the heart center and the spark of the divine there, undefended. Rest in that space, empty of all self, and radiate loving-kindness. Then turn your memory to some moment today when you felt a bit threatened, when the small ego self moved to protect itself. Re-experience that move from center to what seems the closing of the heart. And notice, Aaron says, that the light does not fade. It is simply blocked. A cloud has come between you and the sun. Instead of getting caught in the darkness, focus on the sun. It is a skill. A learnable skill.

Thank you for listening.

title: Clouds Before the Sun
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: clouds before the sun.

The next morning, still March of nineteen ninety three, Aaron and Q'uo continue their dialogue on opening the heart. Yesterday they laid the groundwork. The heart never closes, the light is always there, the work is with the wall. Today they go into the tools.

Aaron begins with a homework report. Did you experience those moments of separating, they ask, the window shades drawn tightly closed? It is a painful experience, and not necessary to incarnation. Then they walk into the mechanics. There is careful looking, and there is the presence of fear. Who is afraid? Afraid of what? There is a cycle. You experience fear and separation. There must be the illusion of a solid self, separate, subject and object. As you experience the self as solid, the fear becomes more solid, bringing you further from your true self.

They quote a poem by Rumi that the channel had encountered that morning. The moment I heard of his love, I thought to find the beloved I must search with body, mind and soul. But no. To find the beloved, we must become the beloved. You need not seek God elsewhere. The divine is within yourself. As soon as you experience yourself as separate from the divine, the self solidifies, fear increases, and the darkness closes in further.

The image Aaron gives for working with this is a blue sky with a brilliant sun and small wisps of clouds. The winds shift. The clouds gather into what seems a storm cloud blocking the sun. Now you have two choices. React as if the cloud were solid and move to protect yourself, fetching your jacket or your umbrella. Or remember the sun is still shining. There is nothing solid here, just bits of the same material you have seen floating through the sky. Of course, if it begins to pour, you put up an umbrella. But is the umbrella to protect you from harm, or to keep you warm and dry? There is a difference.

That difference is the whole teaching. When you relate to the clouds in your life as personally threatening, fear solidifies, self solidifies, and your response becomes a war with the clouds. You believe they must be gotten rid of at all costs so you can return to the experience of the sun. But when you can note the existence of the clouds without feeling personal threat, just clouds coming through, you can still put up the umbrella skillfully, without fear, always knowing the sun is shining above. If someone is raging at you, you may still step back or leave the room, but without reacting with fear. The fear and pain of the other can be seen for what they are.

There is a moment, Aaron says, where the self begins to solidify and you experience perceived threat. I could be hurt. My needs might not be met. There must be attention to that moment, and to the arising of anger, should it be there. With strong mindfulness, that first perception becomes like a waving warning flag. Can there be compassion for this seeming self that is feeling fear? Turn to the light within me. Remember the sun is still shining. When you offer compassion to yourself, you begin to be able to offer it to the catalyst. Then self and other dissolve, not immediately, but slowly. It is no longer my fear, but our fear, our pain.

Q'uo takes up the same thread with the old sage and the child, one of the archive's strangest parables. A sage lived in one room, meditating and praying. A young stranger burst in with a newborn, naming the sage as the father. He did not argue. He took the babe and went to work as a laborer to feed it. Years later the mother returned and took the child away. Again he did not argue, but simply returned to his meditation. To resist one's pain, Q'uo says, is to intensify it. The moment of the impulse to pain is a red flag saying pay attention. Look with attentive caring. Let this be as it is.

Aaron capsulates it into a principle. Do not dialogue with fear. This does not mean get rid of fear. It means do not give fear permission to be in control. When you relate to what leads you into fear with more fear and a need to get rid of it in order to come back to love, you are dialoguing with fear. When you can simply be present with what is, you are no longer reactive to it. There is just fear. There is just pain. It no longer has the capacity to shut out the light. You allow its presence, you move with compassion to the being experiencing it, and immediately you are in the light.

And then the closing exercise, which I will not spoil by explaining too much. Q'uo guides the listener through the first impulse of heavy negative emotion striking, the body flattened on the dust of a barren land. And then the turning. Take this body into your arms. Rock with this poor pained child. Sing the lullaby of faith, of hope. And rise in spirit singing. What is being healed here is not just the pain but the separation. This, too, is holy.

Thank you for listening.

title: Cherish Yourselves
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: cherish yourselves.

Later that same March day, nineteen ninety three, the third Aaron and Q'uo dialogue takes up a question from the homework they assigned. When you practiced moving back into the light, did you find resistance to that light? One listener reports her pattern. She feels good doing the practice, and then as she comes out into the world she moves from being in control to being out of control. Q'uo says the feeling of out-of-controlness is not a fault. It is just a feeling. And what follows is one of the most direct statements in the whole series about how the lower energy centers are actually cleared.

Q'uo begins by naming something many spiritual traditions rush past. The difficulty of incarnation is to be spiritual in the mud. There is in each the spiritual and also the human, the animal, which is in many ways the most beautiful part of each of you. The work here is not to starve it but to cherish it. You must cherish yourself, they say, as you would cherish any other self you love very much, perhaps more. And the lower centers do not clear through the refusal of earthly instinct but through its acceptance.

This is where the homework report becomes the teaching. The feeling of losing control is exactly the place where the animal nature is unquiet. Q'uo is emphatic that no judgment should be made of such feelings. The red center needs no clearing, for it is the seat of pure beingness. The centers above it do need their unquietness calmed, and it can only be calmed by acceptance of the unquietness and those that cause it. When there is a failure, it is a golden opportunity, for then one can take the failing entity up as a baby and say, you poor tired baby, and feel all the love of a parent toward a tired, crying child. The way to perfect love is through perfect understanding of imperfection.

Aaron's contribution to the session goes straight at the heart of why so many of us feel self-loathing. The ego believes it must control fear, control the unhappiness of the small self, and it holds the view that it is possible to fix the distortions in the personality self. What Aaron calls the biggest challenge of the spiritual path is the realization that you cannot fix the distortion within the personality self. Some things you can heal. But you cannot heal them through fighting with them. The catalyst of seeing clearly into the distorted areas moves through forgiveness and compassion. Then there can be a healing of it, an embracing of it, and a letting go.

They use the image of the small self as a small human baby that has fallen and skinned its knee. With love we take it up and tend it. We do not say to it, you wicked child, why did you fall? We simply express love and care to the small self. The distortion does not need to be fixed. It needs to be allowed.

Aaron then talks about fear directly, and their words here are blunt. Do not look at fear as an enemy. Do not set fear aside. Do not consider that you would be happier without your fear. Be willing to embrace it with gentleness. It is part of your incarnational experience, part of the earthsuit. We do not take away the experience of fear. We let it be there and embrace it, and so we move beyond it.

The middle of the session is the part I have replayed more than any other. One seeker asks about the word love as it is used in the channelings, saying that when it is applied to all the feelings she experiences, she cannot feel that love and becomes confused. Q'uo answers with the parable of the prodigal son. The Father ran down the road to welcome the son and there was a great feast. The prodigal may not ever have become the steady younger son, but he was welcomed into the embrace of love just as he was. So too, they say, does the Creator of us all look at each and say, there is perfection in each as each is. Not the changing, but the acceptance.

The session ends with two exercises, and I will give them here the way they were given. The first is the forgiveness meditation. Sit and picture yourself in every situation that arises within the heart today, as a separate entity to whom you may forgive all transgressions. Do this daily. Forgiveness is a process, Aaron says, and the more it becomes habit, the deeper it settles into the heart until it begins to express itself naturally.

The second is almost mischievous. Q'uo suggests that during the waking day, one may try, just once, to be completely and utterly human. Set the spiritual self aside and enjoy every animal and spiritual attribute of the mind and body as a little boy watches with delight the bugs in the ground. Get completely wrapped up in some desire or preference, and see what happens. Notice that the world does not come to an end. Note that the Creator still loves. To be human does not cut one off from spiritual life. To be human is a good thing.

Thank you for listening.

title: Open the Shutters
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: open the shutters.

March twenty third, nineteen ninety three, and the last of the four Aaron and Q'uo dialogues on opening the heart. This one goes to the place the earlier sessions kept circling but had not entered. Faith. Not the faith that comes with reassurance, but the faith that has to live in a closed room with the shutters drawn, in the dark.

Aaron begins with the report from the previous session's homework, the forgiveness meditation, and they linger on a simple observation. Once you begin to practice forgiveness and compassion toward yourself, your heart starts to soften toward others too. There is nothing else that is needed.

The metaphor comes from the channel, who has been talking about how, in the darkest times, she tends to close herself into a small dark closet and refuse to come out until someone rescues her, with doors open and light streaming in and the angels playing violins. Aaron refines the image. Think of a room with shutters on the window. A breeze comes up and the shutters close. Then a storm blows and they are latched. You are in a small, dark room with the shutters latched. It is cold and dark. You sit there waiting for the day the storm will end and the light will stream in.

And the real question, they say, is how you sit there. There are two very different ways. One way is in fear and darkness and doubt, feeling separate and afraid. Another way is in faith, to open yourself to the divine within the darkness, to be patient, to trust. It is easy to trust when the shutters are open and you can see the angels walking in the garden and the flowers growing and the light shining. But in the darkness, when the light is gone, how do you trust? They put it with a blade of clarity. Faith is trust in something you cannot know. You are being asked to trust precisely when you cannot see anything to trust in.

Q'uo takes this further than Aaron does, and the passage deserves to be heard whole. When you are in the midst of your darkest fears, sitting in that dark closet, they say, what is it that you do? You do not let yourself experience your fear of the dark. You are too busy waiting to be rescued. And so all of the time is spent in the dark waiting for light, while all the time the light is there. They repeat it. All the time the light is there.

To have faith, Q'uo says, is to let the heart's eye see what the world's eye cannot. It is to be in a place of darkness and yet to know that there is light because you are the light. The darkness is not the absence of light. It is a place where the eye cannot yet see the light. Faith is the quality that allows the heart to rest in the certainty that the light is there even when the eye cannot perceive it. That is the line I want to underline. Faith is the quality that allows the heart to rest.

Then Q'uo tells a story from the channel's memory that Aaron's earlier session on love had asked her to remember, and it is a devastating little story. Her mother was dying. The hospital chaplain had said that prayer would make things better. The mother believed this completely. When she kept getting worse, the mother was furious, not only with the chaplain but with God. If prayer could not make things better, what good was it? Q'uo's response is gentle but unflinching. The mother's faith had been a faith that asked for proof. Give me the light, and I will believe. But the deeper faith is the one that rests in darkness without proof.

Aaron brings in the story of Thomas, the apostle who needed to put his hand in the wound. It is fine, Aaron says, to be a Thomas sometimes. But the invitation is to move beyond needing to touch in order to believe. When the dark comes, and it will, do not ask why. Ask, how do I rest in this? How do I let the heart's eye see what the world's eye cannot?

The practice at the end of the session is the gentlest of the four dialogues. Sit in your inner room with the shutters closed. Do not try to open them. Simply rest there and breathe. Let the heart's eye do what the world's eye cannot do. And notice that you are not alone in the dark. The light has been there all along, because you are the light. The darkness is not your enemy. It is the place where faith is born.

Thank you for listening.

title: Clear the Screen
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: clear the screen.

Late March, nineteen ninety three, a Sunday, and the question comes from a seeker who has noticed a pattern in his own mind. Something happened in his younger days. Something unwise. And ever since, when he reaches a certain point in his thinking, the thought of that past failure cuts in and he cannot continue. He asks Q'uo how this mechanism works, and what it has to do with regret, and with the healing of memory. What follows is one of Q'uo's most practical teachings on the mind.

Q'uo begins with a metaphor the seeker already lives with. The thought patterns of the mind are like computer programs. Each has a beginning, a middle, and an end. These thought patterns may be run at a high rate of speed. Like an athlete training the body by repeated movement, the mind becomes more and more adroit at running its patterns. The process is not much different from any other learning process. It is repetition that makes the thought pattern what it is.

Here is where the teaching turns sharp. When the mind is programmed with a given set of instructions, it will tend to run the program fully each time it is run. The mind has a difficulty in doing otherwise. Like the seeker says, as soon as he hits that point in his thinking, he becomes disabled in continuing. That is the program running to completion. The regret is not a feeling that visits. It is a program that executes.

But Q'uo does not leave it at mechanics. The thought pattern is not just running. It is also teaching. The seeker, in his younger days, did something unwise, and the memory of that unwisdom became attached to a point in the pattern where judgment occurs. Every time the pattern runs, the judgment fires. What the seeker calls regret, Q'uo calls the memory of a lesson learned in a painful way, now repeating the lesson long after the learning has been done.

The deeper question is what regret is for. Q'uo distinguishes between regret that teaches and regret that merely repeats. When the pattern first formed, it served a function. It said, look here, you acted unwisely, and here is the pain that came of it. That is a program worth running once, or even several times. But once the lesson has been taken into the heart, the program's continued running serves nothing. It is the mind being loyal to an instruction long after the instruction has stopped being useful.

The healing of memory, then, is not the erasing of memory. Q'uo is clear about this. You do not forget the unwisdom. You remember it differently. The healing is in the reprogramming, in teaching the mind that the lesson has been learned, that the program has completed its function and may be retired. And the way this is done is not through argument with the mind, which is just another program running. It is done through forgiveness.

Forgiveness here is not a moral performance. It is the recognition that the entity who did the unwise thing was doing the best that entity could do at that time, with the light that entity had. When you can see the younger self clearly, not excused and not condemned, the judgment point in the pattern loses its charge. The pattern may still begin to run, out of old loyalty, but it no longer has anywhere to go. It winds down on its own.

There is a companion teaching running beneath this one about the nature of time itself. Q'uo speaks of the mind's tendency to treat the past as still present, to run the old program as though the unwisdom were happening now. But the past is not present. The self that did the unwise thing no longer exists. The self that runs the program is a new self, running old software. Healing of memory is the updating of that software, the quiet, patient reprogramming of the thought patterns until the mind runs clean.

The closing note of the session is worth keeping close. Q'uo reminds the seeker that this work cannot be forced. The mind will run its patterns at its own pace, and the attempt to suppress the pattern by force is just the writing of a new, more subtle program on top of the old one. Instead, meet the pattern with compassion when it runs. Notice it. Forgive the self that wrote it. Forgive the self that runs it. And in time, the screen clears.

Thank you for listening.

title: Daily Bread
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: daily bread.

The end of March, nineteen ninety three, and Hatonn is speaking in an intensive meditation. Hatonn's voice in this archive is unmistakable, plain and practical, and today he takes on the most ordinary of anxieties. How does one get one's daily bread? Not the poetry of abundance. The bread itself. The rent, the groceries, the supply that keeps body and soul together in a world that feels less stable every year.

He begins with a word of encouragement that has the feel of a friend putting a hand on your shoulder.
