No matter what the conditions of the mundane world may be, he says, there is the possibility of a rich and full life. And then he says something I have turned over many times since reading it. The less stable the world becomes, the more the seeker who lives by faith may enjoy an enhanced and intensified appreciation of each day's beauties. Instability, which the world mind reads as loss, can become a kind of sharpening.

Hatonn's real question is how one gets the daily bread without worrying oneself into a knot about it. His answer starts with the distinction between desire and worry. Desire in itself is not the enemy. It is the fuel. The problem is the mind's habit of fastening onto the gap between desire and supply and living in the gap. He talks about the seeker who wants security and spends the whole day rehearsing the absence of it, and the result is a life spent staring at an empty pantry instead of cooking with what is there.

The center of the session is the teaching on control. There are things you can control and things you cannot, and the daily bread belongs mostly to the second category. What you can control, Hatonn says, is your attitude. That sounds small until he shows how large it is. Attitude is the instrument by which you receive the day. Two seekers can have the same pantry and live in two different worlds, one of sufficiency and one of lack, and the difference is entirely in how each one meets what arrives.

He gives the image of steering by hunch and hope. In a world where the old maps no longer match the terrain, the rational planner keeps redrawing plans that keep failing, and the faithful seeker learns to steer by something subtler. Hunch and hope are not excuses for passivity. They are the names for what guidance feels like when the outer world gives no reliable signals. You move. You watch. You adjust. You trust that the steering itself, done in faith, is the way the supply finds you.

There is a passage about the ocean that I want to read closely, because it is the heart of Hatonn's whole philosophy of incarnation. Welcome to the ocean of incarnational experience, he says. The maps are faulty. The charts are outdated. The winds change without warning. And yet the voyage is not a mistake. You chose the ocean. The daily bread is not found by standing on the shore demanding that the sea deliver it. It is found by sailing, by doing the next thing in front of you, by trusting that faithfulness in the small work is what brings the supply.

Hatonn also speaks about the relationship between the seeker and the world that seems to withhold. The world is not your enemy, he says. It is your classroom. When the supply seems thin, the question is not only how do I get more, but what am I being taught about my relationship to having? Some seekers learn, in seasons of leanness, that they needed less than they thought. Others learn that their real poverty was not in the pantry but in the imagination. The daily bread, taken in this larger sense, includes everything the soul needs for the day's lessons, and it is always given.

The closing of the session is a benediction on ordinary life. Hatonn does not ask the seeker to transcend the need for bread. He asks the seeker to receive it, day by day, without the poison of worry, with the simplicity of an attitude turned toward gratitude. Do the work in front of you. Steer by hunch and hope. Let the ocean be the ocean. The bread will be there.

Thank you for listening.

title: Prayer as Flow
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: prayer as flow.

Mid April, nineteen ninety three, and the question is one that many seekers carry but few ask out loud. How does prayer actually work? Not whether it works, but how. What happens in the unseen when a person prays for healing, for another, for the self? Q'uo answers with a model of energy that is worth hearing carefully, and worth holding the way they ask us to hold everything, with our own discrimination, as their opinion rather than as fact.

They begin where they so often begin, with the admission that the mechanics of prayer are not fully knowable from inside the illusion. But they offer an image that has stayed with me. Prayer is like the opening of a channel, or better, like the turning of a key in a lock that has always been there. The energy that flows when a seeker prays is not created by the prayer. It is the infinite energy of the Creator, always present, always available, and prayer is the act of consenting to let it move.

The questioner wants to know about healing specifically, and Q'uo describes what they see happening when healing is requested. There is the one who prays, there is the one prayed for, and there is the energy that moves between them. The prayer organizes the seeker's own energies and points them, and in that pointing there is a release. What is released is not the healer's personal power. It is the universal love that the healer has consented to carry for a moment. The healer is a hollow reed. The wind does the work.

I want to pause here and say something this series takes seriously. When Q'uo speaks of energy moving through prayer, they are offering a spiritual reflection, not a medical claim. Nothing in this session replaces the care of a physician, and nothing in it should be read as a promise about outcomes in the body. The archive itself is careful on this point, and we are careful with it too. What is being described is an inner practice, a way of relating to suffering and to the mystery, and its value lives in that realm.

With that held, the teaching itself is beautiful. Q'uo says that prayer for another does not impose the prayer's will upon the other's destiny. The energy offered in prayer is like light offered to a room. The room may receive it or not. The one prayed for retains complete freedom, and the prayer is effective not because it forces an outcome but because it makes the light available. This is why Q'uo can say, in a line that stops me every time, that prayer is never wasted. Even when nothing visible changes, the offering has been made, and the offering itself changes the one who offers.

There is a further subtlety. Q'uo distinguishes between praying for a specific outcome and praying in the spirit of thy will be done. The first has its place. It focuses the energies and gives the heart something definite to pour itself into. But the second, the prayer of release, is the deeper practice, because it does not ask the infinite to conform to the finite mind's picture of what healing looks like. It asks only that love move as love will. The seeker who prays in this way is not giving up on the outcome. The seeker is giving the outcome to larger hands.

The session also touches on the prayer of the healer for the self, the one who gives and gives and wonders why the giving leaves them empty. Q'uo's answer is practical. The healer who prays only for others and never opens to receive is like a channel that flows in one direction until it runs dry. Prayer must be circular. The same opening that lets the energy move outward must let it move inward. Rest, they say. Receive. Let yourself be prayed for, by others and by the silence itself.

The closing image is of a river. Prayer is not the building of a dam to hold the water where you want it. It is the clearing of the riverbed so the water can go where it goes. The water knows its way. Your work is the clearing. And the clearing is never finished, which is why the practice is daily, which is why it is called a practice at all.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Sphere of Being
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the sphere of being.

Late April, nineteen ninety three, and the question is about balance. The seeker wants to know what balance really is, and Q'uo answers by quietly demolishing the most common picture of it. Balance, they say, is not a fixed point. It is not the stillness of a statue. It is the rolling of a sphere.

Think of a sphere, they say. Not a pyramid, not a tower, but a round thing in motion. The balanced entity is not the one who has found the perfect unmoving center and frozen there. The balanced entity is the one who can roll with the terrain, adjusting continuously, never arriving at a final posture, always in the living act of balancing. I find this image liberating, because so many of us treat balance as a destination we keep failing to reach. Q'uo says it is not a destination. It is a way of moving.

The session then turns to one of the great unbalancing forces, and that is fear. Q'uo does not ask the seeker to get rid of fear. They ask the seeker to change the relationship to it. Make fear your guest, they suggest, or even your ally. When fear arrives, do not bar the door and do not hand it the keys to the house. Offer it a chair. Ask what it has come to say. Fear, in this teaching, is often the messenger of a part of the self that has not been heard, and the message is usually simpler than the terror suggests.

There is a companion teaching about the seasons of the inner life. Q'uo speaks of the seeker moving through periods of activity and periods of fallowness, times of clarity and times of confusion, and the temptation to judge the fallow seasons as failures of balance. But the sphere rolls through all weathers. The winter field is not a failed summer field. It is a field at rest, gathering itself. The seeker who can accept the season without fighting it is already practicing the deepest balance of all, the balance between striving and allowing.

Q'uo also addresses the questioner who feels pulled between the spiritual life and the demands of the world, the job, the family, the bills. The teaching here is not to choose one and starve the other. It is to see that the sphere of being includes all of it. The spiritual life is not the part of the day spent in meditation. It is the whole day, lived with the awareness that every act, from the grandest service to the washing of a dish, is the sphere rolling forward. When the seeker stops dividing the life into the sacred hours and the profane hours, a great deal of the strain that looked like imbalance simply dissolves.

The most practical passage in the session is about the daily return. Q'uo recommends the habit of coming back, again and again, to the center, not as a place of stillness but as a place of honesty. Where am I right now? What am I feeling? What is out of proportion? This is not the harsh audit of the perfectionist. It is the gentle checking of the traveler, the way you might check your bearings on a long walk. The checking itself is the balance. The sphere stays rolling because the traveler keeps feeling the ground.

And then there is the teaching on change, which ties the whole session together. The seeker who wants balance often really wants permanence, a state where nothing more will disturb the peace. Q'uo is tender but firm about this. There is no such state in this density. The only permanence is the love that underlies the motion, the ground on which the sphere rolls. Everything else, every mood, every circumstance, every arrangement of the outer life, is in motion, and the art is not to stop the motion but to move with it gracefully.

The closing image returns to the sphere, and I will leave it with you the way Q'uo leaves it. Picture yourself as round, complete, in motion. The bumps in the road are not interruptions of your journey. They are the journey. The rolling is the balance. Rest in the rolling, and you will find that the peace you were seeking by standing still was waiting for you in the movement all along.

Thank you for listening.

title: Choiceless Awareness
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: choiceless awareness.

Early May, nineteen ninety three, and Q'uo introduces a phrase that has echoed through spiritual literature for centuries and still manages to sound brand new each time it is spoken. The new mind. The questioner wants to know what it is, and Q'uo answers with a teaching on perception itself, on the difference between seeing the world through the old mind's labels and seeing it fresh.

The old mind, they say, is the mind of judgment and categorization. It meets each moment already knowing what the moment is. It has a name for everything, a file for everything, a verdict ready before the evidence is in. This is not a moral failing. It is how the mind learned to survive. But the cost is that the seeker stops seeing what is actually there and starts seeing only the labels. The world becomes a museum of old conclusions, and the living moment keeps arriving and finding no one home to meet it.

The new mind is what remains when the labeling pauses. Q'uo calls it choiceless awareness, borrowing a phrase with deep roots, and they describe it as a state of fresh perception in which the seeker meets each moment without the overlay of past and future. This is not blankness. It is not the switching off of intelligence. It is intelligence operating without the crutch of the already-known. The new mind sees the cup on the table as though no cup had ever been seen before, and in that seeing, the cup becomes, for a moment, a miracle.

I want to be honest about how hard this teaching is to practice, because Q'uo is honest about it too. They do not present the new mind as an achievement to be unlocked. They present it as a direction, a leaning. The old mind will keep doing its work. It has to. You need it to cross streets and pay bills. The practice is not to destroy the old mind but to notice when it has taken over the whole show, and to gently, repeatedly, return to the fresh seeing. Each return is the new mind being born again, and it is born a thousand times a day.

There is a passage about wholeness that I think is the key to the whole session. Q'uo says that the new mind perceives wholeness before it perceives parts. The old mind sees the parts and tries to assemble them into a whole, and the assembly never quite works, because the wholeness was there before the parts were divided. This is why analysis so often leaves the seeker feeling that something essential has been missed. Something essential has been missed. It was the wholeness, which cannot be reached by adding up the pieces.

The questioner asks how this relates to the spiritual path, to seeking itself, and Q'uo's answer has a paradox in it that is worth sitting with. The seeking itself, pursued with the old mind, becomes another project of the ego, another accumulation. I am seeking, therefore I am progressing. The new mind does not seek in that way. It does not grasp at enlightenment as a future possession. It rests in the awareness that what is sought is already present, already here, already the case. Seeking becomes not a journey toward something absent but a deepening into something present.

Q'uo gives a practice, and it is disarmingly simple. Several times a day, pause and look at something, anything, a hand, a tree, a face, as though you had never seen it before. Do not name it. Do not evaluate it. Just let it be present to you. At first the old mind will rush in with its labels, impatient, efficient. Let it chatter. Beneath the chatter, the fresh seeing is still there, waiting. Each time you touch it, even for a breath, you are exercising the new mind, and the exercise accumulates.

The closing of the session returns to the phrase itself. The new mind is not new in time, Q'uo says. It is not a future upgrade of the human operating system. It is the original mind, the mind before the labels, the mind of the child before the world taught it what everything is called. To develop the new mind is really to recover it, to come home to a way of seeing that was never lost, only covered over. The covering was necessary. The uncovering is the work. And the work, like the seeing, begins now, in this moment, with whatever is in front of you.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Healer's Hands
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the healer's hands.

Early May, nineteen ninety three, a special meditation, and the questions come from a seeker who works with her hands. She practices a form of energy healing, and she wants to know about technique. Where exactly should the hands go? What should the healer visualize? How does the energy move? Q'uo answers, but not in the way she expects. They answer by gently moving the whole inquiry from the hands to the heart.

The first thing they say is that the details matter less than the seeker thinks. The healer wants a map of the body, a precise choreography of hand positions, a reliable procedure. Q'uo does not dismiss the desire. Technique has its place. But they insist that what heals is not the technique. What heals is the love that moves through the healer, and the healer's willingness to be a clear channel for it. Two healers can place their hands in exactly the same positions, and one session will sing and the other will fall flat, and the difference will be in the inner state of the one whose hands are doing the work.

This is the central teaching of the session, and Q'uo states it plainly. The healer does not heal. The healer offers. What moves through the offering is the infinite love of the Creator, and whether and how it is received belongs entirely to the one being healed and to the mystery of that one's path. The healer who tries to control the outcome, who needs the healing to happen in a particular way, has picked up a burden that was never theirs to carry, and the burden clouds the very channel they are trying to keep clear.

I want to say something careful here, because this session touches on illness and the body, and this series holds a clear line on such matters. Q'uo speaks throughout of their own opinions, and they ask each listener to use personal discrimination. Nothing here is medical advice. The archive's reflections on healing describe a spiritual practice, a way of being present with suffering, and they stand alongside the care of qualified physicians, never in place of it. If you are carrying an illness, the kindest thing you can do for yourself is to hold both, the inner practice and the outer care, without asking either to be what it is not.

With that held, the teaching on the healer's inner state is worth hearing in full. Q'uo describes the ideal healer as one who has done the work of clearing the self, not perfectly, but honestly, who comes to the session without the need to be the one who heals, without the hunger for results, without the subtle pride of the rescuer. The hands are placed. The heart is opened. The love is allowed to move. And then, and this is the hardest part, the healer lets go of what happens next.

The questioner asks about specific hand positions and visualizations, and Q'uo gives her something better than a diagram. They tell her to trust what her hands already know. The hands of an experienced healer, they say, are wiser than the healer's theories about them. When the heart is open and the intention is pure, the hands find their places. Visualization can help, not because the pictures control the energy, but because they quiet the healer's mind and give the love a clear channel to move through. The picture is for the healer, not for the energy. The energy knows its own way.

There is a tender passage near the end about the healer's own need for healing. Those who give healing to others often neglect to receive it themselves, and Q'uo is direct about this. The channel must be cleared from both ends. Rest. Receive. Let others lay hands on you. The healer who will not be healed is carrying a hidden belief that they must be the strong one, the giver, the exception, and that belief is itself a blockage in the channel.

The session closes with a redefinition that I have carried with me. Healing, Q'uo says, is not the fixing of the body. It is the restoration of the awareness of wholeness, and wholeness was never lost. The healer's hands do not create wholeness. They remind. They witness. They offer the love that says, you were never broken, only dreaming of brokenness. Whether the body follows the reminder is not the healer's business. The offering is the whole of it. The rest belongs to the mystery.

Thank you for listening.

title: Details and Wholeness
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: details and wholeness.

Two days later, another special meditation, and the healer's questions continue. This time she wants to know about detail. Should she study the body's systems in depth? Would a precise mental map of anatomy make her healing work more effective? Q'uo's answer is a small masterpiece on the difference between knowing about a thing and knowing a thing, and it applies far beyond healing.

They begin by honoring the question. There is a genuine love of detail in the questioner, a reverence for the intricate architecture of the body, and Q'uo does not mock it. Detail has its dignity. The study of how things work, pursued with wonder, is itself a form of worship. The trouble begins only when the detail becomes the master instead of the servant, when the healer starts to believe that the map is the territory and that a more accurate map would give more control over the territory.

The teaching that follows is about two kinds of knowing. There is the knowing that takes a thing apart to see how it works, and there is the knowing that beholds a thing whole. Both are real. Both have their uses. But in the work of healing, Q'uo says, it is the second kind that matters, because healing is not a mechanical repair. It is not the fixing of a part. It is the restoration of the whole, and the whole cannot be reached by perfecting the parts. A healer can know every named structure in the body and still miss the person, and a healer who knows almost nothing of anatomy but beholds the person whole may be the clearer channel.

Q'uo uses the image of a mosaic to make this vivid. Stand close to a mosaic and you see only tiles, each one exact, each one separate. Step back and the picture appears, and the picture was never in the tiles. It was in the relationships between them, in the wholeness that the tiles serve. The healer who works from detail alone is standing with their nose against the mosaic, cataloguing tiles. The healer who works from wholeness has stepped back far enough to see the picture, and it is the picture that heals.

The questioner presses on visualization. If she pictures the energy moving through specific pathways, does that direct it more effectively? Q'uo's answer is subtle and, I think, deeply honest. Visualization helps the healer, not the energy. The energy does not need the picture. The picture quiets the healer's chattering mind, focuses the intention, and creates the inner stillness through which the love can move unobstructed. So visualize if it helps you become still. But do not mistake the visualization for the mechanism. The mechanism is love, and love was moving before you pictured anything.

There is a warning here too, gentle but clear. The healer who becomes attached to the details of technique can fall into the trap of believing that a failed healing means the technique was wrong, the hands were in the wrong place, the picture was not vivid enough. This is the mind's way of keeping control, of refusing the deeper truth that the outcome was never the healer's to determine. Q'uo keeps returning the questioner to the same release. Offer the love. Let go of the result. Trust the wholeness.

The session broadens at the end into a teaching about all human knowing. Q'uo suggests that our whole culture is standing with its nose against the mosaic, mistaking ever-finer detail for ever-deeper truth. The scientist, the scholar, the technician, each adding tiles to the catalogue, and the picture receding the closer we look. The contemplative path, they say, is the practice of stepping back. Not abandoning detail, but refusing to be hypnotized by it. The truth is not in the tiles. It never was.

I want to close with the line Q'uo gives the questioner to carry into her practice, because it is the whole session in a sentence. Do not try to heal the part, they say. Behold the whole, and let the whole do the healing. The hands know. The heart knows. The love knows. Your work is the beholding.

Thank you for listening.

title: Offer Yourself Hollow
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: offer yourself hollow.

Early May, nineteen ninety three, a Sunday, and the meditation circle's questions turn inward, to the healer's own instrument. What happens when the energy will not flow? What do the blockages mean? And then, from the same seeker, a quieter question, the kind that is asked in a low voice. She has lost a friend, and she wants to know if there is any service she can offer to one who has passed on. Q'uo answers both questions, and the two answers turn out to be one teaching.

On the blockages, Q'uo is practical and unsentimental. The energy centers can become constricted, they say, when the seeker is carrying unexamined material, fear, grief, resentment, the ordinary sediment of a life lived. This is not a judgment. It is mechanics. A channel that is holding something cannot be fully open. The work is not to force the energy through by effort of will. The work is to look honestly at what is being held, to feel it, to release it, and then to let the flow resume on its own.

The image Q'uo gives for the healer is the hollow reed. Not the full vessel, proud of its contents, but the emptied one, through which the wind can move freely. Offer yourself hollow, they say. Come to the work without the need to be effective, without the story of yourself as the healer, without even the desire for a particular outcome. The hollower the reed, the clearer the music. This is why the session's questions about technique keep receiving the same answer in different forms. The technique is the emptying. The emptying is the technique. Everything else follows.

There is a discipline here that Q'uo spells out for the daily life of the healer. Clear yourself before the work. Sit in silence. Let the day's accumulations settle. Notice where you are holding, in the body, in the heart, in the mind, and breathe into those places with honesty rather than with the demand that they open. A center that is breathed into with patience will open when it is ready. A center that is commanded to open will only tighten further. The body, Q'uo implies, can tell the difference between an invitation and an order, and it always answers the invitation.

Then the second question, about the friend who has died, and Q'uo's tone changes, becomes very gentle. Yes, they say, service can be offered to those who have passed. Prayer, loving thought, the holding of the departed one in light, all of this is real service, and it is received. But they add something I think is meant for every grieving heart listening. The greatest service to the departed is the healer's own continued growth in love, because love is the medium in which all these connections live, and the departed one is not far, only elsewhere in the same love.

I want to pause here, because grief is real and it deserves more than a teaching. If you are carrying the loss of someone you love, these words are offered as companionship, not as instruction. Grief has its own wisdom and its own timing, and no spiritual framework should be used to hurry it or to judge it. If the weight of it feels like more than you can carry alone, please reach for the living hands around you, friends, community, counselors, those whose work is to sit with the grieving. The archive's reflections on the continuity of love are meant to sit beside such support, never to replace it.

The session closes by joining the two questions into one image. The healer hollowed out by honesty, cleared by the daily practice of release, becomes a channel not only for the living but for the whole communion of beings, those in bodies and those beyond them. The grief itself, honestly felt and honestly released, becomes part of the hollowing, part of the clearing. Nothing is wasted. Not the blockage, not the sorrow, not the love that outlives the body. All of it, offered hollow and held in love, becomes music, and the music goes on and on.

Thank you for listening.

title: Beyond the Funhouse
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: beyond the funhouse.

Mid May, nineteen ninety three, and Hatonn opens the Sunday meditation with an image that has stayed famous in this archive. Life, he says, is a carnival, and at the center of the carnival is a hall of mirrors. You walk in, and every mirror shows you a distorted version of yourself, tall and thin, short and wide, rippled and strange. And the great temptation of incarnation is to stand in front of these mirrors arguing with the reflections.

Hatonn's point is not that the world is lying to you. It is that the world is showing you something true but partial, and the distortion is in the taking of the partial for the whole. Every situation that meets you, every person who misunderstands you, every success and every failure, is a mirror, and each mirror is curved. If you try to correct yourself to match the mirrors, you will spend your life twisting into shapes that please reflections. The work is to walk through the hall without stopping to fix what the mirrors show.

I love the plainness of Hatonn's voice here. He does not speak in abstractions. He speaks the way a friend talks on a porch in the evening. And his advice for the hall of mirrors is equally plain. Keep walking. Do not set up camp in front of any single mirror, especially not the flattering ones. The flattering mirrors are the most dangerous, because the distortion that pleases is the hardest to question. The seeker who believes the mirror that says, you are wonderful, is as lost as the seeker who believes the mirror that says, you are worthless. Both have mistaken the reflection for the self.

There is a teaching tucked inside this image about the opinions of others that I think is worth pulling out and holding up to the light. Hatonn suggests that much of our suffering comes from treating the reflections other people show us as verdicts. Someone is cold to you, and the mirror says you are unlovable. Someone praises you, and the mirror says you are great. But other people are walking through their own hall of mirrors, seeing their own distortions, and what they reflect back to you is shaped as much by their mirrors as by anything about you. To take any of it as final is to let someone else's carnival ride determine your worth. The wise seeker learns to thank the mirror for the information and keep walking.

The session then turns to the question of exits. How do you get out of the hall? Hatonn's answer is that there is no secret door. The exit is the same as the entrance. You walk through. The hall is not a trap. It is a passage. The mirrors are not there to stop you. They are there to teach you, by distortion after distortion, what you are not, until the knowing of what you are begins to dawn from the inside rather than from any reflection at all.

And what is on the other side of the hall? Hatonn describes it not as a place but as a quality of seeing. The seeker who has walked through enough mirrors begins to develop an inner steadiness, a sense of self that does not rise and fall with the reflections. This is not arrogance. It is not the refusal to listen. It is the quiet confidence of one who has learned the difference between a mirror and a window. The mirror shows you yourself, distorted. The window shows you the world, and through the world, the Creator. Walk toward the windows.

Later in the session Latwii joins the circle for questions, and the conversation ranges widely, but I am keeping this episode with Hatonn's carnival, because it is the heart of the day. The teaching is complete in itself. You are in a hall of mirrors. Every reflection is distorted. Keep walking. Do not argue with the glass. The one who walks through, steady and unhurried, will come out the other side into a seeing that no mirror can give and no mirror can take away.

Thank you for listening.

title: Fruitful Polarity
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: fruitful polarity.

Late May, nineteen ninety three, and the question is one the archive approaches with unusual delicacy. What is the spiritual significance of sexuality, of the male and the female, of the polarity between them? Q'uo answers at length, and I want to say at the outset how I am holding this session. These are reflections from nineteen ninety three, offered as opinion, and some of what is said about men and women belongs to its time. What endures, and what this episode keeps, is the deeper teaching underneath, about polarity itself, and about the wholeness that contains it.

Q'uo begins with the basic metaphysics. In this density, experience is structured by polarity, the dynamic tension between opposites that makes movement, growth, and choice possible. Sexual polarity is one expression of this deeper structure, and like all polarities it is fruitful. The tension between the two poles generates something neither pole could generate alone. This is true in electricity, and Q'uo suggests it is true in the life of the spirit as well. Where there is genuine difference held in genuine love, something new is born.

The teaching then moves inward, and this is where it becomes universal. Every seeker, Q'uo says, contains both polarities within. There is in each person a reaching, assertive, projective energy, and a receptive, nurturing, allowing energy, and the spiritual life requires both. The seeker who cultivates only the active pole becomes brittle, all thrust and no root. The seeker who cultivates only the receptive pole becomes passive, all root and no thrust. Wholeness is not the victory of one pole over the other. It is the marriage of the two within a single heart.

I find this the most useful part of the session for actual practice. You can watch these two energies moving in your own day. There are moments that ask for the active pole, for clear direction, for the courage to initiate, to speak, to build. And there are moments that ask for the receptive pole, for listening, for allowing, for the patience to let something unfold in its own time. The art of the spiritual life is not to pick one and perfect it. It is to become fluent in both, and to know, moment by moment, which one the moment is asking for. Most of us have a native accent in one pole and need practice in the other, and the practice itself is the growth.

Q'uo speaks about relationship as the great school of this fluency. In the intimate partnership, each person is continually meeting the other pole, both in the partner and in themselves, and the friction of that meeting is the teaching. The question is never really whether the other person is embodying their pole correctly. The question is whether you can meet the polarity without collapsing it, without demanding that the other become like you, or that you become like the other. Love, in this teaching, is the capacity to hold difference without needing to resolve it.

There is a passage about the movement beyond gender that I want to give its full weight. Q'uo suggests that as the seeker matures spiritually, the identification with one pole loosens. The person begins to experience themselves less as a man or a woman in the spiritual sense and more as a whole being in whom both energies dance. This is not the erasing of difference. It is the outgrowing of the need to be defined by it. The polarity remains fruitful, but it is no longer a cage. It becomes a dance floor.

The session closes with a return to the body, and Q'uo is tender here. The physical expression of polarity, they say, is sacred when it is entered into with love and with the awareness of what is being exchanged. It is not sacred or profane in itself. Like everything in this density, it takes its meaning from the consciousness that meets it. Two people can enact the same outer gestures, and one enactment can be a deepening of union while the other is a deepening of separation. The difference is never in the act. It is in the heart.

Thank you for listening.

title: Your Own Master
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: your own master.

Late May, nineteen ninety three, an intensive meditation, and a rare voice takes the circle. Oxal. The question is about teachers. What is the role of the guru, the guide, the one who knows? In a spiritual culture full of authorities and followings, Oxal's answer is quietly revolutionary. Every teacher, they say, is also a student. And every student is ultimately their own master.

Oxal begins by describing what a true teacher does, and it is almost entirely negative, in the sense of what the teacher does not do. The true teacher does not dominate. Does not demand obedience. Does not gather followers as possessions. Does not present themselves as the destination. The true teacher points, and then gets out of the way. If you find yourself in the presence of someone who needs you to need them, Oxal implies, you have not found a teacher. You have found a collector.

The positive description is just as spare. The teacher offers what they have learned, plainly, without embellishment, and leaves the student completely free to take it or leave it. There is no pressure, no recruitment, no subtle manipulation disguised as wisdom. The teaching is laid on the table like bread. Those who are hungry will eat. Those who are not will pass by. The teacher's peace is not disturbed either way, because the teacher was never feeding themselves on the student's hunger.

Then comes the line I have been carrying since I first read this session. Each student is ultimately its own master. Oxal does not mean this as a slogan for spiritual independence, though it is that. They mean it structurally. No one else can do your seeking for you. No one else can walk your hall of mirrors, sit in your dark closet, clear your energy centers, or learn your lessons. A teacher can describe the terrain. A teacher cannot walk it for you. The authority you are looking for outside yourself was always an appointment you had to keep with yourself.

Oxal speaks about inner guidance with the same clarity. Beyond the outer teachers there are inner ones, guides, the deeper self, the quiet voices that speak in meditation and in dreams. But here too the principle holds. The inner guide does not command. It suggests. It nudges. It offers images and feelings and leaves you free. Any inner voice that demands obedience, that speaks in the tones of compulsion and fear, is not guidance. It is something else wearing guidance's clothes. The real thing always respects your freedom, because your freedom is the whole point of the exercise.

There is a related teaching about the temptation to collect teachers the way some collect books, always seeking the next authority, the deeper secret, the teacher behind the teacher. Oxal is gentle about this hunger but clear about its cost. Every hour spent shopping for a master is an hour not spent doing the student's own work, and the work is where the transformation happens. The teaching you already have, practiced deeply, will take you further than a hundred teachings sampled shallowly. Depth, not novelty, is the student's true wealth.

There is a practical teaching here about how to listen. Oxal describes the mind as a room full of chatter, opinions, anxieties, rehearsals, and somewhere in the room, very quietly, the actual guidance speaking. The work is not to silence the chatter by force. The work is to become familiar enough with the sound of your own deepest knowing that you can recognize it under the noise. This takes time. It takes the patience of meditation, of journaling, of paying attention to which inner promptings, followed, led toward greater love. The track record, over time, teaches the ear.

The session closes with Oxal turning the whole question inside out. The seeker came asking how to find a teacher. Oxal's answer is that the finding was never the problem. You are surrounded by teachers. Every person who crosses your path is teaching you something. Every difficulty is instruction. The question was never where to find a teacher. The question was whether you were willing to be a student, and then, in time, to recognize that the student and the teacher were never two.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Ocean of Illusion
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the ocean of illusion.

The end of May, nineteen ninety three, and Hatonn is speaking again on a Sunday, returning to waters he charted two months earlier. The archive holds two sessions on the daily bread, the supply of life, given months apart, and they rhyme with each other the way the sea rhymes with itself. This episode stays with the second sailing, and with the image that gives it its title. Welcome, Hatonn says, to the ocean of incarnational experience.

The ocean is not a metaphor for trouble. It is a metaphor for the whole thing. You are in it. You chose it. Before this life, Hatonn says, you looked at these waters and you chose to sail them, knowing the charts were faulty and the weather uncertain. There is something bracing about being reminded of that choice. The instability of the world is not a malfunction. It is the agreed-upon condition of the voyage. You did not sign up for a harbor. You signed up for the sea.

Hatonn's concern, as before, is the practical one. How do you live on this ocean without being consumed by worry about the supply? His answer this time leans into the image of navigation. The old maps do not match the current waters. The rational mind keeps trying to plot a course by instruments that were calibrated for a different sea, and keeps running aground on the difference between the chart and the reality. The alternative is not to drift. It is to learn a different kind of steering.

He calls it steering by hunch and hope, and I want to rescue that phrase from sounding vague, because in Hatonn's mouth it is precise. Hunch is the name for the quiet inner signal, the felt sense of the right direction that arrives without a full argument attached. Hope is the name for the trust that keeps you moving when the signal is faint. Together they are not the absence of navigation. They are navigation by a subtler instrument, the one the soul brought with it, calibrated before birth for exactly these waters.

There is a passage about desire that deepens the earlier session's teaching. Desire, Hatonn says, is the wind in the sails. Without it the ship does not move. The spiritual traditions that preach the killing of desire have mistaken the wind for the storm. What drowns the sailor is not desire but the clutching at it, the demand that the wind blow from exactly one quarter at exactly one strength. Set the sails to catch what comes. Trim them as the weather changes. The wind is not yours to command. It is yours to use.

And what of control? Hatonn returns to the one thing the sailor can actually govern, and it is the same as before. Your attitude. Not the sea, not the weather, not the other ships, not the supply waiting in the next port. Your attitude is the rudder, the one instrument that is truly yours, and a steady hand on the rudder matters more than a perfect chart. Two sailors in the same storm live in two different oceans, and the difference is made at the helm.

Hatonn also speaks to the fear that rises when the shore disappears from view, the particular dread of the open water where no landmark offers reassurance. Every sailor knows this hour. The temptation is to turn back toward the familiar coast, even a coast that offered nothing, simply because it was known. Hatonn's counsel is to hold the course. The open water is not emptiness. It is the place where the hunch grows clearest, because there is nothing else to listen to. What feels like being lost is often the first honest moment of the voyage.

The closing of the session is Hatonn at his most characteristic, plainspoken and warm. Do the next thing. Tend the sails you can reach. When the hunch comes, honor it. When the hope falters, rest, and let it return on its own tide. The ocean does not need your permission to be the ocean. Your work is the sailing. And the bread, the daily bread, the supply for the day's voyage, is given with the day, as it has always been, to those who are actually at sea.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Yeast of Faith
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the yeast of faith.

Early June, nineteen ninety three, and the Sunday question is about worry and prayer. The circle has noticed something true and a little embarrassing. When you worry about a situation long enough and hard enough, you seem to feed it. The worry becomes a kind of prayer in reverse, sowing the seeds of the very outcome you fear. Is there a better way? Q'uo's answer is one of the most complete teachings on prayer in the whole archive, and it begins with a defense of worry itself.

Yes, you will worry, Q'uo says. They legalize it, almost. In this density, with the veil drawn and the future hidden, it would be miraculous not to worry. There is a continual stream of circumstance you cannot control, and the returning of the mind to the concern is natural. The question is never how to become a person who never worries. The question is what you do with the worry once you notice it is running.

Q'uo describes the situation that produces worry as the common coin of incarnation. Before this life, you chose the veil of forgetting, chose to make your choices in blindness, and every worrying moment you now face is one you moved toward step by step, not by mistake. You did not come here to dispel worry and be comforted. You came to strive in darkness. Your greatest sight is the blind but loving heart, for one sees with the heart the light which is not visible to the mind. I read that sentence twice every time. The heart sees what the mind cannot.

Then the image that gives this episode its shape. Q'uo recalls the story of Peter on the water. He saw his teacher walking on the waves and leapt from the boat in excitement, and for a moment he walked too. Then he realized he was doing the impossible, and he began to sink. And the teacher reached out a hand, and Peter walked again. That reaching of the hand, Q'uo says, is the essence of prayer. It is the direct communication with the infinite intelligence that surrounds and makes possible the illusion. To pray is to organize the energies within the self and point them at that communication.

Here is the turn that makes the whole session. Prayer needs not to be answered to be effective. It is not given that the seeker will see clear answers to every prayer. What is given is that the communication itself does something. Worry, Q'uo says, makes the connection with the divine in an unorganized way. Prayer organizes it. The very process of putting the concern into words before infinite intelligence causes the seeker to refine it, reconsider it, restate it, and begin to see the truer dimensions of the situation. The prayer is not a vending machine. It is a conversation that changes the one who speaks.

Q'uo actually suggests retiring the word prayer, because in this culture it carries the shadows of unworthiness and the suggestion that some are more entitled to it than others. They propose instead the word conversation. A conversation with infinite intelligence. The seeker speaks the mind as it is given to speak. Infinite intelligence responds in silence and in power. And the reflex of that conversation, the answer that is not an answer, is a spirit that enlivens hope and faith, which in turn organizes the intellectual mind so that it is more worry-resistant the next time the situation arises.

The most practical part of the session comes in the follow-up questions, when the circle asks for a trigger, a tripwire in consciousness that catches the worrying as it starts and turns it toward the conversation. Q'uo's answer is honest about how personal this is. The threshold varies. Each entity must learn to notice the moment when worry has worn out its usefulness, when it has alerted the deeper self and the guides and all possible action has been taken, even if the action is only preparation. At that point, the entity must trust. Must have faith that all that can be done has been done. And that faith, Q'uo says, is like yeast in the mix of catalyst, affecting the outcome in the most appropriate manner.

Yeast. Not a lever, not a command, not a technique for controlling destiny. A quiet ferment, working invisibly through the whole lump, changing its nature from the inside. That is what faith does in the situation you have been worrying about. It does not guarantee the outcome you wanted. It guarantees that whatever comes will meet a self that has been changed by the conversation, enlarged in identity, more aware of itself as a universal self. The worry sowed seeds of fear. The conversation sows seeds of possibility. Both grow. You choose, moment by moment, which garden you are tending.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Lonesome Valley
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the lonesome valley. The question on this June afternoon in nineteen ninety three is simple and deep: what is solitude for.

Q'uo begins with an honest admission, that there is no one clear answer, because solitude has as many uses as there are seekers. But there is a way to judge it. Ask yourself what you are working toward. If you are trying to bring your own vibration closer to the one great original thought, which is love, then solitude has a part to play. If your work is mainly to serve other people, you will find solitude less fitting, because to serve people you must spend time with them.

That sounds clean, but Q'uo warns that most of us do not arrive at solitude that cleanly. In our culture, the one who seeks solitude is usually not some serene sage. More often, they are looking for relief from suffering and pain. So let us look at the right use of this gift, they say.

There is the solitude of crisis. Think of the desert experience, the forty days in the wilderness. In this crisis the seeker has been overstimulated, the senses overtaxed by noise, opinions, the sheer press of other people. And so they walk alone. As the old folk song says, you have got to walk that lonesome valley by yourself, because no one else can walk it for you. You walk through the valley of the shadow of death, and although your guides and your higher self are with you, the learning itself cannot be delegated.

Then there is the solitude of sensitivity. Some people, often because of something that happened when they were young, find company itself uncomfortable. The discomfort builds until they reach a solitary place, and there at last is safety and relaxation. It is almost, Q'uo says, as though the mind and emotions were another organ, like the lungs. The lungs must breathe for the body to live. So the sensitive person must be solitary for the inner life to stay sharp. Deny it, and the emotions go without oxygen.

Such a person is right to claim the solitude. But there is a caution. The seeker must consider how to use it well, because there is a pull toward distraction. Q'uo leaves a deliberate blank here. Create what, the channel asks, irritably? They leave it blank on purpose. Those who use solitude well are often given creations in it, fantasies of the heart and mind and spirit. And if riches pour into you, they say, pour them through you into the world, so that what was given in the darkness of your own inner sanctum can bless everyone who sees or hears it.

Then they name the harder thread, the one that tangles itself into almost every solitude. There is a service to self element in the desire to be alone, the habit of treating the self as separate from everything else. Solitude, they say, is itself an illusion. There is no solitude in a full and teeming creation. You cannot imagine how crowded the universe is. It bursts with life.

There is no one right amount of solitude, no one best path. But there is one form of solitary practice that deserves notice above all else, and that is the solitude in which you turn to the holy of holies within the self. In meditation a link is sought in spiritual solitude, and through that solitude the purified desire reaches out, and the silence answers in thought too deep for words. Treasure those moments with the infinite One, they say, and know that every moment the Creator has been sought lightens the consciousness of your people.

When the circle turns to questions, Carla asks about the one thing Q'uo has not said: what about when people are depressed and want to be alone? Q'uo answers that depression is its own special case of sensitivity. The entity is oversensitive and yet numb to hope and faith, and so retreats into a smaller, safer, solitary place, the way a turtle pulls into its shell. It is trying to lick its wounds.

I want to say this plainly, because it matters. If solitude has become the place where you hide from a sadness that will not lift, you do not have to stay hidden. Reach out to someone you trust, a counselor, a friend, a helpline where you live. There is no shame in needing company in the valley.

The session ends with a rare sweetness. Q'uo thanks the group for the shorter session, grateful to please the channel with a more succinct answer than usual. It is a small, human moment in a cosmic teaching, and I keep it.

Thank you for listening.

title: Follow Your Nature
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: follow your nature. A group asks whether there is spiritual value in deliberately choosing the harder path.

Q'uo answers with a garden. Walk with them along the brick paths and look at the flowers and shrubs, the clover and the rose. Each leaf and blossom is perfect. The lilies of the field are dressed more splendidly than any king, and they did no work to earn it. It was simply the Creator's gift. Now turn inward and ask: how is your own inner self arrayed? Did your character come to you by effort, or was it given?

The spiritual journey, they say, is mostly a journey of taking away what is not natural, until the natural beauty of the self stands uncovered and free. The self is like a light bulb, a clear empty channel. Place it where it can receive energy, open the pathway, and it becomes radiant, the way the lily radiates the love of the infinite One.

So should you choose the bicycle ride or the concert? One is physically hard, the other easy. Q'uo refuses the whole frame. Ask instead which is more natural to you. One seeker finds joy in activity, in the muscles working, the wind of the world on the skin. Another finds joy sitting still in music, expanding inward with praise. There is no intrinsic virtue in discomfort and no virtue in ease. What matters is which choice lets the original vibration sound most clearly through you.

The word they keep returning to is transparent. When you are transparent to the original thought, then whatever touches you colors you, and you let the radiance pour through. The natural self is not something you build with effort. It is something you uncover by dropping what is not yours. Every choice becomes a chance to let one more false layer fall away.

They note, gently, how old this question is. In every generation there are those who wear the hair shirt next to the skin, who take the hardest jobs and befriend the most difficult people, all for the sake of the infinite One. If that is your true nature, they say, go and do it. But the path to the infinite is simply the path that most purely realizes the natural self.

And here is the part I find most comforting. You do not need to go hunting for difficulty, because difficulty will find you. To all who listen to the voice of spirit come suffering, limitation, loss, and death. Choose the easy path and difficulties will come. Choose the hard path and difficulties will come. Every seeker has great trials in the past and in the future. That is the nature of the illusion.

So the well made choice is not the choice of difficulty but the choice of greatest service. How may I serve in this environment, the transparent one asks, looking at the bicycle and the concert. If you vibrate more radiantly while active, that is the greater path. If you shine as a listener, sit and shine in praise. The choice turns on rightness, not on pain.

This holds even for the great choices, the mate, the vocation. Those are harder to read, Q'uo admits. But the same rule applies: become transparent to the original thought, and choose the life in which you can most deeply bear witness to love and light. It takes growing awareness of your true nature, and the Creator does not ask you to choose what is unnatural.

They close the session with something quietly pointed. The group had come that day without a clear and burning desire to seek, yet they chose to sit faithfully in the circle anyway. Was that the more difficult choice? Probably. But that was not why it was the right choice. It was right because it was made in service, and in the desire to seek truth. In that, Q'uo says, you fulfilled your nature.

Turn like the flowers, then. Toward the sun.

There is one more promise folded into this teaching. As you keep choosing the natural over the unnatural, you become more transparent to the original thought, until what is natural to you simply stands in front of you, obvious as a flower. You no longer have to reason it out. The transparent one simply gazes on each activity and asks, how may I serve in this environment. And the rightness of the choice can be felt. It is the feeling of praise and service lining up inside you, the sense that this, and not that, is where your radiance pours through.

Thank you for listening.

title: Fear No Evil
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: fear no evil. A special session, called to ask what it is like, metaphysically, to walk through the valley of the shadow of death while still alive.

The group asks about the times when a seeker feels worn out, burned out, angry, resentful, feeling that the Creator and the creation have let them down, that things are not the way they should be. Q'uo reaches for the psalm: yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for thou art with me.

Third density, they say, is the first density of self conscious life, and so it is the density of the paradox of life and death. A flower knows only the moment; it turns to the light and flourishes or wilts in utter contentment. We do not have that simplicity. We are the first ones who know we will end, and that knowing shadows everything.

When a seeker wakes up and begins the pilgrimage, each new level of awareness brings a new level of unknowing. Q'uo calls this initiation, and asks us to see it almost as a compliment. When the darkness deepens, it means the earlier work has been integrated and the soul is being trusted with more. The testing is also a graduation. They ask the seeker to do something startling: to rejoice at the new awareness that bites like a sword, and then to offer the infinite One the one thing it most delights to hear.

What it delights to hear, they say, is not your composure but your complaint. Bring it your anger, your disappointment, your sorrow. Share the whole of it, seemingly good and seemingly bad, in honest heartfelt dialogue. Every emotion, refined through this offering, becomes a gift to the infinite One, and the infinite One becomes more than it was.

Then comes a quiet exercise. Q'uo asks the circle to touch into the pool of sorrow, to let it grow intense, and to give it to the infinite One. In the silence that follows there is an answer, silent and unmanifest. Each sorrow, they say, is a treasure, and the love of the Creator speaks directly to that deep heart within where true intelligence lives.

The valley can be seen two ways at once, and both are true. It is the valley, and it is also the high place. It is the dark path, and it is also the path streaming with light. To refuse either view is to refuse wholeness.

The teaching turns practical at the end. When the time of testing comes and the new lesson begins, there is an opportunity to say yes to it deliberately, to accept the lesson and rediscover, through harsh experience, the joy at the heart of the self. Not quickly, not before the inspiration is real, but when the foolish heartfelt impulse comes, leap. You cannot create order out of chaos by forcing it, Q'uo warns. Any order you impose to avoid pain also avoids self knowledge.

In the questions that follow, one seeker speaks of a year in which the valley shook the very foundation of her magical life, the part of her she thought could never be attacked. Q'uo answers with tenderness: it is not your magical personality that has been harmed. That part of you is unblemished. What you feel is the pathway to it growing faint, the way a trail looks faint when the forest around it has burned. The tempering is by fire, and fire seems to destroy. But the path remains, and aid walks with you whether you feel it or not.

And then Carla asks the question that must have been sitting in every heart in that room. She speaks of the time after Don died, when she felt suicidal and hopeless, when the only thing that kept her going was the habit of turning to the light, and even that did not make it less terrifying. Is there any way to reduce the terror of walking through it?

Q'uo answers honestly: there is little comfort in the transformation itself. What there is, is faith, continually exercised. Faith that there is an end to this experience. Faith that there is strength within to outlast what seems overwhelming. And the assurance that when you look back from beyond this illusion, you will rejoice at the very darkness, because you will see the light and love and faith that were blessed into it.

I want to pause here and say this in my own voice. If you are in a valley like that now, if hopelessness has settled on you, you do not have to walk it on faith alone. Please reach out to someone you trust, a counselor, a crisis line or helpline in your country. The archive honors faith, but faith and help are not enemies.

Rest then in shadow and in sunlight, and have compassion for your own courage.

Thank you for listening.

title: Praise and Thanksgiving
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: praise and thanksgiving. A group wonders why the Creator would want praise at all. Would the one who made everything really need an audience. Probably not.

Q'uo begins by dissolving the question. The Creator, as far as they can feel this mystery, does not desire one response over another. The Creator acts; it does not react. No particular mode of address is preferred. Praise and thanksgiving are accepted without emotion, the way the sun accepts whatever turns toward it.

Then why do so many sources say it is good and just to offer praise? Here is their answer. In the beginning the Creator expressed itself in one great original thought, which we call love. Everything that exists is made of that love, built of articulated light. So when a seeker offers love, blessing, thanks, what is really happening is a matter of vibration. The entity is tuning itself to match the frequency of the original thought.

It is not that a hungry Creator demands homage. It is that love reflects in love, and in that infinite reflection lies truth. The closer the seeker comes to the frequency of love, the more the seeker's very nature reads as praise and thanksgiving, beneath words, beneath thought, in the way creation itself is built.

Then the group pushes deeper. It is one thing to praise in a sunlit room. What about the horrific scenes of the world, the wars, the starvation? Must we convert our anger and despair into compassion, or is it wrong to feel them at all?

Q'uo does not ask anyone to look away. They say that when a seeker is struck by the suffering of the world, a good response is to enter into it. Become, in thought, one of those who suffers. Do not touch it and leave. Stay with the suffering, keep company with it, embrace it, until your whole vibration echoes with it. Then offer that frame of mind to the infinite One, as you would offer money at an altar. For this suffering has been suffered in love of the fellow self.

This is a strange and difficult teaching. They do not discourage sending light to those situations. But they say there is a deeper resource in each of us, a deep mind in which all entities are together, where moving in sympathy into another's illusion can actually relieve, by that imagining, the bite of pain for all.

The last question turns to a teaching from the ones called Yom: that human beings find the choiceless, compassionate stance deeply threatening. Why? Q'uo traces it to the second density self inside us, the animal mind whose instincts sort and judge everything for survival. To that mind, withholding judgment looks like madness. How can you note choicelessly that something is blocking your airway? Action is needed. The threat is the clash between the creature that must judge to survive and the consciousness that would see all without bias.

The seeker, then, needs both. Choose decisively the direction of your seeking, and at the same time learn to perceive without attraction or repulsion. You will fail at the second, Q'uo says frankly. Almost surely. But the practice is to keep turning back. When you feel fear or threat, stop, go to meet that fearful inner entity, put your arms around it metaphysically, and witness with it each iota of pain. Accept it. Then move forward in praise until the next snag.

The rate of spiritual learning, they say, is greater for the one who turns back for the lagging parts of the self than for the one who leaps from good thought to good thought and leaves the frightened parts behind. Do not drag your consciousness into compassion. Go back and fetch it with love.

The exchange about Yom goes deeper still. Carla wonders aloud whether part of what threatens us is the task of going back into ourselves to fetch the frightened inner parts, the ones we left behind when we first started reaching for compassion. Q'uo agrees that it is often easier to pour love on one particular other self in trouble than to hold the generality of suffering humankind. But the resource is the same. The deep mind in which all entities are together does not sort its love. When you truly enter another's pain, you are also, quietly, going back for the frightened parts of yourself.

Thank you for listening.

title: The First Channeling
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the first channeling. This is a session from an intensive meditation in July of nineteen ninety three, and it is really about beginnings, about what it takes to learn to receive.

Hatonn is delighted to be working with a new instrument, the one known as M. Each new voice, they say, adds one more universe of possible ways to state the simple truth they carry. And they begin with the thing new channels ask about most: the conditioning, that physical sensation that says contact is happening.

Conditioning is real, Hatonn says, but it is a byproduct, not the point. One may request it, and they will try to intensify it, but its true value is as a focal point for a beginner who is worried about whether anything is actually happening. It steadies the channel and builds confidence. The experienced instrument here does not request it. She has learned something better: trust, built after the real work of tuning and challenging has been done.

The real work comes first. Tune carefully. Learn the self. Exalt the mental and emotional energies. The more purely the instrument desires to serve, the more stable the contact can be, and the higher the range it can hold. Hatonn asks the whole circle to picture light energy moving clockwise around them, like a battery, because this genuinely helps every instrument hold the contact steady.

There is a lovely practical instruction here for M. Relax, they say, and go with the flow. Rome was not built in a day, and neither are channels. What is wanted is not perfection but willingness, the courage to begin speaking before you are sure. Hatonn suggests that the first several times, the new channel simply begin with the greeting, I am Hatonn, and trust that beginning. Sometimes the very act of venturing the opening words breaks the dam of concern.

M does venture it, briefly, with difficulty, and Hatonn is overjoyed. The leap from the cliff has been taken. They thank M for the courage, and note something worth remembering: the contact is subtle, and what the instrument is really learning is that thoughts can arrive in the mind of one who is willing to say one thing quickly and then hear another.

Through another instrument, S, Hatonn describes how the thoughts come. Concepts blossom in the deeper, less conscious part of the mind, and the instrument supplies words for them, the way two energies blend. The fear that separates self from self falls away gradually, like the petals of a spent blossom, even as the blossom closer to the heart keeps unfurling.

There is also care for the body. M feels discomfort in the head and neck, and Hatonn is matter of fact about it. This is not unusual for a new instrument. The unfamiliar position of the body becomes a stress point. They will keep working to ease it.

The mark of a maturing instrument, they say, is the willingness to speak with less and less expectation about what will be said. There is always some anticipation, a horizon unfolding as the words are supplied for the concepts. But the deeper faith is that the concepts will keep blossoming even when no structure has been laid out in advance. You reach down to the source and can no longer tell where you end and the contact begins, because both are embraced in the same infinite love.

And there is care for the circle. Those who stay silent serve as surely as those whose tongues wag most eloquently. All serve. Each one offers only the portion most readily available, trusting the greater process to bring every serving home to the right guest.

There is an honest admission tucked into the middle of the session. Hatonn tells the new channel that some of what they tried to convey did not come through cleanly, that certain concepts got tangled on the way into words. They do not apologize the way we would. They simply note that with practice, the contact will improve. I find this encouraging beyond the circle. Every real skill begins with a few garbled transmissions. The teacher is not asking for perfection. Only for the willingness to keep the line open.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Harvest of Loss
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the harvest of loss. The question is how we can use the losses of our lives as fuel for the spiritual search, and Hatonn gives the word passion as the key.

Passion has a sorrowful side as well as a joyful side, they say. A life lived with an eye only to joy is bereft of half of life's full passion. To live a life of passion means to love living, and that includes one's sorrow. The task is to immerse fully in the process of living, to feel the full brunt and carry the full weight in all earnestness.

The passion with which you live the incarnation is what gives you the full range of response, joy and pain together, so that you have the whole vibrational keyboard to play in forming the character of the seeker. Fewer notes would mean less music. It is advanced work to remember that all is one and there is no true loss or gain. That realization comes more finely tuned as you feel both the joy and the pain.

When the seeker beholds the harvest of joy, praise comes easily. But the passionate heart cannot reason how to praise and give thanks for the harvest of loss, even though, looking back, it can see how that very harvest graded the road to a new level of awareness and made it passable.

Loss, Hatonn says, speaks of separation. When someone dies, the separation is obvious: you can no longer speak in the old familiar ways. But beneath that there is a deeper disharmony, a feeling of being torn out of a world that was nurturing and welcoming, and set down in a hostile land. The cut goes deep.

And yet loss sensitizes. To feel the pain of loss is to awaken the very qualities that also feel joy. It is the same instrument, tuned finer. The healing comes when the feeling of loss is placed inside a larger frame, so the mind and emotions can feel whole again within a harmonized universe, keeping the increased sensitivity and going forth to gather catalyst anew.

There is a passage here I keep returning to. Hatonn pictures the seeker stranded on a hostile beach, mile upon mile of heat and dust and thirst, and asks how, from that desolation, one could bring forth thanks and praise. The answer is a faith that is truly and completely blind. Not the wisdom that says this is all an illusion, which would only anesthetize the self and rob it of the experience it came for. The pain, they say plainly, is there to be felt. It is not to be circumvented.

Think of the passion of the teacher known as Jesus. It was not a comfortable experience or a wise one. It was a humble seeker reaching as deeply as possible into a compassion that opened like a floodgate of pain. The pain was there to be felt.

What loss makes, if you let it, is compassion. First for yourself, in the healing of your own loss. Then for others who feel the same loss. Eventually, for all entities who suffer any loss. The seeker begins to see that everyone in this illusion knows both the exhilaration of gaining what is valued and the pain of its removal. And that shared pattern becomes a bridge.

How blessed are those who suffer, Hatonn says near the end. With what riches are they furnished. Only the one who has found the strength to offer praise and thanksgiving, not in spite of suffering but because of it, can speak the greater passion and joy that endures through all experience.

One of the questions asks what happens when loss keeps coming, when a life seems to be nothing but grief. Hatonn answers with the image of the hollowed vessel. The loss of something loved hollows you out, they say, and that very hollowness becomes the capacity to carry more light. The grieving entity, emptied of its old certainties, grows light enough in spirit to carry ever more love. It is not that the pain is good. It is that the emptying it leaves behind can become a larger room, if you let the grief do its slow work.

Thank you for listening.

title: Branches of One Vine
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: branches of one vine. The question is about relationships, and why we choose the particular people we choose.

Hatonn begins with the image of a vine with many branches. One branch seems to have nothing to do with some far flung branch of the same rambling vine. Only by tracing the path of growth backward to the common root can the two begin to grasp the union that is the true nature of their relationship. For there is truly one being, one great self, one great thought which is love, and in that creative love are all.

Yet within the illusion, this union looks like folly. How could two people's deepest reality be oneness? None of it is apparent, and that is the point. The illusion exists so that you will not grasp union too quickly. It is in the experience of differences, in the testing of spiritual principles, that the lessons of love are brought forward and laid before each mind and heart.

Why this branch and not another? Hatonn suggests that the entities you are close to now have been in relationship with you many times before, lifetime after lifetime, working at the tips of the vine. Each time, as each entity's choices deepen it, the two move a little farther down toward the common root, a little closer to the unity at the heart of the vine. That is why one person can move you so profoundly. You have worked many incarnations to reach this depth of pain, of joy, of choosing love.

Every relationship is, at bottom, a relationship with the self. Each other person is a mirror reflecting your own face, your nature, your issues, your lessons. What you admire and encourage in another, you are encouraging in yourself. What you judge and question in another, you are questioning in yourself.

I find this one of the most practical lines in the whole session. If you can hold this, it takes so much pain out of dealing with another. Then, when you are angry, you know the issue lies within yourself, and what flows from you, even if it is a hard truth, flows without the taint of anger or disappointment. It shines.

There is also a strange comfort in the scale of it. Each of you, Hatonn says, is in truth a universe, as infinite within as can be imagined. What you see outwardly is, metaphysically speaking, less real than the universe within. It is in that inner universe that you can best position yourself to grow.

The goal of every relationship, if you can hold it, is to help each other learn the lessons of love. That is the commonality to look for. And whatever you do or say, let it be colored by that far away perfection, that ideal love, so that your responses carry the openness through which infinite love can flow.

In the questions, Carla asks about a twenty five year friendship that ended over a single letter. What is the purpose of that kind of heartache? Hatonn answers that all experience exists to extend the limits of love within you. Each of us feels pain, and each of us wonders whether there is love enough to heal it. And as you explore the reasons for the pain, you may find the reasons to heal, with love as the primary force.

The human heart has only a limited amount of love. But the energy that created you has infinite love, because love is the nature of consciousness at that level. Open the heart, and serve shiningly.

There is one more image I want to keep from this session. Hatonn describes love as a well of unlimited supply. When you draw from it to give to another, not only does the recipient benefit, but so does the giver. The drawing itself keeps the water fresh. That is why the relationships that ask the most of us can also feed us the most. Every act of choosing love at the tip of the vine keeps the channel open, and the common root keeps sending up more.

And the last line of the session is the one to carry out the door. Open the heart, and serve shiningly. Not serve perfectly, or serve when you feel like it. Shiningly. The vine does not measure how much light each branch gets. It just keeps growing toward the sun.

Thank you for listening.

title: The Fivefold Practice
transcript:
Voices from the Archive. Tonight: the fivefold practice. The question is about the spiritual attention span, about how to keep remembering that this is an illusion when the workday keeps swallowing you whole.

One member of the circle worries that he spends his days buried in work and only remembers the deeper truth when he gets home. Another worries that she has too many projects and cannot give any of them her best. A third asks about the focus of the creative artisan. Q'uo is delighted by the questions and offers five techniques.

But first, the reassurance. Even if you buried yourself in distraction and labor, you would still move forward along the path of evolution. There is no ultimate resistance possible to the truth.
